subtopics.guide: Creating a sketch of y = f(x) from information given or from a context, including transferring a graph from screen to paper with key features labelled; using technology to graph the sum and difference of two functions.

skills.name: Sketch a graph from its equation, transferring it from the GDC
examTypes: Sketch the graph of y = f(x) for −2 ≤ x ≤ 5, labelling the intercepts and turning points
On the grid, sketch the graph of f, showing any asymptotes
Sketch the curve, indicating the coordinates of the endpoints

methods.name: Graph on the GDC and copy the key features
methods.summary: Set a window matching the domain, find intercepts, max/min and endpoint values with the GDC, then plot them and join smoothly.

methods.name: Find key features by hand, then join
methods.summary: Calculate intercepts, turning points and asymptotes algebraically and draw the shape between them.

methods.name: Transform a known parent graph
methods.summary: Recognise f as a shifted or stretched x², 1/x, e^x or ln x and move the parent's key points.

methods.name: Plot from a table of values
methods.summary: Tabulate f at sensible x-values (by hand or GDC table), plot and join with a smooth curve.

misconceptions: Draws the curve crossing or bending away from a vertical asymptote
Ignores the given domain, drawing past the endpoints or omitting endpoint coordinates
Copies a distorted GDC window so turning points appear in the wrong place relative to the axes

threads.echo: Most sketches start from a parent you know (x², 1/x, e^x) moved and stretched: track its key points and the whole curve follows.

skills.name: Sketch a graph from given information or a context
examTypes: Sketch a possible graph of f given f(0) = 3, f(2) = 0 and that f is decreasing
Sketch a graph showing how the temperature of the tea changes over time
Sketch a function with vertical asymptote x = 1 and horizontal asymptote y = 2

methods.name: Plot the given facts first
methods.summary: Mark the given points, asymptotes and turning points, then join them with a curve that obeys the increasing/decreasing information.

methods.name: Reason from the context
methods.summary: Ask what happens at the start, in the long run, and whether the quantity changes quickly or slowly at each stage.

methods.name: Pick a function family with the right features
methods.summary: Choose a family (linear, quadratic, exponential, rational) whose shape matches, then adjust it to fit the facts.

misconceptions: Draws a curve that fails the vertical line test
Lets a quantity that cannot be negative (time, population, temperature above room level) go below its limit
Shows a long-run level as a turning point instead of an asymptote

skills.name: Read values and solutions from a graph
examTypes: Use the graph to write down f(2)
Use the graph to solve f(x) = 1
Write down the number of solutions of f(x) = k
Write down the value of f(f(1))

methods.name: Up from x, across to y
methods.summary: Find x on the horizontal axis, move vertically to the curve and read the y-value.

methods.name: Draw y = k and read off x
methods.summary: Draw the horizontal line y = k; each crossing with the curve gives a solution of f(x) = k.

methods.name: GDC trace, value or intersect
methods.summary: If the equation is known, use the GDC to read values precisely and confirm the graph reading.

misconceptions: Reads 'solve f(x) = 1' as 'find f(1)'
Gives only one solution when y = k crosses the curve several times
Misreads the scale when the axes are not 1 unit per square

threads.echo: Solving f(x) = k is finding where the curve meets the horizontal line y = k: every equation is an intersection of graphs.

skills.name: Graph sums and differences of functions with technology
examTypes: Sketch the graph of y = f(x) + g(x)
Use your GDC to sketch h(x) = f(x) − g(x) and find its zeros
Find the maximum value of f(x) + g(x)

methods.name: Define Y3 = Y1 + Y2 on the GDC
methods.summary: Enter f and g, then graph their sum or difference as a new function and analyse it with the usual tools.

methods.name: Add heights point by point
methods.summary: At several x-values add (or subtract) the two y-values read from the graphs and plot the results.

methods.name: Combine the formulas first
methods.summary: Add or subtract the expressions and simplify before graphing, e.g. (x² + 1) + (2x − 3) = x² + 2x − 2.

misconceptions: Adds the x-values instead of the y-values
Thinks the zeros of f + g are the zeros of f together with the zeros of g
Assumes the maximum of f + g occurs where f or g has its own maximum

threads.echo: f(x) = g(x) is the same as f(x) − g(x) = 0: the zeros of the difference graph are the crossing points of the two original graphs.

skills.name: Match equations to graphs
examTypes: Which of the following graphs could be y = f(x)?
Match each equation with its graph
Justify why graph B cannot represent f

methods.name: Check intercepts
methods.summary: Compute f(0) and the zeros and rule out graphs that do not pass through them.

methods.name: Check shape, sign and asymptotes
methods.summary: Use the family (parabola up or down, growth or decay, 1/x branches) and the asymptotes to eliminate options.

methods.name: Substitute a convenient point
methods.summary: Evaluate f at an easy x-value and see which graph contains that point.

methods.name: Plot on the GDC and compare
methods.summary: When a calculator is allowed, graph the equation and pick the matching picture.

misconceptions: Picks a graph with the right shape but the wrong y-intercept
Confuses a^x with a > 1 (growth) and 0 < a < 1 (decay)
Ignores the sign of the leading coefficient and picks a parabola opening the wrong way

threads.echo: Recognising a graph means spotting its parent and how it was moved: a parabola with vertex (2, −1) is y = x² translated.
The vertex, or the point where the asymptotes cross, shows where the parent's origin moved to: that displacement is the translation vector.

subtopics.title: Key features of graphs and intersections
subtopics.guide: Determining key features of graphs: maximum and minimum values, intercepts, symmetry, vertex, zeros of functions or roots of equations, and vertical and horizontal asymptotes, using technology where appropriate; finding points of intersection of two curves or lines using technology.

skills.name: Find the zeros and intercepts of a function
examTypes: Find the x-intercepts of the graph of f
Write down the y-intercept
Find the zeros of f(x) = x³ − 4x
Find the root of f(x) = 0 in the given interval

methods.name: Solve f(x) = 0 and evaluate f(0)
methods.summary: Factorise or rearrange f(x) = 0 for the x-intercepts; substitute x = 0 for the y-intercept.

methods.name: Read zeros from factorised form
methods.summary: If f(x) = a(x − p)(x − q)…, the zeros are p, q, … at sight.

methods.name: GDC zero/root function
methods.summary: Graph f and use the zero function on each crossing, or use the polynomial solver.

methods.name: Read crossings from a given graph
methods.summary: Read where the curve crosses each axis, using the scale carefully.

misconceptions: Confuses the zeros (x where f(x) = 0) with the y-intercept f(0)
From f(x) = (x + 2)(x − 5) gives zeros −5 and 2 (wrong signs)
Divides by x when solving x³ = 4x and loses the zero x = 0

threads.echo: A zero of f, a root of f(x) = 0 and an x-intercept of the graph are three names for the same point.

skills.name: Find maximum and minimum points and values
examTypes: Find the coordinates of the local maximum point
Write down the minimum value of f
Find the maximum height reached

methods.name: GDC maximum/minimum
methods.summary: Graph f and use the max or min function, giving coordinates to 3 significant figures.

methods.name: Read the turning point from the equation's form
methods.summary: For a(x − h)² + k or another transformed parent, the turning point (h, k) is visible in the equation.

methods.name: Solve f′(x) = 0
methods.summary: Differentiate, set the derivative to zero, and substitute back for the value (the Topic 5 method).

methods.name: Read from the graph
methods.summary: Locate the highest or lowest point on a given graph and read its coordinates.

misconceptions: Gives the x-coordinate when the maximum value (the y-value) is asked for, or vice versa
On a restricted domain, misses an endpoint that is higher than the local maximum
Gives GDC answers to fewer than 3 significant figures

threads.echo: Every 'biggest' or 'smallest' question, from a parabola's vertex to optimisation and amplitude, is a hunt for these turning points.

skills.name: Identify vertical and horizontal asymptotes
examTypes: Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote of y = 3e^(−x) + 2
Write down the equations of the asymptotes of the graph of f
Write down the equation of the vertical asymptote of y = ln(x − 4)

methods.name: Find where the function is undefined
methods.summary: A vertical asymptote sits where a denominator is zero or where a log's argument reaches zero.

methods.name: Look at large |x|
methods.summary: Terms such as e^(−x) or 1/x vanish as x grows, leaving the horizontal asymptote.

methods.name: Move the parent's asymptote
methods.summary: e^x has y = 0, so e^x + 2 has y = 2; ln x has x = 0, so ln(x − 4) has x = 4.

methods.name: Check with a GDC table
methods.summary: Tabulate f at very large x and close to the suspected gap to confirm where the curve levels off or blows up.

misconceptions: Writes an asymptote as a number (2) instead of an equation (y = 2)
Swaps vertical and horizontal, writing x = 2 for a horizontal asymptote
Gives ln(x − 4) the vertical asymptote x = −4

threads.echo: Asymptotes move with the graph: a horizontal translation shifts a vertical asymptote, a vertical translation shifts a horizontal one.
Translating by the vector (a, b) moves x = 0 to x = a and y = 0 to y = b, so the asymptotes' crossing point is the vector itself.

skills.name: Use the symmetry of a graph
examTypes: Write down the equation of the line of symmetry
The graph is symmetric about x = 3 and passes through (1, 5); write down another point on the graph
A(−1, 4) and B(7, 4) lie on a parabola; find the x-coordinate of the vertex

methods.name: Average the x-values of two points at the same height
methods.summary: Points with equal y-values on a symmetric curve sit equally either side of the axis, so the axis is x = (x₁ + x₂)/2.

methods.name: Reflect a known point in the line of symmetry
methods.summary: A point d units left of x = h has a twin d units right of it with the same y-value.

methods.name: Read the line of symmetry from the equation
methods.summary: y = a(x − h)² + k is symmetric about x = h; functions built only from even powers of x, such as x⁴ − 2x², are symmetric about the y-axis.

misconceptions: Thinks the line of symmetry passes through the y-intercept
Reflects a point the wrong distance or to the wrong side
Assumes every curve with a turning point is symmetric (e.g. a cubic)

threads.echo: Knowing one half of a symmetric graph gives you the other half for free, the same trick as related angles on the unit circle and the normal curve.

skills.name: Find the points of intersection of two curves or lines
examTypes: Find the coordinates of the points where the graphs of f and g intersect
Write down the x-coordinate of the point of intersection
Hence solve f(x) = g(x)

methods.name: GDC intersect
methods.summary: Graph both functions and use intersect at each crossing, zooming out to be sure none are missed.

methods.name: Set f(x) = g(x) and solve
methods.summary: When the algebra allows (linear, quadratic), equate, solve, and substitute back for y.

methods.name: Zeros of f(x) − g(x)
methods.summary: Graph h = f − g and use the zero function; handy when the curves cross at a shallow angle.

methods.name: Sketch both graphs to count and locate crossings
methods.summary: A quick sketch shows how many intersections to look for and roughly where.

misconceptions: Gives only the x-coordinate when coordinates are asked for
Finds one intersection and misses others hidden outside the GDC window
Rounds x early and substitutes, giving an inaccurate y-coordinate

threads.echo: Every equation f(x) = g(x) is two graphs meeting: the GDC finds the meeting point, algebra explains it, and each checks the other.

subtopics.title: Composite functions, identity and inverse functions
subtopics.guide: Composite functions (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)); the identity function and the property (f ∘ f⁻¹)(x) = (f⁻¹ ∘ f)(x) = x; finding the inverse function f⁻¹(x), including restricting the domain of f so that an inverse exists.

skills.name: Evaluate a composite function at a value
examTypes: Find (f ∘ g)(2)
Find f(g(−1))
Using the table, find (g ∘ f)(3)

methods.name: Work from the inside out
methods.summary: Evaluate g(2) first, then feed that number into f.

methods.name: Find f(g(x)) first, then substitute
methods.summary: Form the composite expression, simplify, and then substitute the value.

methods.name: Chain two readings from graphs or tables
methods.summary: Read g(a) from g's graph or table, then look up that value on f's.

misconceptions: Applies f first for (f ∘ g)(x), evaluating g(f(x)) instead
Multiplies f(2) × g(2) instead of composing
Applies the same function twice

skills.name: Find and use a composite function expression
examTypes: Find an expression for (g ∘ f)(x)
Show that (f ∘ g)(x) = 4x² − 3
Hence solve (f ∘ g)(x) = 13
Given f(x) and (f ∘ g)(x), find g(x)

methods.name: Replace every x in f with g(x)
methods.summary: Write f with empty brackets, put g(x) into every bracket, then expand and simplify.

methods.name: Follow a flow diagram
methods.summary: Chain g's operations then f's operations and apply them to x in that order.

methods.name: Check with a test value
methods.summary: Compute f(g(1)) numerically and compare with your expression at x = 1 to catch order errors.

misconceptions: Computes g(f(x)) when f(g(x)) is asked for
Replaces only one of the x's in f with g(x)
Assumes f ∘ g = g ∘ f

threads.echo: y = f(x − a) + b is a composite: shift the input with x ↦ x − a, apply f, then shift the output by b, so every transformation is a composition with a simple linear function.

skills.name: Find the inverse function f⁻¹(x) algebraically
examTypes: Find f⁻¹(x)
Find an expression for f⁻¹(x) where f(x) = (2x + 1)/(x − 3)
Find f⁻¹(x) for f(x) = e^(2x) − 1
Find f⁻¹(x) where f(x) = (x − 2)² + 1, x ≥ 2

methods.name: Swap x and y, then make y the subject
methods.summary: Write y = f(x), interchange x and y, and rearrange for y.

methods.name: Make x the subject, then rename
methods.summary: Rearrange y = f(x) for x, then replace y with x to write f⁻¹(x).

methods.name: Undo the operations in reverse order
methods.summary: List what f does to x (×2, then +1), then undo each step in the reverse order (−1, then ÷2).

methods.name: Check the reflection on the GDC
methods.summary: Graph f, your f⁻¹ and y = x; the two curves must be mirror images in y = x.

misconceptions: Writes f⁻¹(x) = 1/f(x)
Undoes the operations in the original order, e.g. for 2x + 1 gives x/2 − 1
For a quadratic on a restricted domain keeps the ± instead of choosing the sign that matches the domain

threads.echo: Finding f⁻¹ is the algebra of undoing: the same reverse-the-steps thinking turns e^x into ln x and powers inverse normal calculations.
Swapping x and y is the algebra of reflecting the graph in the line y = x.

skills.name: Find the domain and range of f⁻¹, and restrict a domain so f⁻¹ exists
examTypes: Write down the domain of f⁻¹
State the range of f⁻¹
Find the largest value of k such that f⁻¹ exists for x ≤ k
Explain why f does not have an inverse

methods.name: Domain of f⁻¹ = range of f, and vice versa
methods.summary: Find the range of f (from its graph, vertex or asymptote) and that is the domain of f⁻¹.

methods.name: Cut the domain at the turning point
methods.summary: A quadratic is one-to-one on each side of its vertex, so find h (by −b/2a or completing the square) and restrict to x ≥ h or x ≤ h.

methods.name: Horizontal line test on the graph
methods.summary: Choose the largest interval on which every horizontal line meets the graph at most once.

methods.name: Locate the turning point on the GDC
methods.summary: Use max/min on the GDC to find where the graph turns back, which is where the domain must be cut.

misconceptions: States the domain of f⁻¹ as the domain of f
Restricts the domain at the y-intercept instead of at the turning point
Thinks every function has an inverse

threads.echo: An inverse can only undo when each output came from exactly one input, which is why arcsin and inverse functions need restricted domains.
The natural place to cut a quadratic's domain is its vertex, the extreme point where the graph turns back on itself.

skills.name: Use the identity function and (f ∘ f⁻¹)(x) = x
examTypes: Show that (f ∘ g)(x) = x and hence state the relationship between f and g
Write down the value of (f ∘ f⁻¹)(5)
Solve f⁻¹(x) = 3

methods.name: Compose and simplify to x
methods.summary: Start from (f ∘ g)(x), substitute and simplify line by line until you reach x.

methods.name: Use f(f⁻¹(x)) = x directly
methods.summary: (f ∘ f⁻¹)(5) = 5 with no working, and f⁻¹(x) = 3 means x = f(3).

methods.name: Check the graphs are reflections in y = x
methods.summary: If f and g are mirror images in y = x, each undoes the other.

misconceptions: Thinks (f ∘ f⁻¹)(x) = 1 rather than x
Solves f⁻¹(x) = 3 by writing x = f⁻¹(3) instead of x = f(3)
Believes (f ∘ f)(x) = x for any function

threads.echo: Doing then undoing gets you back where you started: ln(e^x) = x and e^(ln x) = x are this same identity.

subtopics.title: Quadratic functions
subtopics.guide: The quadratic function f(x) = ax² + bx + c: its graph, y-intercept (0, c) and axis of symmetry; the form f(x) = a(x − p)(x − q) with x-intercepts (p, 0) and (q, 0); the form f(x) = a(x − h)² + k with vertex (h, k).

skills.name: Find the axis of symmetry of a parabola
examTypes: Write down the equation of the axis of symmetry
Find the equation of the axis of symmetry of y = 2x² − 12x + 5
The graph has x-intercepts −1 and 5; write down the equation of the axis of symmetry

methods.name: x = −b/(2a)
methods.summary: Read a and b from ax² + bx + c and substitute into x = −b/(2a).

methods.name: Midpoint of the x-intercepts
methods.summary: The axis lies halfway between the zeros p and q: x = (p + q)/2.

methods.name: Read h from a(x − h)² + k
methods.summary: In vertex form the axis is x = h at sight; complete the square first if needed.

methods.name: Solve f′(x) = 2ax + b = 0
methods.summary: The axis passes through the turning point, where the gradient is zero.

misconceptions: Uses x = b/(2a), dropping the minus sign
Writes the axis as y = h, or just the number h, instead of x = h
Reads h from a(x + 3)² as +3

threads.echo: The axis cuts the parabola into mirror halves, so two points at the same height or the two roots pin it down at once.

skills.name: Find the vertex and the maximum or minimum value
examTypes: Write down the coordinates of the vertex of f(x) = 3(x − 2)² + 5
Find the coordinates of the vertex of y = x² − 6x + 1
Find the minimum value of f
Hence write down the range of f

methods.name: Read (h, k) as the translation of y = ax²
methods.summary: a(x − h)² + k is ax² moved by the vector (h, k), so its vertex is (h, k).

methods.name: Complete the square
methods.summary: Rewrite ax² + bx + c as a(x − h)² + k and read off the vertex.

methods.name: x = −b/(2a), then substitute for y
methods.summary: Find the x-coordinate from the formula and evaluate f there for the y-coordinate.

methods.name: Midpoint of the roots, then substitute
methods.summary: The vertex lies on the axis halfway between the zeros, so average them and evaluate f.

methods.name: Set f′(x) = 0
methods.summary: Differentiate, solve 2ax + b = 0 and substitute back.

methods.name: GDC maximum/minimum
methods.summary: Graph f and use max or min to read the vertex.

misconceptions: From a(x + 3)² − 4 gives the vertex (3, −4) instead of (−3, −4)
Finds the x-coordinate of the vertex but not the y-coordinate
Calls the vertex a minimum when a < 0

threads.echo: The vertex is the parabola's extreme point, your first optimisation; in Topic 5 you will find the same point with f′(x) = 0.
y = a(x − h)² + k is y = ax² moved so its vertex goes from (0, 0) to (h, k).
The vertex (h, k) is exactly the translation vector that carries y = ax² into place: vertex form is a vector in disguise.

skills.name: Express a quadratic in vertex form a(x − h)² + k
examTypes: Express x² − 8x + 11 in the form (x − h)² + k
Write 2x² + 12x + 7 in the form a(x − h)² + k
Hence describe the transformation that maps y = x² onto y = f(x)

methods.name: Complete the square
methods.summary: Take out a, halve the x-coefficient to get h, then correct the constant: x² − 8x + 11 = (x − 4)² − 16 + 11 = (x − 4)² − 5.

methods.name: Expand a(x − h)² + k and compare coefficients
methods.summary: Expand to ax² − 2ahx + ah² + k and match the x and constant terms to find h and k.

methods.name: Find the vertex, then write the form
methods.summary: Use h = −b/(2a) and k = f(h), keep the original a, and write a(x − h)² + k.

misconceptions: Forgets to subtract the square of half the coefficient, writing x² − 8x + 11 = (x − 4)² + 11
When a ≠ 1, does not multiply the correction term by a
Gets the sign of h wrong, writing (x + 4)² for x² − 8x + …

threads.echo: ax² + bx + c and a(x − h)² + k are the same function; the second form reveals the vertex, just as different line forms reveal different facts.
Completing the square tells you how y = x² was changed: a is a vertical stretch and h, k are a translation.
The h and k you produce form the translation vector (h, k) that carries y = ax² onto y = f(x).

skills.name: Use the factorised form a(x − p)(x − q) and the x-intercepts
examTypes: Write down the x-intercepts of f(x) = 2(x + 1)(x − 4)
Express f(x) in the form a(x − p)(x − q)
Use the graph to write down the values of p and q

methods.name: Factorise ax² + bx + c
methods.summary: Take out a common factor, then split the middle term or inspect to find the two brackets.

methods.name: Find the roots, then write the factors
methods.summary: Solve f(x) = 0 by formula or GDC; roots p and q give f(x) = a(x − p)(x − q).

methods.name: Read p and q from the graph, then a from another point
methods.summary: Use the x-intercepts for p and q and the y-intercept or another point to find a.

misconceptions: From (x + 1)(x − 4) gives the intercepts 1 and −4
Leaves out the leading coefficient a when writing a(x − p)(x − q)
Thinks the y-intercept is pq rather than apq

threads.echo: Factorised form shows the zeros, vertex form shows the turning point, standard form shows the y-intercept: one parabola, three views.
Each factor (x − p) is an x-intercept on the graph: the algebra and the picture say the same thing.

skills.name: Find a quadratic from its graph or from given points
examTypes: The graph has vertex (3, −2) and passes through (5, 6); find f(x)
The graph meets the x-axis at −1 and 4 and the y-axis at −8; find a, b and c
The curve passes through three given points; find a, b and c

methods.name: Start from a(x − h)² + k and use a point for a
methods.summary: Put the vertex into vertex form, then substitute the other point to find the stretch a.

methods.name: Start from a(x − p)(x − q) and use a point for a
methods.summary: Put the zeros into factorised form, then use the y-intercept or another point to find a.

methods.name: Substitute three points into ax² + bx + c
methods.summary: Each point gives a linear equation in a, b, c; solve the system by elimination.

methods.name: GDC simultaneous solver or quadratic regression
methods.summary: Enter the three equations in the solver, or the points as data and run quadratic regression.

misconceptions: Assumes a = 1 without checking against another point
Writes (x − 1) for an intercept at x = −1
Substitutes the vertex into ax² + bx + c as if it were just another point and forgets it is a turning point

threads.echo: Once the vertex is known, the quadratic is y = ax² translated to (h, k); the only thing left to find is the stretch a.
Choose the form that fits the information: vertex given → vertex form, roots given → factorised form, three points → standard form.

skills.name: Sketch a quadratic showing its key features
examTypes: Sketch the graph of y = f(x), showing the vertex and the axis intercepts
Which graph represents y = −2(x − 1)² + 3?
On the same axes, sketch y = f(x) and y = g(x)

methods.name: Plot the intercepts, vertex and axis, then join
methods.summary: Compute the y-intercept, zeros and vertex, mark the axis, and draw a smooth U or ∩ through them.

methods.name: Transform y = x²
methods.summary: Stretch by a (reflecting if a < 0), then translate by the vector (h, k).

methods.name: Graph on the GDC and transfer
methods.summary: Graph f, find the key points with the GDC and copy them onto the axes.

misconceptions: Draws the parabola opening upwards when a < 0
Draws a pointed V-shaped vertex instead of a smooth curve
Puts the vertex at the y-intercept

threads.echo: Every parabola is y = x² stretched and translated, so sketching one is just moving the key points of x².

skills.name: Model and optimise with a quadratic in context
examTypes: Find the maximum height reached by the ball
Find the dimensions that maximise the area of the enclosure
Find the time at which the ball hits the ground
Interpret the vertex in the context of the question

methods.name: Find the vertex and interpret it
methods.summary: Use −b/(2a) or completing the square, then say what the vertex means (time and maximum height, width and maximum area).

methods.name: GDC maximum
methods.summary: Graph the model on a sensible window and use max.

methods.name: Differentiate and set to zero
methods.summary: Solve h′(t) = 0 for the time of the maximum, then evaluate h.

methods.name: Use the symmetry of the path
methods.summary: A projectile is highest halfway between two times when it is at the same height, such as launch and landing at ground level.

misconceptions: Gives the time of the maximum when the maximum height is asked for, or vice versa
Keeps a negative time or length when solving h(t) = 0
Writes area as a function of two variables without using the constraint (e.g. the fixed perimeter) to remove one

threads.echo: Maximum height and maximum area are vertex questions now and derivative questions later: same goal, new tool.

subtopics.title: Solving quadratic equations and inequalities; the discriminant
subtopics.guide: Solving quadratic equations and inequalities, using factorisation, completing the square, the quadratic formula and technology; the discriminant Δ = b² − 4ac and the nature of the roots: two distinct real roots, two equal real roots, or no real roots.

skills.name: Solve a quadratic equation
examTypes: Solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0
Solve 2x² + 3x − 4 = 0, giving your answers in exact form
Find the zeros of f
Solve the equation, giving your answers correct to 3 s.f.

methods.name: Factorise and use the zero-product rule
methods.summary: Write the quadratic as a product of brackets equal to 0 and set each bracket to 0.

methods.name: Quadratic formula
methods.summary: Substitute a, b, c into x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/(2a) and simplify, leaving surds for exact answers.

methods.name: Complete the square and square-root
methods.summary: Rewrite as a(x − h)² + k = 0, isolate the square and take ± square roots.

methods.name: GDC polynomial solver or graph zeros
methods.summary: Enter a, b, c in the polynomial solver or graph the quadratic and find its zeros.

misconceptions: Divides both sides of 3x² = 6x by x and loses the root x = 0
From (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0 gives x = −2 or x = −3
Forgets the ± when square-rooting, so x² = 9 gives only x = 3

threads.echo: The roots of ax² + bx + c = 0 are where the parabola crosses the x-axis; factorising and the GDC's zero function find the same points.
Factorised form makes the equation solvable by the zero-product rule; vertex form makes it solvable by square-rooting: pick the form that does the work.

skills.name: Use the discriminant to determine the nature of the roots
examTypes: Find the value of the discriminant
Hence state the number of real roots
Show that the equation has no real solutions
Explain why the graph of f does not meet the x-axis

methods.name: Compute Δ = b² − 4ac and compare with 0
methods.summary: Δ > 0 gives two distinct real roots, Δ = 0 two equal roots, Δ < 0 no real roots.

methods.name: Compare the vertex with the x-axis
methods.summary: With a > 0, a vertex above the axis means no real roots, on the axis means equal roots, below means two roots.

methods.name: Count x-intercepts on a GDC graph
methods.summary: Graph the quadratic and count how many times it meets the x-axis (a check, not a proof).

misconceptions: Mishandles the sign of −4ac when c < 0, e.g. writes 25 − 4(1)(−6) = 1
Thinks Δ < 0 means two negative roots rather than no real roots
Uses b² + 4ac or √(b² − 4ac) as the discriminant

threads.echo: Δ > 0, Δ = 0 and Δ < 0 are the algebra for 'the parabola crosses the x-axis twice, touches it, or misses it'.
Δ = 0 is the tipping point where the vertex just touches the axis, the same tangency idea as a line just grazing a curve.

skills.name: Find parameter values for a given number of roots, or for tangency
examTypes: Find the values of k for which x² + kx + 9 = 0 has equal roots
Find the range of values of k for which the equation has no real roots
The line y = mx − 1 is a tangent to y = x² + 3; find the possible values of m
Show that the line never meets the curve

methods.name: Set Δ = 0, Δ > 0 or Δ < 0 and solve for k
methods.summary: Rearrange to ax² + bx + c = 0 (for a line and curve, equate them first), write Δ in terms of k and solve the equation or inequality.

methods.name: Complete the square and place the vertex
methods.summary: Write the quadratic in vertex form and require k (the vertex height) to be 0, positive or negative as needed.

methods.name: Match gradients for tangency
methods.summary: Set the curve's derivative equal to the line's gradient, find the point of contact, and require it to lie on both.

methods.name: Vary the parameter on the GDC
methods.summary: Use a slider or try values of k to see where the graph changes from two crossings to none, then confirm algebraically.

misconceptions: Reads a, b, c before rearranging to '= 0', e.g. keeps the line's terms on the other side
Solves k² − 36 < 0 as k < ±6 instead of −6 < k < 6
Uses Δ > 0 for 'real roots' and forgets the equal-roots case (Δ ≥ 0)

threads.echo: Tangency is a boundary case: the line sits at the extreme position where two intersections merge into one, so Δ = 0.
Counting roots is counting where two graphs meet; the discriminant does the counting without drawing anything.

skills.name: Solve a quadratic inequality
examTypes: Solve x² − x − 6 > 0
Find the set of values of x for which f(x) ≤ 0
Hence find the range of values of k (from an inequality in k)

methods.name: Find the roots and sketch the parabola
methods.summary: Solve the equation, sketch the U or ∩ through the roots and read off where the graph is above or below the x-axis.

methods.name: Sign table of the factors
methods.summary: Tabulate the sign of each factor on each interval between the roots and multiply the signs.

methods.name: Test a point in each interval
methods.summary: Substitute one value from each interval to see whether the inequality holds there.

methods.name: Graph on the GDC and read the interval
methods.summary: Graph the quadratic, find its zeros and read the x-values where it is above or below the axis.

misconceptions: Solves x² > 9 as x > ±3, or as x > 3 only
Writes x < −2 or x > 3 as the single interval −2 < x < 3
Divides by a negative leading coefficient without reversing the inequality

threads.echo: 'Where is x² − x − 6 > 0?' means 'where is the parabola above the x-axis?', and the picture makes the answer obvious.

skills.name: Solve equations that reduce to a quadratic
examTypes: Solve e^(2x) − 5e^x + 6 = 0
By letting u = 2^x, solve 4^x − 3(2^x) − 4 = 0
Solve x + 6/x = 5
Solve ln x + ln(x − 2) = ln 3

methods.name: Substitute u for the repeated expression
methods.summary: Let u = e^x (so e^(2x) = u²), solve the quadratic in u, then convert each u back to x.

methods.name: Clear fractions or combine logs, then rearrange
methods.summary: Multiply through by the denominator, or use log laws to combine, until you reach ax² + bx + c = 0.

methods.name: Graph both sides on the GDC
methods.summary: Use intersect to find or check the solutions, which also shows when a root must be rejected.

misconceptions: Stops at u = 2 or u = 3 instead of solving e^x = 2 and e^x = 3 for x
Keeps an impossible solution such as 2^x = −1 or a negative x inside a log
Writes 4^x as 2(2^x) instead of (2^x)²

threads.echo: After solving for u = e^x you still have to undo the exponential with ln, so the last step is an inverse function.
Seeing e^(2x) as (e^x)² is rewriting in an equivalent form that turns a scary equation into a familiar quadratic.

subtopics.title: Reciprocal and rational functions
subtopics.guide: The reciprocal function f(x) = 1/x, x ≠ 0: its graph and self-inverse nature; rational functions of the form f(x) = (ax + b)/(cx + d) and their graphs; equations of vertical and horizontal asymptotes.

skills.name: Recognise the graph and properties of y = 1/x
examTypes: Sketch the graph of y = 1/x, stating the equations of its asymptotes
Show that f(x) = 1/x is self-inverse
Write down f⁻¹(x) for f(x) = 4/x

methods.name: Find the inverse algebraically
methods.summary: Swap x and y in y = 1/x and rearrange; getting y = 1/x back shows it is self-inverse.

methods.name: Use symmetry about y = x
methods.summary: The hyperbola is its own mirror image in y = x, so its inverse is itself.

methods.name: Plot a table including fractions and negatives
methods.summary: Use x = ±1/4, ±1/2, ±1, ±2, ±4 to see both branches approach the axes.

misconceptions: Thinks self-inverse means f(x) × f⁻¹(x) = 1
Draws y = 1/x touching or crossing the axes
Draws the branches in the second and fourth quadrants (that is y = −1/x)

threads.echo: 1/x is its own undo button: applying it twice returns x, which is why its graph is symmetric in y = x.
y = 1/x is symmetric in both y = x and y = −x, so one branch tells you everything about the other.

skills.name: Find the asymptotes of f(x) = (ax + b)/(cx + d)
examTypes: Write down the equation of the vertical asymptote
Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote
The graph has asymptotes x = 2 and y = 3; find the values of the unknown constants

methods.name: x = −d/c and y = a/c
methods.summary: The vertical asymptote is where cx + d = 0; the horizontal asymptote is the ratio of the x-coefficients.

methods.name: Rewrite as a/c + k/(cx + d)
methods.summary: Split the numerator to separate a constant part (the horizontal asymptote) from a fraction that blows up at x = −d/c.

methods.name: Divide top and bottom by x and let x grow
methods.summary: (a + b/x)/(c + d/x) tends to a/c as x gets large, giving the horizontal asymptote.

methods.name: Check with a GDC table
methods.summary: Tabulate f for very large x and near x = −d/c to confirm both asymptotes.

misconceptions: Gives the vertical asymptote as x = d/c (sign error)
Gives the horizontal asymptote as y = b/d (the ratio of constants) instead of y = a/c
Thinks there is no horizontal asymptote because the numerator is not a constant

threads.echo: The asymptotes x = −d/c and y = a/c are the axes of y = 1/x moved by a translation, which is why there is always one of each.
The asymptotes cross at (−d/c, a/c): that point is the translation vector that carried the centre of y = 1/x away from the origin.

skills.name: Write a rational function as a transformed 1/x
examTypes: Express f(x) = (2x + 1)/(x − 3) in the form A + B/(x − 3)
Hence describe a sequence of transformations that maps y = 1/x onto y = f(x)
Write down the translation vector that maps y = 7/x onto y = f(x)

methods.name: Combine A + B/(x − 3) and compare
methods.summary: Put A + B/(x − 3) over a common denominator and match the numerator with 2x + 1.

methods.name: Read A and the shift from the asymptotes
methods.summary: The horizontal asymptote gives A and the vertical asymptote gives the horizontal shift; one point then fixes B.

misconceptions: Gives the translation vector as (−3, 2) because of the '− 3' in x − 3
Forgets the vertical stretch B and treats every rational function as a translated 1/x
Splits the numerator wrongly, e.g. 2x + 1 = 2(x − 3) + 1

threads.echo: Every (ax + b)/(cx + d) is 1/x stretched and translated, so the whole family has the same shape with its centre moved.
A + B/(x − h) is B/x moved by the vector (h, A): the same translation-by-vector rule as vertex form a(x − h)² + k.
(2x + 1)/(x − 3) and 2 + 7/(x − 3) are the same function; the second form shows the asymptotes and the transformation at a glance.

skills.name: Sketch a rational function showing its intercepts and asymptotes
examTypes: Sketch the graph of f, showing the asymptotes and axis intercepts
Find the coordinates of the x- and y-intercepts
Which graph shows y = (x + 2)/(x − 1)?

methods.name: Draw the asymptotes, mark the intercepts, add the branches
methods.summary: Find x = −d/c, y = a/c, the x-intercept (numerator = 0) and y-intercept (b/d), then draw the two branches through the intercepts.

methods.name: Transform y = 1/x
methods.summary: Write f as A + B/(x − h) and move the branches of 1/x (flipped if B < 0) to the new asymptotes.

methods.name: Graph on the GDC and transfer
methods.summary: Graph f, read the intercepts and asymptotes, and copy the shape carefully near the asymptotes.

misconceptions: Puts the branches in the wrong pair of quadrants relative to the asymptotes
Finds the x-intercept by setting the denominator to zero
Draws the curve crossing the vertical asymptote

threads.echo: Sketching (ax + b)/(cx + d) is sketching 1/x with its asymptote cross moved, so draw the cross first and the branches follow.

skills.name: Find the inverse of a rational function, with its domain and range
examTypes: Find f⁻¹(x) where f(x) = (3x − 1)/(x + 2)
Write down the domain and range of f⁻¹
Show that f(x) = (2x + 5)/(x − 2) is self-inverse

methods.name: Swap x and y, multiply out, collect the y-terms
Reflect the asymptotes in y = x
methods.summary: f⁻¹'s vertical asymptote is f's horizontal one and vice versa, which gives the domain and range of f⁻¹ immediately.

methods.name: Use the pattern (ax + b)/(cx + d) ↦ (−dx + b)/(cx − a)
methods.summary: Swap a and d and change both their signs to check your algebra; when d = −a the function is its own inverse.

misconceptions: Cannot collect the y-terms after cross-multiplying and leaves y on both sides
Gives the domain of f⁻¹ as x ≠ −d/c (f's excluded value) instead of x ≠ a/c
Thinks only 1/x can be self-inverse

threads.echo: The inverse undoes f, so the output f can never reach (its horizontal asymptote) becomes the input f⁻¹ cannot accept.
f and f⁻¹ are mirror images in y = x, so their asymptotes swap; when the graph is symmetric in y = x, f is self-inverse.

skills.name: Use a rational function as a model
examTypes: Find the average cost per item when 50 items are made
Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote and interpret it in context
Find the least number of items needed for the average cost to fall below $8

methods.name: Read the horizontal asymptote as the long-run value
methods.summary: As the input grows the model approaches y = a/c, e.g. the average cost tends to the cost per item.

methods.name: Set the model equal to the target and solve
methods.summary: Multiply through by the denominator, solve the linear equation, and round in the direction the context needs.

methods.name: Graph the model and the target line
methods.summary: Use intersect, or a table, to find where the model crosses the target value.

misconceptions: Thinks the model eventually reaches its horizontal asymptote value
Rounds a number of items down when the condition needs rounding up
Interprets the vertical asymptote as a real value of the quantity in context

subtopics.title: Exponential and logarithmic functions
subtopics.guide: Exponential functions f(x) = a^x (a > 0) and f(x) = e^x, and their graphs; logarithmic functions f(x) = log_a x and f(x) = ln x (x > 0), and their graphs; exponential and logarithmic functions as inverses of each other.

skills.name: Sketch and describe exponential graphs, including transformed ones such as e^(x − a) + b
examTypes: Sketch y = 2^x and y = (1/2)^x on the same axes
Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote of y = 3e^(x − 1) + 2
Write down the y-intercept and the range of f(x) = e^(−x) − 4
Which graph represents y = 0.5^x?

methods.name: Plot the intercept, asymptote and a couple of points
methods.summary: Evaluate at x = 0 and x = 1, mark the horizontal asymptote, and join with the growth or decay shape.

methods.name: Move e^x or a^x by its transformations
methods.summary: e^(x − a) + b is e^x translated by the vector (a, b): (0, 1) goes to (a, 1 + b) and the asymptote y = 0 goes to y = b.

methods.name: Use the base to decide growth or decay
methods.summary: a > 1 grows, 0 < a < 1 decays, and a^(−x) = (1/a)^x is the reflection of a^x in the y-axis.

methods.name: Graph on the GDC and copy the key features
methods.summary: Graph the function and read the intercept and the level the curve flattens towards.

misconceptions: Puts the y-intercept of e^(x − 1) + 2 at (0, 3), ignoring the horizontal shift
Gives the asymptote of e^x + b as y = 0
Thinks (1/2)^x is the reflection of 2^x in the x-axis rather than the y-axis

threads.echo: a^x multiplies by the same factor a for every step of 1 to the right: the continuous version of a geometric sequence.
e^(x − a) + b is e^x shifted right a and up b, so the asymptote moves to y = b and the point (0, 1) moves to (a, 1 + b).
Translating e^x by the vector (a, b) gives e^(x − a) + b: the same vector rule as vertex form and A + B/(x − h).

skills.name: Sketch and describe logarithmic graphs as reflections of exponentials
examTypes: Sketch y = ln x and y = e^x on the same axes
Write down the equation of the vertical asymptote of y = ln(x − 2) + 1
Write down the x-intercept of y = log₃ x
State the domain of f(x) = ln(2x − 6)

methods.name: Reflect y = a^x in y = x
methods.summary: Swap the coordinates of key points of a^x: (0, 1) becomes (1, 0) and the asymptote y = 0 becomes x = 0.

methods.name: Use (1, 0), (a, 1) and the asymptote x = 0
methods.summary: log_a 1 = 0 and log_a a = 1 give two points; the curve rises slowly and plunges down the y-axis.

methods.name: Translate ln x by its vector
methods.summary: ln(x − a) + b is ln x moved by (a, b): the asymptote becomes x = a and (1, 0) moves to (1 + a, b).

methods.name: Graph on the GDC and copy
methods.summary: Graph the function, noting that the GDC may not show the steep drop near the asymptote clearly.

misconceptions: Draws the log graph with a horizontal asymptote
Gives the vertical asymptote of ln(x − 2) as x = −2
Thinks ln 0 = 0, so the graph starts at the origin

threads.echo: ln x undoes e^x, so its graph is e^x reflected in y = x: the asymptote y = 0 becomes x = 0 and (0, 1) becomes (1, 0).
ln(x − a) + b is ln x translated, so the vertical asymptote moves from x = 0 to x = a.
Under y = ln(x − a) + b every point of ln x, including (1, 0), moves by the same vector (a, b).

skills.name: Switch between exponential and logarithmic form to evaluate or solve
examTypes: Solve log₂ x = 5
Solve e^(2x) = 7, giving your answer in exact form
Write down the value of ln(e⁴) and of e^(ln 3)
Write down the inverse of f(x) = 3^x

methods.name: Use log_a x = y ⇔ a^y = x
methods.summary: Rewrite the log statement as a power (or the power as a log) and read off the unknown.

methods.name: Take ln of both sides
methods.summary: Isolate the exponential, apply ln to both sides so ln(e^(2x)) = 2x, then solve.

methods.name: Write x = log_a b and evaluate as ln b / ln a
methods.summary: For a^x = b with an awkward base, x = log_a b = ln b / ln a, exact or on the GDC.

methods.name: Intersect y = e^(2x) with y = 7
methods.summary: A graphical solution gives a decimal to check against the exact answer.

misconceptions: Solves e^(2x) = 7 as x = 2 ln 7 or x = ln 7 − 2 instead of x = (ln 7)/2
Converts log₂ x = 5 to x = 5² instead of 2⁵
Writes x = 7/(2e), treating e as a coefficient to divide by

threads.echo: Logs exist to undo exponentials: log₂ x = 5 just asks 'what is 2⁵?', the same undoing as f⁻¹.
log_a x = y and a^y = x are one fact written two ways; switch to whichever form isolates the unknown.

skills.name: Model exponential growth and decay
examTypes: Find the population after 6 years
Given that the mass halves every 5 hours, find the value of k
Find the time taken for the temperature to fall below 30°C
Interpret the value 0.85 in the model V = 2000(0.85)^t

methods.name: Substitute into P = P₀a^t or P = Ae^(kt)
methods.summary: Identify the initial value and growth factor (or rate k) and evaluate at the required time.

methods.name: Use logs to find an unknown exponent or rate
methods.summary: Isolate the exponential, take ln of both sides and solve for t or k.

methods.name: Graph the model and the target value
methods.summary: Use intersect, or scan a table, to find when the model reaches the target.

methods.name: Multiply by the growth factor step by step
methods.summary: Build a table year by year, as for a geometric sequence, to check or estimate the answer.

misconceptions: Uses r instead of 1 + r as the growth factor (0.05 instead of 1.05 for 5% growth)
Computes P₀ × r × t (linear growth) instead of P₀ × r^t
Treats the initial value as P(1) instead of P(0), so the exponent is off by one

threads.echo: An exponential model multiplies by the same factor each unit of time, exactly like a geometric sequence or compound interest.
Finding when the model reaches a target means undoing the exponential, so ln does the work.

skills.name: Find unknown constants in an exponential or log function from a graph or points
examTypes: The graph of y = a·b^x + c has asymptote y = 3 and passes through two given points; find a, b and c
The graph of f(x) = ln(x − k) has vertical asymptote x = 2; write down the value of k
Given f(x) = 5e^(kx) and f(2) = 10, find the exact value of k

methods.name: Read the vertical shift from the asymptote
methods.summary: The horizontal asymptote y = c gives c, the y-intercept then gives a + c, and another point gives b.

methods.name: Substitute points and solve
methods.summary: Substitute two points, divide one equation by the other to eliminate a, then use logs for the base or rate.

methods.name: Exponential regression for data
methods.summary: When the points come from data, use exponential regression on the GDC to estimate the parameters.

misconceptions: Reads the y-intercept of a·b^x + c as a instead of a + c
Uses the asymptote value as the y-intercept
Takes ln of a sum term by term, e.g. ln(a·b^x + c) = ln a + x ln b + ln c

threads.echo: The constant c is a vertical translation, so it shows up as the asymptote; a and b control the stretch and steepness.

subtopics.title: Solving equations graphically and analytically
subtopics.guide: Solving equations both graphically and analytically; using technology to solve a variety of equations, including those where there is no appropriate analytic approach; applications to real-life situations.

skills.name: Solve equations that need technology
examTypes: Solve e^x = x + 3
Solve ln x = 4 − x², giving your answers correct to 3 s.f.
Find the solutions of f(x) = g(x) for 0 ≤ x ≤ 5

methods.name: Graph each side and use intersect
methods.summary: Enter the left side as Y1 and the right side as Y2 and find every intersection in the domain.

methods.name: Rearrange to h(x) = 0 and find the zeros
methods.summary: Graph h(x) = left side − right side and use the zero function on each crossing.

methods.name: Find a sign change in a table, then refine
methods.summary: Tabulate h(x) and look for a change of sign, then shrink the step to locate the root.

misconceptions: Misses a solution outside the default GDC window
Rounds intermediate values or gives answers to fewer than 3 s.f.
Takes ln of both sides of e^x = x + 3 and writes x = ln x + ln 3

threads.echo: When algebra cannot isolate x, the graph still can: every equation is just two graphs meeting.

skills.name: Solve equations analytically and check with a graph
examTypes: Solve ln(2x − 1) = 3, giving an exact answer
Solve log₂ x + log₂(x − 2) = 3
Find the exact solutions of the equation

methods.name: Apply inverse operations to both sides
methods.summary: Isolate the function and undo it: exponentiate a log, take ln of an exponential, multiply out a fraction.

methods.name: Combine and rearrange into a polynomial
methods.summary: Use log laws or clear fractions until you have a linear or quadratic equation, then solve and check each root.

methods.name: Sketch or graph both sides to check
methods.summary: A graph shows how many solutions to expect and exposes any root that must be rejected.

misconceptions: Keeps a solution that makes a log argument negative or a denominator zero
Applies ln term by term, writing ln(a + b) = ln a + ln b
Multiplies only one side by the denominator when clearing fractions

threads.echo: Analytic solving is a chain of undoing: every step applies an inverse operation to both sides.
An exact algebraic answer should match the GDC intersection to 3 s.f.; if it does not, one of them is wrong.

skills.name: Find the number of solutions, or the values of k that give a certain number
examTypes: Write down the number of solutions of f(x) = 2
Find the values of k for which f(x) = k has exactly two solutions
Hence explain why the equation has no solution for x > 3

methods.name: Slide a horizontal line y = k across the graph
methods.summary: Count crossings as the line moves up and note the k-values where the count changes.

methods.name: Use turning-point values and asymptotes as boundaries
methods.summary: The number of solutions only changes at a maximum or minimum value or at an asymptote, so those y-values bound the intervals for k.

methods.name: Use the discriminant for a quadratic
methods.summary: If f(x) = k rearranges to a quadratic, Δ > 0, = 0, < 0 gives two, one or no solutions.

methods.name: Graph and count on the GDC
methods.summary: Graph y = f(x) and y = k for trial values and count the intersections.

misconceptions: Counts two solutions when y = k only touches the graph at a turning point (one solution)
Counts intersections outside the given domain
Counts an asymptote value as giving a solution

threads.echo: The number of solutions of f(x) = k is the number of times the horizontal line y = k crosses the graph.
The count changes exactly at the maximum and minimum values, so the turning points set the boundaries for k.

skills.name: Solve inequalities graphically or with technology
examTypes: Find the values of x for which f(x) > g(x)
Solve e^x > 3x, giving your answer correct to 3 s.f.
Find the set of values of t for which the population exceeds 1000

methods.name: Find the intersections, then read which graph is above
methods.summary: Use intersect for the boundary x-values and read off the intervals where f lies above g.

methods.name: Graph f(x) − g(x) and find where it is positive
methods.summary: Plot the difference; the solution is where its graph is above the x-axis.

methods.name: Solve the equality, then test the intervals
methods.summary: Find the boundary points algebraically where possible, then test one value in each interval.

misconceptions: Gives the intersection points instead of an interval
Chooses the interval where f is below g
Misses that the solution set can be in two separate pieces

threads.echo: f(x) > g(x) means 'where is the graph of f above the graph of g?', so find where they cross and look.

skills.name: Set up and solve an equation from a real-life model
examTypes: Find when the two populations are equal
Find the time at which the temperature first reaches 60°C
Find the value of t when the tank is half full and interpret your answer

methods.name: Graph the model and the target, and intersect
methods.summary: Plot the model and the line y = target (or a second model) on a window matching the context.

methods.name: Rearrange and solve analytically
methods.summary: Isolate the unknown, using ln for exponential models, then interpret the result.

methods.name: Scan a GDC table for the first value that works
methods.summary: Useful when the answer must be a whole number of years or items.

misconceptions: Rounds the wrong way for the context (e.g. 4.2 years becomes 4 when 5 complete years are needed)
Keeps a solution outside the model's domain, such as a negative time
Answers 'how much' when the question asks 'when'

threads.echo: Real-world 'when does it reach…' questions are still intersections: the model's graph meets the line y = target.

subtopics.title: Transformations of graphs
subtopics.guide: Transformations of graphs: translations y = f(x) + b and y = f(x − a), including translation by the vector (a, b); reflections in the x-axis (y = −f(x)) and the y-axis (y = f(−x)); vertical stretch y = p f(x) with scale factor p; horizontal stretch y = f(qx) with scale factor 1/q; composite transformations.

skills.name: Apply a translation given as a vector (a, b) or in words
examTypes: The graph of f is translated by the vector (3, −2); write down the equation of the new graph
Write down g(x) after f is translated 4 units to the left
Find the coordinates of the image of the vertex after the translation
Write down the equation of the new asymptote

methods.name: Replace x with x − a, then add b
methods.summary: Translation by (a, b) turns y = f(x) into y = f(x − a) + b; substitute and simplify if f is given.

methods.name: Move key points by the vector
methods.summary: Add the vector to every key point, (x, y) ↦ (x + a, y + b), then rebuild the equation from the new vertex or asymptotes.

methods.name: Shift the vertex, centre or asymptotes
methods.summary: For a parabola move the vertex to (h + a, k + b); for 1/x, e^x or ln x move the asymptotes by a and b and write the new form directly.

methods.name: Graph both on the GDC and compare
methods.summary: Plot f and your answer and check that every point has moved a right and b up.

misconceptions: Writes f(x + 3) − 2 for a translation by (3, −2), getting the horizontal sign wrong
Puts the vertical component inside the bracket, writing f(x − 3 − 2)
Moves the curve's points but leaves the asymptote where it was

threads.echo: The vector (a, b) means 'a right, b up'; the same vector appears as the vertex in a(x − h)² + k, the centre of A + B/(x − h) and the (−c, d) shift in a·sin(b(x + c)) + d.
A translation moves every point by the same amount, so the shape is untouched and only the position changes.
f(x − a) moves right because the new graph must undo the '− a' before f sees the same input: changes inside the bracket act backwards.

skills.name: Apply reflections in the x-axis and the y-axis
examTypes: Write down the equation of the graph after a reflection in the x-axis
Find an expression for g(x) = f(−x)
Write down the coordinates of the image of P(2, 5) after a reflection in the y-axis

methods.name: Negate the whole function or replace x with −x
methods.summary: Reflection in the x-axis gives −f(x), so negate every term; reflection in the y-axis gives f(−x).

methods.name: Flip key points
methods.summary: (x, y) ↦ (x, −y) for the x-axis and (x, y) ↦ (−x, y) for the y-axis.

methods.name: Graph both on the GDC and compare
methods.summary: Check the result is the mirror image of f in the correct axis.

misconceptions: Reflects y = x² + 1 in the x-axis as y = −x² + 1, negating only one term
Confuses −f(x) (x-axis) with f(−x) (y-axis)
Writes (−x)² + 1 for a reflection in the x-axis, not noticing it gives the same graph

threads.echo: A minus sign on the output flips the graph vertically; on the input it flips it horizontally: outside affects y, inside affects x.
If f(−x) = f(x), reflecting in the y-axis changes nothing, which is exactly why x² and cos x are symmetric about the y-axis.

skills.name: Apply vertical and horizontal stretches
examTypes: Describe the transformation that maps y = sin x onto y = 3 sin(2x)
Write down g(x) after a horizontal stretch with scale factor 1/2
Find the image of (4, 6) on the graph of y = 2f(x)

methods.name: p f(x) scales y by p; f(qx) scales x by 1/q
methods.summary: Multiply outside for a vertical stretch and replace x with qx for a horizontal stretch of scale factor 1/q.

methods.name: Scale key points
methods.summary: (x, y) ↦ (x, py) for a vertical stretch and (x, y) ↦ (x/q, y) for a horizontal one.

methods.name: Use invariant points to check
methods.summary: x-intercepts do not move under a vertical stretch, and the y-intercept does not move under a horizontal stretch.

methods.name: Graph both on the GDC and compare
methods.summary: Compare heights or widths of the two graphs to confirm the scale factor.

misconceptions: Thinks f(2x) is a horizontal stretch with scale factor 2 (it is 1/2)
Thinks 2f(x) moves the x-intercepts
Describes a stretch without its direction or scale factor

threads.echo: Multiplying the output stretches the graph vertically; multiplying the input squashes it horizontally by the reciprocal, because inside changes act in reverse.

skills.name: Apply a sequence of transformations and write the resulting function
examTypes: The graph of f is stretched vertically by scale factor 2 and then translated by the vector (1, −3); find g(x)
Write g(x) in the form a f(b(x + c)) + d
Explain why the order of the transformations matters
Find the image of a point under the combined transformation

methods.name: Apply one change at a time to the equation
methods.summary: Start from y = f(x) and apply each transformation in the given order, replacing x or multiplying the whole right-hand side each time.

methods.name: Follow one point through every step
methods.summary: Pick a point such as the vertex, move it through each step, and use the final position to check the equation.

methods.name: Read a·f(b(x + c)) + d as stretches then one translation
methods.summary: Stretch by 1/b horizontally and by a vertically, then translate by the vector (−c, d).

methods.name: Check with a GDC overlay
methods.summary: Graph the original and the result and verify that a tracked point lands where expected.

misconceptions: Writes f(2x − 3) for 'horizontal stretch by 1/2, then translate 3 right' (it is f(2(x − 3)))
Writes 2(f(x) + 3) for 'vertical stretch by 2, then translate up 3' (it is 2f(x) + 3)
Assumes the order of transformations never matters

threads.echo: a·sin(b(x + c)) + d in trigonometry is this exact recipe applied to sin x, so every trig graph question is a transformations question.
After the stretches, whatever is left is a single translation vector (−c, d), whether the parent is x², 1/x, e^x or sin x.

skills.name: Describe fully the transformations that map one graph onto another, including the translation vector
examTypes: Describe fully the transformation that maps the graph of f onto the graph of g
Write down the translation vector that maps y = x² onto y = (x + 2)² − 5
Describe a sequence of two transformations that maps y = e^x onto y = 3e^x − 1
Given g(x) = f(x − 1) + 4, describe the transformation

methods.name: Rewrite g in terms of f and read each change
methods.summary: Express g as a·f(b(x + c)) + d (completing the square if needed, e.g. x² − 6x + 4 = (x − 3)² − 5) and name each part.

methods.name: Compare where key points and asymptotes moved
methods.summary: The displacement of the vertex or asymptote crossing gives the translation vector; ratios of heights or widths give the stretch factors.

methods.name: Compare the two graphs directly
methods.summary: Sketch or graph both, then look for flips, stretches and shifts between them.

misconceptions: Describes f(x + 2) as a translation 2 to the right, or gives the vector (2, 0)
Says 'moved' or 'shifted' without direction and size, or 'enlarged' instead of 'stretched'
Gives a stretch without saying parallel to which axis

threads.echo: Final vertex minus starting vertex gives the translation vector directly, just like a displacement.
Reading g(x) = a·f(b(x + c)) + d as stretches and a translation is the skill you will reuse for every sin, cos, e^x and normal curve.
Completing the square turns x² − 6x + 4 into (x − 3)² − 5, the equivalent form that shows the translation (3, −5).

skills.name: Find the image of a point, or the original point, under transformations
examTypes: A(2, 5) lies on y = f(x); find the image of A on y = 2f(x − 1) + 3
Write down the coordinates of the minimum point of y = f(2x) − 1
The point (6, 4) lies on the graph of g; find the corresponding point on f

methods.name: Use (x, y) ↦ (x/b − c, ay + d)
methods.summary: For y = a·f(b(x + c)) + d, apply the rule to the coordinates in one step.

methods.name: Move the point one transformation at a time
methods.summary: Apply each stretch, reflection and translation to the point in order.

methods.name: Set the inside equal to the original x
methods.summary: Solve b(x + c) = x₀ for the new x, then compute the new y as a·y₀ + d.

misconceptions: Moves the point the wrong way horizontally: (2, 5) on f becomes (1, 5) on f(x − 1)
Applies the vertical translation before the vertical stretch
Doubles the x-coordinate for f(2x) instead of halving it

threads.echo: A translation by (a, b) adds the vector to every point, so the image of P is simply P + (a, b).
Going back from g to f undoes the transformation, just as z = (x − μ)/σ undoes a shift by μ and a stretch by σ to standardise a normal variable.

skills.name: Sketch a transformed graph from the graph of f
examTypes: On the same axes, sketch the graph of y = f(x − 2) + 1
Sketch y = −f(x), showing the images of A, B and C
Which graph shows y = f(2x)?

methods.name: Transform the labelled points and asymptotes, then redraw
methods.summary: Find the image of every labelled point and asymptote, plot them, and redraw the same shape through them.

methods.name: Sketch each intermediate graph
methods.summary: For several transformations, draw a light sketch after each step so no change is missed or misordered.

methods.name: Check on the GDC when f is known
methods.summary: If f's equation is given, graph the transformed function to confirm the sketch.

misconceptions: Moves the curve but leaves the asymptote in its original place
Stretches away from the wrong axis, e.g. moves points vertically for f(2x)
Sketches f(x − 2) shifted to the left

threads.echo: Sketching a transformed graph is moving labelled points: if you know where the vertex, intercepts and asymptotes go, the curve follows.
Under a translation every labelled point and every asymptote moves by the same vector (a, b).

subtopics.title: 3D distance and midpoint, volume and surface area of solids, angles in 3D
subtopics.guide: Distance between two points and the midpoint of a segment in three-dimensional space. Volume and surface area of right pyramids, right cones, spheres, hemispheres and their combinations; the angle between two intersecting lines or between a line and a plane.

skills.name: Find the distance between two points in 3D
examTypes: Find the distance between A(1, −2, 3) and B(4, 2, 15)
Show that triangle ABC is isosceles
Given that AB = 7, find the possible values of k
Find the length of the space diagonal of a cuboid

methods.name: 3D distance formula
methods.summary: Square the differences in x, y and z, add them, then square-root: d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)² + (z₂ − z₁)²).

methods.name: Pythagoras twice
methods.summary: Find the diagonal across the floor from the x and y moves, then use it and the vertical z move as the legs of a second right triangle.

methods.name: Work with d² for an unknown coordinate
methods.summary: Set the sum of squared differences equal to d² (no roots), solve the quadratic in k and expect two values, one on each side.

misconceptions: Adding the differences before squaring: (Δx + Δy + Δz)² instead of Δx² + Δy² + Δz²
Mishandling a negative coordinate, e.g. taking 4 − (−2) as 2
Giving only one value of k from (k − 3)² = 16

threads.echo: The move from A to B is a 3D vector (Δx, Δy, Δz); the distance is just the length of that movement, Pythagoras with one more direction added.

skills.name: Find the midpoint of a segment in 3D, or an endpoint given the midpoint
examTypes: Find the coordinates of the midpoint M of [AB]
M(2, 5, −1) is the midpoint of [AB] and A is (6, 3, 4). Find B
Find the centre of a sphere given the ends of a diameter

methods.name: Solve one equation per coordinate
methods.summary: For a missing endpoint, set (x + 6)/2 = 2 and so on, and solve each coordinate equation separately.

methods.name: Half the journey, or the same step again
methods.summary: The midpoint is A plus half the displacement A→B; to get B from A and M, repeat the step A→M once more, so B = 2M − A.

misconceptions: Subtracting instead of adding: M = ((x₂ − x₁)/2, ...)
Finding the endpoint by averaging A and M instead of extending past M
Halving the midpoint coordinates to get the endpoint

threads.echo: The midpoint is where you land after half of the displacement from A to B; take that same step again from M and you reach B.

skills.name: Find volumes of pyramids, cones, spheres, hemispheres and composite solids
examTypes: Find the volume of a right cone with radius 4 cm and slant height 5 cm
A solid is a cone on top of a hemisphere; find its total volume
The volume of a sphere is 288π cm³; find its radius
Find the height of the pyramid, hence find its volume

methods.name: Substitute into the booklet formula
methods.summary: Choose V = ⅓Bh, ⅓πr²h, (4/3)πr³ or (2/3)πr³ for a hemisphere and substitute.

methods.name: Split a composite solid into standard pieces
methods.summary: Break the solid into cones, hemispheres, cylinders or pyramids, find each volume, then add (or subtract a removed piece).

methods.name: Find the perpendicular height first
methods.summary: When only a slant height or slant edge is given, use a right triangle through the apex to get h before using ⅓Bh.

methods.name: Rearrange for a missing dimension
methods.summary: Set the formula equal to the given volume and rearrange, e.g. r³ = 3V/(4π) then cube-root.

methods.name: Solve a composite volume equation on the GDC
methods.summary: When the equation mixes r² and r³ terms, graph V(r) against the target volume or use the solver.

misconceptions: Using the slant height instead of the perpendicular height in V = ⅓πr²h
Forgetting the ⅓ for a cone or pyramid, or using (4/3)πr³ for a hemisphere
Using the diameter as the radius

threads.echo: A cone is a stack of thin circular discs shrinking to a point; adding up all those slices is where the ⅓ comes from, the same 'add up small pieces' idea as integration.

skills.name: Find surface areas of pyramids, cones, spheres, hemispheres and composite solids
examTypes: Find the total surface area of a solid hemisphere of radius 3 cm
Find the curved surface area of a cone given its height and base radius
Find the total surface area of a square-based right pyramid
Find the cost of painting the outside of the composite solid

methods.name: Booklet formulas for each surface
methods.summary: Use πrl for a cone's curved surface, 4πr² for a sphere and 2πr² for a hemisphere's curved part, finding l = √(r² + h²) first if needed.

methods.name: Sketch the net and add exposed faces
methods.summary: List every exposed face (base, triangles, curved surfaces), leave out faces hidden where solids join, and add their areas.

methods.name: Unroll the cone into a sector
methods.summary: The curved surface opens into a sector of radius l with arc 2πr, so its area is ½ × l × 2πr = πrl.

misconceptions: Using the vertical height h in πrl instead of the slant height l
Giving a solid hemisphere's surface as 2πr², forgetting the flat face πr² (or counting a face hidden at a join)
Using 4πr² for a hemisphere

skills.name: Find the angle between a line and a plane
examTypes: Find the angle between the diagonal AG and the base ABCD of the cuboid
Find the angle between a slant edge of the right pyramid and its base
Find the angle the slant height of the cone makes with its base

methods.name: Project onto the plane and use tan
methods.summary: Drop a perpendicular from the top of the line to the plane, join it to where the line meets the plane, and use tan θ = height / horizontal projection.

methods.name: Use sin with the full line length
methods.summary: If the line's length is known (e.g. from the 3D distance formula), sin θ = vertical height / line length directly.

methods.name: Read rise and run from coordinates
methods.summary: Place the solid on axes; the rise is Δz and the horizontal run is √(Δx² + Δy²), so tan θ = Δz / √(Δx² + Δy²).

misconceptions: Measuring the angle to an edge of the base instead of to the line's projection onto the plane
Using the face diagonal as the vertical side of the triangle
Mixing up the slant edge of a pyramid with the slant height of a triangular face

threads.echo: Split the line's 3D movement into a horizontal part across the floor and a vertical part Δz; tan θ is rise over run, exactly the gradient idea.

skills.name: Find the angle between two intersecting lines in a 3D solid
examTypes: Find the angle between the diagonals AG and BH of the cuboid
Find the angle between two slant edges at the apex of the pyramid
Points A, B and C have given 3D coordinates; find angle ABC

methods.name: Three sides, then the cosine rule
methods.summary: Find all three side lengths with 3D Pythagoras or the distance formula, then use the cosine rule for the angle.

methods.name: Spot a right angle
methods.summary: If one line runs along an edge perpendicular to the face containing the other, the triangle is right-angled and SOH CAH TOA is quicker.

methods.name: Halve an isosceles triangle
methods.summary: With two equal sides (e.g. slant edges), drop the perpendicular from the apex and use sin(θ/2) = (half base) / (equal side).

misconceptions: Assuming an angle in a 2D drawing of a 3D solid is 90° because it looks like it
Using a face diagonal where a space diagonal is needed
Putting the side opposite the wanted angle in the wrong place in the cosine rule

threads.echo: An isosceles triangle has a mirror line through its apex; cutting along it turns one awkward triangle into two right-angled halves.

subtopics.title: Right-angled and non-right-angled triangle trigonometry
subtopics.guide: Use of the sine, cosine and tangent ratios to find sides and angles in right-angled triangles. The sine rule, the cosine rule and area of a triangle = ½ab sin C for any triangle (the ambiguous case is in SL3.5).

skills.name: Write down a trig ratio from a right-angled triangle
examTypes: Write down the value of sin θ as a fraction
Write down cos θ in terms of the sides p, q and r
Find the exact value of tan θ

methods.name: Label the sides, then SOH CAH TOA
methods.summary: Mark the hypotenuse, then the opposite and adjacent sides relative to θ, and pick the matching ratio.

methods.name: Pythagoras for the missing side
methods.summary: If the side you need is not given, find it with Pythagoras first, then form the ratio (exact surds allowed).

methods.name: Scale to hypotenuse 1
methods.summary: Divide every side by the hypotenuse; in the scaled triangle sin θ is the height and cos θ the base, just as on the unit circle.

misconceptions: Labelling opposite and adjacent relative to the wrong angle
Writing the ratio upside down, e.g. sin θ = hypotenuse / opposite
Treating the longer leg as the hypotenuse when the right angle is drawn in an unusual position

skills.name: Find a side in a right-angled triangle
examTypes: Find the length of BC
Find the height of the tree
Find the exact length of AB

methods.name: Choose the ratio and rearrange
methods.summary: Pick the ratio linking the known side, the unknown side and θ; multiply if the unknown is on top, divide if it is underneath.

methods.name: Use the other acute angle
methods.summary: Switch to the angle 90° − θ so the unknown side is on top of the ratio and no division is needed.

methods.name: Pythagoras
methods.summary: If two sides are already known, use a² + b² = c² and skip trig.

methods.name: Scale a special triangle
methods.summary: For 30°, 45° or 60° on Paper 1, scale the 1 : 1 : √2 or 1 : √3 : 2 triangle to get an exact length.

misconceptions: Rearranging sin θ = 12/x as x = 12 sin θ instead of x = 12 / sin θ
Using the hypotenuse as the adjacent side
Calculator in radian mode when the angle is in degrees

skills.name: Find an angle in a right-angled triangle
examTypes: Find the size of angle θ
Find the angle the ladder makes with the ground
Show that angle ABC = 60°

methods.name: Inverse trig on the ratio
methods.summary: Form the ratio from the two known sides and apply sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹.

methods.name: Find the third side, use another ratio
methods.summary: Get the third side by Pythagoras and use a different ratio, useful as a check or when the given pair is awkward.

methods.name: Recognise an exact ratio
methods.summary: Ratios such as 1/2, √3/2, 1/√2 or 1 give 30°, 60° or 45° with no calculator.

misconceptions: Writing θ = tan(5/12) instead of θ = tan⁻¹(5/12)
Reading tan⁻¹ x as 1 / tan x
Using adjacent / opposite for tan θ, which gives the other acute angle

threads.echo: tan⁻¹ undoes tan: you know the ratio and want the angle back, just as a log undoes an exponential.

skills.name: Use the sine rule to find a side or an angle
examTypes: Find the length of AC
Find the size of angle B
Show that BC = 5√2
Find the perimeter of triangle PQR

methods.name: Sides on top for a side
methods.summary: Use a / sin A = b / sin B with the unknown side on top, so it is a single multiplication.

methods.name: Sines on top for an angle
methods.summary: Flip to sin A / a = sin B / b so the unknown sine is on top, then apply sin⁻¹.

methods.name: Drop an altitude
methods.summary: Drop a perpendicular h from the shared vertex; h = b sin C = c sin B in the two right triangles, which is the sine rule itself.

methods.name: Angle sum to make a matching pair
methods.summary: If two angles are known but not the one opposite the known side, use the 180° angle sum first to create a side–angle opposite pair.

misconceptions: Pairing a side with an angle that is not opposite it
Rearranging b / sin 40° = 8 / sin 65° as b = 8 sin 65° / sin 40°
Trying the sine rule with SAS information, where no opposite pair is known (needs the cosine rule)

skills.name: Use the cosine rule to find a side from two sides and the included angle
examTypes: Find the length of BC
Find PR, giving your answer to 3 significant figures
Find the exact length of AB
Find the distance between the two ships

methods.name: Cosine rule
methods.summary: Substitute into a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A, with A the angle between b and c, then square-root.

methods.name: Two right triangles and Pythagoras
methods.summary: Drop a perpendicular to split the triangle, find the height and base pieces with SOH CAH TOA, then use Pythagoras.

methods.name: Exact cosines on Paper 1
methods.summary: With 60°, 90° or 120° use cos 60° = ½, cos 90° = 0, cos 120° = −½ to keep the answer exact; a negative cosine makes the side longer.

misconceptions: Evaluating (b² + c² − 2bc) cos A instead of b² + c² − (2bc cos A)
Forgetting to square-root a²
Using an angle that is not between the two given sides

skills.name: Use the cosine rule to find an angle from three sides
examTypes: Find the size of the largest angle
Find angle ABC
Show that cos B = −1/4
Find the angle between the two paths

methods.name: Rearranged cosine rule
methods.summary: Use cos A = (b² + c² − a²) / (2bc), with a the side opposite the wanted angle, then cos⁻¹.

methods.name: Substitute, then solve for cos A
methods.summary: Substitute all three sides into a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A and solve the linear equation for cos A.

methods.name: Sign of b² + c² − a²
methods.summary: Negative means the angle is obtuse, zero means a right angle (Pythagoras), positive means acute; useful for 'show that' and as a check.

misconceptions: Using (a² + b² − c²) / 2ab when the angle wanted is A
Thinking a negative cosine is an error, when it just means the angle is obtuse
Using the sine rule for the largest angle and missing that it is obtuse

threads.echo: cos⁻¹ gives exactly one angle between 0° and 180°, the full range of triangle angles, so unlike sin⁻¹ there is never a second answer to hunt for.

skills.name: Find the area of a triangle using ½ab sin C, or work backwards from the area
examTypes: Find the area of triangle ABC
The area is 20 cm²; find the possible values of angle C
Find the exact area of the triangle
Given the area, find x

methods.name: ½ab sin C
methods.summary: Use ½ab sin C with C the angle between sides a and b.

methods.name: Base and perpendicular height
methods.summary: Take one side as the base, find the perpendicular height as b sin C, then use ½ × base × height.

methods.name: Reverse with two angles
methods.summary: For a given area, solve sin C = 2 × Area / (ab) and keep both C and 180° − C.

misconceptions: Using an angle that is not between the two given sides
Finding only the acute angle when working back from an area
Forgetting the ½

threads.echo: sin C = sin(180° − C), so one area allows two included angles that mirror each other about 90°.

subtopics.title: Applications of right and non-right trigonometry
subtopics.guide: Applying Pythagoras, right-angled trigonometry, the sine rule and the cosine rule in context, including angles of elevation and depression and bearings, and constructing labelled diagrams from written statements.

skills.name: Use angles of elevation and depression to find heights and distances
examTypes: Draw a labelled diagram to represent this information
Find the height of the cliff
Find the angle of depression from the top of the tower to the boat
Find the horizontal distance from the observer to the building

methods.name: One right triangle with tan
methods.summary: Sketch the horizontal, the vertical height and the line of sight, then use tan θ = height / horizontal distance (or sin/cos if the sloping length is involved).

methods.name: Move the angle of depression
methods.summary: An angle of depression from the top equals the angle of elevation from the bottom (alternate angles between horizontals), so place it inside the triangle at ground level.

misconceptions: Measuring the angle of depression from the vertical instead of the horizontal
Putting the angle of depression inside the triangle at the top vertex
Forgetting to add the observer's eye height

threads.echo: tan of the angle of elevation is the gradient of the line of sight: metres of rise per metre of horizontal run.

skills.name: Find a height from two angles of elevation taken at different points
examTypes: From A the angle of elevation of the top is 30°; 50 m closer it is 45°. Find the height
Find the distance BT, hence find the height of the tower
Show that h = 50 tan α tan β / (tan β − tan α)

methods.name: Sine rule, then right-angled trig
methods.summary: In the non-right triangle formed by the two observation points and the top, the top angle is β − α; use the sine rule for the sloping side, then SOH CAH TOA for the height.
