methods.name: Two tan equations
methods.summary: With x the nearer distance, h = x tan β and h = (x + 50) tan α; equate, solve for x, then find h.

methods.name: Intersect the two height expressions
methods.summary: Graph y = x tan β and y = (x + 50) tan α and read the intersection: x is the distance and y the height.

misconceptions: Using the 50 m between observers as the distance to the foot of the tower
Taking the angle at the top as α + β instead of β − α
Using a right-triangle ratio in the triangle that has no right angle

threads.echo: Two expressions for the same height are two straight lines; solving them simultaneously is finding where the lines cross.

skills.name: Interpret bearings, draw the journey diagram, and find distances and bearings
examTypes: A ship sails 12 km on a bearing of 070°, then 8 km on 150°. Draw a diagram
Find the distance of the ship from its starting point
Find the bearing of the port from the ship
Write down the bearing of A from B

methods.name: Angle chase, then cosine and sine rules
methods.summary: Draw north lines at each point, use co-interior angles (sum 180°) to find the angle inside the triangle, then the cosine rule for distance and the sine rule for the direction.

methods.name: East and north components
methods.summary: Resolve each leg into east = d sin(bearing) and north = d cos(bearing), add the components, then use Pythagoras for the distance and tan⁻¹ for the direction.

methods.name: Back bearing ± 180°
methods.summary: The bearing of A from B is the bearing of B from A plus or minus 180°.

misconceptions: Measuring a bearing anticlockwise or from east instead of clockwise from north
Giving the bearing of A from B when asked for B from A
Using the bearings themselves as angles inside the triangle without angle chasing

threads.echo: Each leg of a journey is a displacement vector; splitting it into east and north parts and adding them is exactly how vectors add.

skills.name: Solve multi-step problems across connected triangles, choosing the right rule at each step
examTypes: Find BD, hence find angle BCD
Find the area of quadrilateral ABCD
Find the perimeter of the field
Show that the length of the fence is 23.6 m

methods.name: Classify what each triangle gives you
methods.summary: Right angle → SOH CAH TOA or Pythagoras; SAS or SSS → cosine rule; a side with its opposite angle → sine rule; then carry the shared side into the next triangle.

methods.name: Split into right triangles
methods.summary: Drop perpendiculars to break the shape into right triangles and use only SOH CAH TOA and Pythagoras.

methods.name: Split a quadrilateral along a diagonal
methods.summary: Cut along whichever diagonal gives two triangles with enough information, and add the two ½ab sin C areas.

misconceptions: Rounding the shared side early and carrying the error into the next triangle
Assuming an angle is 90° because it looks like it
Using the sine rule in a triangle where no side–opposite angle pair is known

subtopics.title: The circle: radians, arc length and sector area
subtopics.guide: Radian measure of angles and conversion between degrees and radians. Length of an arc and area of a sector, l = rθ and A = ½r²θ with θ in radians.

skills.name: Convert between degrees and radians
examTypes: Write 150° in radians as a multiple of π
Convert 2.5 radians to degrees
Express 5π/4 in degrees

methods.name: Multiply by π/180 or 180/π
methods.summary: Degrees to radians: multiply by π/180; radians to degrees: multiply by 180/π.

methods.name: Fraction of a full turn
methods.summary: Write the angle as a fraction of 360°, then take the same fraction of 2π: 150° is 5/12 of a turn, so 5π/6.

misconceptions: Multiplying by 180/π when converting degrees to radians
Thinking π radians is 3.14° or that 1 radian is about 1°
Giving a decimal when an exact multiple of π is asked for

skills.name: Find arc length or sector perimeter, or work back to r or θ
examTypes: Find the length of arc AB
Find the perimeter of the sector
The arc length is 12 cm and r = 5 cm; find θ
A pendulum swings through 0.4 rad; find the distance travelled by its tip

methods.name: l = rθ
methods.summary: With θ in radians, l = rθ; rearrange to θ = l / r or r = l / θ.

methods.name: Fraction of the circumference
methods.summary: The arc is the fraction θ / 2π (or θ / 360° in degrees) of the full circumference 2πr.

misconceptions: Using θ in degrees in l = rθ
Forgetting the two radii when finding the perimeter of a sector
Using the minor-arc angle when the major arc is asked for

skills.name: Find sector area, or work back to r or θ
examTypes: Find the area of sector OAB
The sector has area 30 cm² and radius 6 cm; find θ
Find the area of the major sector

methods.name: A = ½r²θ
methods.summary: With θ in radians, A = ½r²θ; rearrange to θ = 2A / r².

methods.name: Fraction of the whole circle
methods.summary: The sector is the fraction θ / 2π of the full area πr².

methods.name: Major sector by complement
methods.summary: Major sector = πr² − minor sector, or use the reflex angle 2π − θ in ½r²θ.

misconceptions: Using θ in degrees in ½r²θ
Squaring θ instead of r: ½rθ²
Giving the minor sector when the major sector is asked for

threads.echo: A sector is a fan of thin triangles, each about ½ × r × (r Δθ); adding them all up gives ½r²θ, the same 'sum of thin slices' idea behind integrals.

skills.name: Find the area or perimeter of a segment or composite shaded region
examTypes: Find the area of the shaded segment
Show that the shaded area is 6π − 9√3 (r = 6, θ = π/3)
Find the perimeter of the shaded region

methods.name: Sector minus triangle
methods.summary: Segment = ½r²θ − ½r² sin θ = ½r²(θ − sin θ).

methods.name: Build from standard pieces
methods.summary: Make the shaded region by adding and subtracting sectors, triangles, rectangles and circles.

methods.name: Chord by cosine rule or 2r sin(θ/2)
methods.summary: For a perimeter, find the straight chord with the cosine rule or 2r sin(θ/2), then add the arc rθ.

misconceptions: Calculator in degree mode when evaluating sin θ for θ in radians
Adding the two radii instead of the chord to the perimeter of a segment
Using ½r² sin θ with θ in degrees in one term and radians in the other

skills.name: Solve sector problems with two conditions (perimeter and area, or arc and area)
examTypes: A sector has perimeter 20 cm and area 24 cm². Find r and θ
Show that θ = (20 − 2r) / r
Hence show that r² − 10r + 24 = 0

methods.name: Eliminate θ and solve a quadratic
methods.summary: Make θ the subject of the perimeter equation, substitute into the area equation and solve the quadratic in r, then check each θ is between 0 and 2π.

methods.name: Intersect the two conditions on the GDC
methods.summary: Write θ from each condition as a function of r, graph both, and read the intersection(s).

misconceptions: Using perimeter = rθ, forgetting the 2r
Accepting a solution with θ > 2π
Keeping only one root when both give a valid sector

threads.echo: Two conditions are two curves; the sector you want sits where they cross, whether you find it by substitution or on the GDC.

subtopics.title: The unit circle, exact values and the ambiguous case
subtopics.guide: Definition of cos θ and sin θ in terms of the unit circle, and tan θ = sin θ / cos θ. Exact values of the trig ratios of 0, π/6, π/4, π/3, π/2 and their multiples; extension of the sine rule to the ambiguous case.

skills.name: Use unit-circle definitions: coordinates, signs by quadrant, tan as gradient
examTypes: P is the point on the unit circle at angle θ; write down its coordinates
Given π/2 < θ < π, state the sign of cos θ and of tan θ
The point (−0.6, 0.8) lies on the unit circle; write down sin θ and cos θ
Explain why tan(π/2) is undefined

methods.name: Read coordinates off the circle
methods.summary: cos θ is the x-coordinate and sin θ the y-coordinate of the point at angle θ, measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis.

methods.name: CAST diagram
methods.summary: Fix the sign from the quadrant: All positive, then Sin, then Tan, then Cos, going anticlockwise from the first quadrant.

methods.name: tan as the gradient of the radius
methods.summary: tan θ = y / x is the gradient of OP, so it is undefined when the radius is vertical.

methods.name: Read from the sin and cos graphs
methods.summary: Check the sign or value at θ on y = sin θ and y = cos θ.

misconceptions: Swapping coordinates: taking sin θ as the x-coordinate
Measuring θ clockwise or from the y-axis
Thinking tan(π/2) = 0 or 1 instead of undefined

threads.echo: Walking 1 unit at angle θ moves you cos θ right and sin θ up: the same east and north components you used for bearings.
tan θ is rise over run for the radius OP, so it is literally the gradient of that line.

skills.name: Write down exact values at 0, π/6, π/4, π/3 and π/2
examTypes: Write down the exact value of cos(π/6)
Write down tan(π/3)
Find the exact value of sin²(π/4) + cos(π/3)

methods.name: Special triangles
methods.summary: Halve an equilateral triangle of side 2 (sides 1, √3, 2) for π/6 and π/3; use the isosceles right triangle (1, 1, √2) for π/4.

methods.name: The √n / 2 pattern
methods.summary: sin of 0, π/6, π/4, π/3, π/2 is √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2; cos is the same list backwards.

misconceptions: Swapping sin(π/6) = 1/2 and cos(π/6) = √3/2
Writing tan(π/6) = √3 instead of 1/√3
Thinking sin(π/4) = 1/2

threads.echo: cos θ = sin(π/2 − θ): reflecting the unit circle in y = x swaps x and y, which is why the cos list is the sin list reversed.

skills.name: Find exact values for any multiple of π/6, π/4 or π/3, including negative and reflex angles
examTypes: Find the exact value of sin(5π/6)
Write down cos(4π/3)
Find tan(−π/4)
Find the exact value of cos(7π/4) + sin(2π/3)

methods.name: Reflect on the unit circle
methods.summary: Locate the angle on the unit circle and reflect its point into the first quadrant; the coordinates keep their size and only the signs change.

methods.name: Reference angle plus CAST
methods.summary: Find the angle to the nearest x-axis (5π/6 → π/6), take the first-quadrant value, then apply the CAST sign.

methods.name: Symmetry of the graph
methods.summary: Use the symmetry of y = sin x about x = π/2 (or y = cos x about x = π) to match the angle with a known value.

methods.name: Related-angle identities
methods.summary: Apply sin(π − x) = sin x, cos(π + x) = −cos x, cos(−x) = cos x, tan(x + π) = tan x directly.

misconceptions: Correct size but wrong sign for the quadrant, e.g. cos(2π/3) = 1/2
Measuring the reference angle from the y-axis, e.g. using π/3 for 5π/6
Treating a negative angle as positive, e.g. sin(−π/6) = 1/2

threads.echo: Every related angle is a mirror image of a first-quadrant angle in an axis of the unit circle, so you only ever need to remember one quadrant.

skills.name: Use exact trig values to find exact lengths and areas in triangles
examTypes: Find the exact area of triangle ABC with AB = 6, AC = 4 and angle A = 120°
Given AB = 3, AC = 5 and angle A = 60°, show that BC = √19
Find the exact value of cos ABC

methods.name: Substitute exact values
methods.summary: Use sin 120° = √3/2, cos 120° = −½ and so on in ½ab sin C or the cosine rule, then simplify surds.

methods.name: Drop a perpendicular onto a special triangle
methods.summary: Create a 30-60-90 or 45-45-90 right triangle and read lengths from its side ratios, then use Pythagoras.

misconceptions: Using cos 120° = +½, which gives a side that is too short
Simplifying √(16 + 9) as 4 + 3
Giving a decimal when an exact surd is required

threads.echo: sin 120° = sin 60° because 120° is the mirror image of 60° in the y-axis of the unit circle.

skills.name: Resolve the ambiguous case of the sine rule (two possible triangles)
examTypes: Find the two possible values of angle B
Find the difference between the two possible lengths of AC
Explain why there are two possible triangles
Given that angle ABC is obtuse, find its size

methods.name: Sine rule, then 180° minus
methods.summary: Get the acute angle B₁ from sin⁻¹, then B₂ = 180° − B₁; keep B₂ only if A + B₂ < 180°.

methods.name: Cosine rule as a quadratic
methods.summary: With the unknown side x, a² = x² + c² − 2xc cos A is a quadratic in x; two positive roots mean two triangles.

methods.name: Swing the side with a compass
methods.summary: Draw the known angle and its adjacent side, then swing the opposite side as an arc and count where it cuts the base line (0, 1 or 2 points).

methods.name: Compare with the altitude
methods.summary: Find the altitude h = c sin A; if h < a < c there are two triangles, if a = h exactly one (right-angled).

misconceptions: Giving only the calculator angle from sin⁻¹
Keeping B₂ = 180° − B₁ even when the angle sum then exceeds 180°
Thinking SAS can be ambiguous, when the included angle fixes a unique triangle

threads.echo: sin⁻¹ returns only one angle, but sin θ = k has two solutions between 0° and 180°; undoing sin needs a second look, just as in trig equations.
sin(180° − θ) = sin θ: the two possible angles are mirror images about 90°.

subtopics.title: Trigonometric identities and relationships between ratios
subtopics.guide: The Pythagorean identity cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 and the double angle identities for sine and cosine. Finding the value of one trig ratio given another, using the quadrant to decide the sign.

skills.name: Find one trig ratio from another, using the quadrant for the sign
examTypes: Given sin θ = 3/5 and θ is obtuse, find cos θ
Given cos x = −1/3 and π < x < 3π/2, find tan x
Given tan θ = 2/√5 and θ is acute, find the exact value of cos θ

methods.name: Pythagorean identity
methods.summary: Substitute into cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ, square-root, then choose the sign from the quadrant.

methods.name: Sketch a right triangle
methods.summary: Draw a right triangle with the given ratio (opposite 3, hypotenuse 5), find the third side by Pythagoras, read off the ratio, then apply the CAST sign.

methods.name: Point on the unit circle
methods.summary: Place the point (x, 3/5) on x² + y² = 1 in the correct quadrant and solve for x.

misconceptions: Ignoring the quadrant and giving cos θ = +4/5 when θ is obtuse
Writing cos θ = 1 − sin θ, dropping the squares

threads.echo: cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 is Pythagoras a² + b² = c² written for the unit circle, where c = 1.

skills.name: Find exact values of sin 2θ and cos 2θ from a given ratio
examTypes: Given sin θ = √5/3 and θ is acute, find cos 2θ
Find the exact value of sin 2θ
Given sin θ = 4/5, show that cos 2θ = −7/25

methods.name: Pick the cos 2θ form that fits
methods.summary: Given sin θ use 1 − 2sin²θ; given cos θ use 2cos²θ − 1; no need to find the other ratio.

methods.name: Find both ratios, then substitute
methods.summary: Find the missing ratio with the Pythagorean identity, then use sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ and cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ.

methods.name: Read ratios from a triangle
methods.summary: Sketch the right triangle for the given ratio, read sin θ and cos θ, and substitute into the double angle formulae.

misconceptions: sin 2θ = 2 sin θ
cos 2θ = 2 cos θ, or cos 2θ = 1 − sin²θ
Losing the negative sign of cos θ for an obtuse θ before substituting into sin 2θ

threads.echo: cos 2θ has three equivalent forms; picking the one that matches your information is like picking vertex form or factorised form for a quadratic.

skills.name: Rewrite and simplify trig expressions using identities
examTypes: Show that (sin x + cos x)² = 1 + sin 2x
Write 3 − 6 sin²x in the form a cos bx
Express 2 cos²x − 1 in terms of sin x
Hence write down the maximum value of 4 sin x cos x

methods.name: Expand, then apply identities
methods.summary: Expand the brackets, then replace sin²x + cos²x by 1 and 2 sin x cos x by sin 2x.

methods.name: Spot a known pattern
methods.summary: Recognise shapes such as 1 − 2sin²x or sin x cos x and replace them in one step, factoring out constants first (3 − 6sin²x = 3(1 − 2sin²x)).

methods.name: Check with a test value
methods.summary: Substitute a value such as x = π/6 into both forms to check they agree (a check, not a proof).

misconceptions: Expanding (sin x + cos x)² as sin²x + cos²x
Writing 4 sin x cos x as 4 sin 2x instead of 2 sin 2x
Reading sin²x as sin(x²)

threads.echo: Rewriting 4 sin x cos x as 2 sin 2x is like completing the square: a new form of the same function makes a feature obvious.
Once the expression is a single sine, its maximum is just the amplitude: 2 sin 2x tops out at 2.

skills.name: Prove a trig identity (show that LHS = RHS)
examTypes: Show that sin 2θ / (1 + cos 2θ) = tan θ
Prove that (1 − cos 2x) / sin 2x = tan x
Show that cos⁴x − sin⁴x = cos 2x

methods.name: Start from the more complicated side
methods.summary: Transform the busier side step by step, one identity per line, until it equals the other side.

methods.name: Convert everything to sin x and cos x
methods.summary: Rewrite tan and the double angles in terms of sin x and cos x, then cancel common factors.

methods.name: Spot a factorisable structure
methods.summary: Use structures such as a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b), then cos²x + sin²x = 1 collapses one factor.

misconceptions: Working on both sides at once as if solving an equation, then concluding 0 = 0
Cancelling across a sum, e.g. (1 + cos 2x) / cos 2x = 1 + 1
Choosing a form of cos 2θ that does not cancel the 1, e.g. cos²θ − sin²θ in 1 + cos 2θ

threads.echo: A 'show that' proof turns one form into another using the LHS → RHS layout from SL1.6 deductive proof.

subtopics.title: Circular functions and their graphs
subtopics.guide: The circular functions sin x, cos x and tan x: amplitude, periodic nature and graphs. Composite functions of the form f(x) = a sin(b(x + c)) + d, transformations, and real-life periodic contexts.

skills.name: Write down amplitude, period, principal axis, maximum, minimum and range
examTypes: Write down the amplitude and period of f(x) = 3 sin(2x) + 1
Write down the range of f
Write down the maximum value of g and the first x at which it occurs
State the period of y = tan(x/2)

methods.name: Read the parameters
methods.summary: Amplitude |a|, period 2π/b (π/b for tan), principal axis y = d, maximum d + |a|, minimum d − |a|.

methods.name: Transform the base graph's features
methods.summary: Start from sin x (range [−1, 1], period 2π) and push each number through: stretch by a, period divided by b, lift by d.

methods.name: Graph and read on the GDC
methods.summary: Plot the function in radian mode, find a maximum and minimum, and deduce the rest.

misconceptions: Period = b instead of 2π/b
Amplitude = a + d, or a negative amplitude when a < 0
Giving tan x an amplitude

threads.echo: a, b and d are the vertical stretch, horizontal stretch and vertical shift from SL2.11, now applied to a wave.
The maximum d + |a| and minimum d − |a| come straight from the stretch and shift, just as the vertex comes straight from vertex form.

skills.name: Describe or apply the transformations that map sin x or cos x to a sin(b(x + c)) + d
examTypes: Describe a sequence of transformations that maps y = sin x to y = 3 sin(2x − π/3) + 1
The graph of f is translated by the vector (π/4, −2); write down the equation of the image
Given g(x) = f(x − p) + q, find p and q
The graph is stretched horizontally with scale factor ½; write down the new equation

methods.name: Factor b out of the bracket
methods.summary: Write sin(2x − π/3) as sin(2(x − π/6)) so the horizontal shift is read as π/6, not π/3.

methods.name: Track key points
methods.summary: Send a maximum, a minimum and a zero of sin x through each transformation in turn and plot the images.

methods.name: Read the translation vector
methods.summary: After the stretches, the shift is the vector (−c, d): the horizontal part has the opposite sign to the +c inside the bracket.

methods.name: Overlay on the GDC
methods.summary: Graph the original and the image and check the proposed transformations line them up.

misconceptions: Reading sin(2x + π/3) as a shift of π/3 left instead of π/6
Using scale factor b for the horizontal stretch instead of 1/b
Translating right for a +c inside the bracket

threads.echo: f(x + c) moves left and f(x) + d moves up, exactly the SL2.11 rules; a trig wave obeys the same laws as any other graph.
The shift is the translation vector (−c, d), the same move as vertex form a(x − h)² + k shifting by (h, k) and z = (x − μ)/σ undoing a shift by μ.

skills.name: Find a, b, c and d from a graph or from given maximum and minimum points
examTypes: The graph has a maximum at (π/4, 5) and a minimum at (3π/4, −1). Find a, b, c and d
Write f(x) in the form a cos(b(x − c)) + d
Write down the equation of the principal axis

methods.name: Half-range and average
methods.summary: a = (max − min)/2, d = (max + min)/2, period = 2 × (gap from a maximum to the next minimum), b = 2π / period.

methods.name: Use cosine so c is a maximum
methods.summary: With a cos(b(x − c)) + d, c is simply the x-coordinate of a maximum, so no phase calculation is needed.

methods.name: Substitute a known point
methods.summary: After finding a, b and d, substitute a point on the curve and solve for c, choosing the value that fits the graph.

methods.name: Plot the model to check
methods.summary: Graph the candidate model and confirm it passes through the given points.

misconceptions: Taking the period as the gap from a maximum to the next minimum
Using a = max − min, forgetting to halve
Getting the sign of c wrong in a cos(b(x − c)) + d

threads.echo: Finding the model is undoing the transformations: which stretches and shifts turn the basic wave into this one?
The maximum and minimum alone fix the amplitude and the principal axis; the extremes carry most of the information.

skills.name: Sketch the graph of a circular function on a given domain
examTypes: Sketch y = 2 cos x − 1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π, marking the maximum, minimum and intercepts
Sketch y = tan x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π, showing its asymptotes
Which graph shows y = −sin(2x)?

methods.name: Five key points per period
methods.summary: Split one period into quarters, tabulate the five key points (axis, max, axis, min, axis for sine) and join with a smooth wave.

methods.name: Transform sin x or cos x
methods.summary: Start from the basic graph and apply the stretches, reflections and shifts to its key features.

methods.name: Graph on the GDC and transfer
methods.summary: Use a radian window that matches the domain and copy the shape, intercepts and turning points to paper.

misconceptions: Drawing tan x with turning points instead of vertical asymptotes at x = π/2 + kπ
Starting a cosine graph on the axis instead of at a maximum
Drawing a zigzag of straight lines instead of a smooth curve

threads.echo: Sketching from sin x by stretches and shifts is the SL2.11 method applied to a wave.

skills.name: Model a real-life periodic situation (tides, Ferris wheel, temperature, daylight)
examTypes: Find the height of the seat after 10 minutes
Find the first time the water depth is 4 m
Find for how long in each rotation the seat is above 30 m
Write down the minimum depth and interpret it in context

methods.name: Substitute the time
methods.summary: Put the time into the model, in radian mode, to get the height or depth.

methods.name: Intersect with y = k on the GDC
methods.summary: Graph the model and the horizontal line y = k and read every intersection time inside the domain.

methods.name: Rearrange and solve
methods.summary: Rearrange to sin(b(t + c)) = (k − d)/a, find the principal solution, then use symmetry and the period for the rest.

methods.name: Use symmetry about the peak
methods.summary: Find one crossing time; the other is equally far beyond the maximum, and the time above k is the gap between them.

misconceptions: Calculator in degree mode for a radian model
Giving only the first intersection when all times in the interval are asked for
Reading the period as b rather than 2π/b, e.g. b = π/6 means a 12-hour cycle

threads.echo: 'When is the depth 4 m?' is the intersection of the wave with y = 4; GDC and algebra must give the same times.
A wave is symmetric about each peak, so if it crosses a level 2 hours before the peak it crosses again 2 hours after.

subtopics.title: Solving trigonometric equations
subtopics.guide: Solving trigonometric equations in a finite interval, both graphically and analytically. Equations leading to quadratic equations in sin x, cos x or tan x.

skills.name: Solve sin x = k, cos x = k or tan x = k in a finite interval
examTypes: Solve 2 sin x = 1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π
Solve cos x = −0.4 for −180° ≤ x ≤ 180°
Solve √3 tan x = 1 for 0 ≤ x < 2π, giving exact answers

methods.name: Reference angle in every valid quadrant
methods.summary: Find the reference angle, place it in each quadrant where the ratio has the right sign (CAST), and list those inside the interval.

methods.name: Symmetry of the graph
methods.summary: From the principal value α: sin also gives π − α, cos gives −α (or 2π − α), tan gives α + π; then add or subtract whole periods to stay in range.

methods.name: Intersect on the GDC
methods.summary: Graph y = sin x and y = k over the interval and read off every intersection.

misconceptions: Stopping at the calculator's principal value
Using 180° − α for cos instead of 360° − α
Missing solutions in a negative interval such as −π ≤ x ≤ π

threads.echo: sin⁻¹ gives one answer, but sin x = k has many; undoing a periodic function needs symmetry to recover the rest.
The second solution of sin x = k is the mirror image of the first in the line x = π/2, the same symmetry as related angles on the unit circle.

skills.name: Solve equations with a transformed argument, e.g. sin 2x = k or cos(x + π/4) = k
examTypes: Solve sin 2x = √3/2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ π
Solve 2 cos(x + π/4) = 1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π
Solve tan 3x = 1 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 180°

methods.name: Substitute u and change the interval
methods.summary: Let u = 2x, transform the interval to 0 ≤ u ≤ 2π, solve for every u, then divide back to get x.

methods.name: Add multiples of the new period
methods.summary: Find one or two solutions for x, then add multiples of the new period 2π/b until you leave the interval.

methods.name: Intersect on the GDC
methods.summary: Graph y = sin 2x and y = k and count the crossings; twice the frequency means twice as many solutions.

misconceptions: Solving for 2x without extending the interval, losing half the solutions
Dividing only the principal value by 2 and forgetting the others
Undoing x + π/4 by adding π/4 instead of subtracting

threads.echo: sin 2x is sin x squeezed horizontally by a factor ½, so twice as many waves fit in the interval and there are twice as many solutions.

skills.name: Solve equations that lead to a quadratic in sin x, cos x or tan x
examTypes: Solve 2 sin²x − sin x − 1 = 0 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π
Show that 2 cos²x + 3 sin x = 3 can be written as 2 sin²x − 3 sin x + 1 = 0; hence solve it
Solve cos 2x = sin x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π
Solve 3 tan²x = 1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ π

methods.name: Identity, substitute u, factorise
methods.summary: Use cos²x = 1 − sin²x or a double angle identity to get a single trig function, let u = sin x, factorise, then solve each factor.

methods.name: Quadratic formula in u
methods.summary: If it does not factorise, solve for u with the quadratic formula, then reject any root outside [−1, 1].

methods.name: Graph the whole equation
methods.summary: Graph LHS − RHS over the interval and read its zeros (a Paper 2 method or check).

misconceptions: Accepting sin x = 2 as giving solutions
Taking only the positive root of tan²x = 1/3
Using cos 2x = 2cos²x − 1 when the equation also contains sin x, leaving two different functions

threads.echo: The identity rewrites the equation in terms of sin x alone; after that it is just an SL2.7 quadratic in disguise.
Each root sin x = k is a horizontal line meeting the sine wave; count the crossings to count the solutions.

skills.name: Solve equations by factorising or converting to tan x, without losing solutions
examTypes: Solve sin 2x = cos x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π
Solve sin x = √3 cos x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π
Solve sin 2x = sin x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π
Solve sin x(2 cos x − 1) = 0

methods.name: Collect and factorise
methods.summary: Bring everything to one side and take out the common factor, e.g. cos x(2 sin x − 1) = 0, then solve each factor.

methods.name: Divide to get tan x
methods.summary: For sin x = k cos x, divide by cos x to get tan x = k, after checking that cos x = 0 gives no solutions.

methods.name: Graph both sides
methods.summary: Sketch or plot both sides and count the crossings to make sure no solution was lost.

misconceptions: Cancelling cos x from 2 sin x cos x = cos x and losing x = π/2 and 3π/2
Getting tan x = 1/√3 from sin x = √3 cos x (it is √3)
Turning sin 2x = sin x into 2x = x

threads.echo: Dividing by cos x silently deletes some intersections; the graph shows every crossing, so it catches lost solutions.

skills.name: Solve trig equations graphically, including ones with no algebraic method, and count solutions
examTypes: Solve sin x = 0.3x for −π ≤ x ≤ π
Write down the number of solutions of f(x) = 2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 4π
Find the values of k for which f(x) = k has exactly two solutions
Solve 2 cos x = e^(−x) for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π

methods.name: GDC intersect
methods.summary: Graph both sides in radian mode with a window matching the interval and use intersect for every crossing.

methods.name: Sketch and count crossings
methods.summary: Sketch both graphs by hand and count the crossings to give the number of solutions without solving.

methods.name: Reason from the maximum and minimum
methods.summary: y = k meets a sin(bx) + d only when d − |a| ≤ k ≤ d + |a|; at k equal to the max or min the line just touches, which changes the count.

misconceptions: Using a GDC window that cuts off part of the interval and missing solutions
Including the boundary values of k where the line only touches at a maximum or minimum
Leaving the GDC in degree mode

threads.echo: When algebra cannot isolate x, the equation is still the intersection of two graphs, so the GDC finds what algebra cannot.
The number of solutions changes exactly when y = k passes a maximum or minimum, the same idea as a line touching a parabola at its vertex.

subtopics.title: Collecting data: populations, samples and sampling
subtopics.guide: Population, sample and random sample; discrete and continuous data; reliability of data sources and bias in sampling; interpreting outliers; simple random, convenience, systematic, quota and stratified sampling and how effective each is.

skills.name: Identify the population and the sample, and decide whether a sample is random
examTypes: Write down the population in this study
State whether the sample is a random sample. Justify your answer

methods.name: Who is the conclusion about, and who was measured?
methods.summary: The population is the whole group the conclusion is about, the sample is the part actually measured, and the sample is random only if every member of the population had an equal chance of being chosen.

misconceptions: The population is the people who answered the survey (that is the sample)
Choosing whoever walks past is 'random' (it is a convenience sample: not everyone has an equal chance)

skills.name: Classify data as discrete or continuous
examTypes: State whether the data are discrete or continuous
Write down which of these variables is continuous

methods.name: Counted or measured?
methods.summary: Data you count (people, goals, shoe sizes) are discrete; data you measure on a continuous scale (time, mass, height) are continuous.

methods.name: Can it take a value in between?
methods.summary: Pick two neighbouring possible values and ask whether a value between them is possible in principle; if not, the data are discrete.

misconceptions: Any data with decimals is continuous (money in cents and shoe size 7.5 are discrete)
Data recorded to the nearest whole number must be discrete (height to the nearest cm is still continuous)

skills.name: Identify, describe and evaluate a sampling technique
examTypes: Identify the sampling technique used
Describe how a systematic sample of 20 students could be taken
Suggest one disadvantage of this sampling method

methods.name: Run the feature checklist
methods.summary: Ask in turn: is there a fixed interval (systematic)? Are groups filled in proportion (stratified if chosen randomly within each group, quota if not)? Does everyone have an equal chance (simple random)? Is it just whoever is easiest to reach (convenience)?

methods.name: Eliminate by what could go wrong
methods.summary: Look at who could never be chosen or who is over-represented, and rule out the techniques that would not have that flaw.

misconceptions: Quota sampling and stratified sampling are the same (quota fills each group without random selection)
Systematic sampling is fully random (only the starting point is random; the rest follows the interval)
Stopping people in the street is simple random sampling

skills.name: Calculate how many to select from each group in a stratified sample
examTypes: Find the number of Year 12 students that should be included in the sample
Complete the table showing the number sampled from each stratum

methods.name: Stratum's share of the sample
methods.summary: Number from a stratum = (stratum size ÷ population size) × sample size, rounded sensibly.

methods.name: One scale factor for every group
methods.summary: Work out sample size ÷ population size once, multiply every stratum by it, then check the rounded numbers add up to the sample size.

misconceptions: Splitting the sample equally between the strata instead of in proportion to their sizes
Rounding each stratum so the numbers no longer add up to the required sample size

skills.name: Comment on bias in a sample and the reliability of data
examTypes: Explain why this sample may be biased
Suggest how the reliability of the results could be improved
Give a reason why this data source may not be reliable

methods.name: Who is left out or over-represented?
methods.summary: Picture the whole population, name the group the method cannot reach (or reaches too often), and say which way that would push the results.

methods.name: Compare the sample's make-up with the population's
methods.summary: Compare the proportion of each group in the sample with the proportion in the population; a large mismatch signals bias.

misconceptions: A larger sample removes bias (it improves reliability, but a biased method stays biased)
A random sample is always perfectly representative

skills.name: Decide in context whether an outlier should be kept or removed
examTypes: The value 250 is an outlier. Suggest whether it should be removed. Justify your answer
Explain the effect of removing the outlier on the mean and on the median

methods.name: Is it a mistake or a genuine extreme?
methods.summary: Remove a value only if it is impossible or clearly a recording error in context (a student 17 m tall); keep genuine extremes (a very tall basketball player).

methods.name: Reason about which measures it affects
methods.summary: An outlier drags the mean, range and standard deviation but barely moves the median and IQR, so decide which summary to trust.

misconceptions: Every outlier must be deleted
Removing an outlier changes the median as much as it changes the mean

subtopics.title: Presentation of data
subtopics.guide: Frequency tables with class intervals written as inequalities; frequency histograms with equal class widths; cumulative frequency tables and graphs used to find the median, quartiles, percentiles, range and IQR; drawing and interpreting box-and-whisker diagrams, marking outliers more than 1.5 × IQR from the nearest quartile, and comparing distributions.

skills.name: Read and complete frequency tables and equal-width histograms
examTypes: Write down the value of p in the frequency table
Draw a histogram to represent the data
Write down the number of students who took between 20 and 30 minutes

methods.name: Read frequencies from bar heights
methods.summary: With equal class widths the height of each bar is the frequency of that class, so read each one off the vertical axis.

methods.name: Use the total frequency
methods.summary: If one frequency is missing, subtract the known frequencies from the given total to find it.

misconceptions: Putting a value of exactly 20 into the class 10 ≤ x < 20
Leaving gaps between bars, as in a bar chart, for continuous data

skills.name: Build a cumulative frequency table and graph, and recover class frequencies from it
examTypes: Complete the cumulative frequency table
Draw the cumulative frequency graph
Find the number of values in the class 40 < x ≤ 50

methods.name: Running total
methods.summary: Add each class frequency to the total so far; the last cumulative frequency must equal n.

methods.name: Subtract consecutive cumulative values
methods.summary: Going backwards, the frequency of a class is its cumulative frequency minus the cumulative frequency before it.

methods.name: Plot at upper class boundaries
methods.summary: Plot each cumulative frequency against the upper boundary of its class, start at zero on the lower boundary of the first class, and join with a smooth curve.

misconceptions: Plotting cumulative frequencies at class midpoints instead of upper boundaries
Reading a cumulative frequency as the frequency of that single class

threads.echo: Cumulative frequency is a running total of everything so far, the same 'keep adding the pieces' idea as a partial sum of a series or the area built up under a curve.

skills.name: Find the median, quartiles, percentiles and IQR from a cumulative frequency graph
examTypes: Use the graph to find the median
Find the interquartile range
Find the 90th percentile

methods.name: Across from the cumulative frequency, down to the value
methods.summary: Go across from n/2 (median), n/4 (Q1), 3n/4 (Q3) or k% of n (kth percentile) on the vertical axis to the curve, then down to read the data value.

methods.name: Interpolate within the cumulative frequency table
methods.summary: Find the class containing the (n/2)th value and estimate how far through that class it lies, proportionally.

misconceptions: Reading the median halfway along the horizontal axis instead of from n/2 on the vertical axis
Finding Q3 − Q1 on the cumulative frequency axis instead of on the data axis
Reading the 90th percentile from 90 on the vertical axis when n is not 100

skills.name: Estimate how many values lie above, below or between given values, or find a cut-off
examTypes: Estimate the number of students who scored more than 65
Find the percentage of plants taller than 40 cm
The top 30 students receive a grade A. Find the minimum mark for an A

methods.name: Up to the curve, across, then subtract from n
methods.summary: Go up from the value to the curve and across to read how many are at or below it; subtract from n for 'more than'. Reverse the route (across from n − 30, then down) to find a cut-off.

methods.name: Interpolate in the table
methods.summary: With only a table, assume values are spread evenly through the class and take the matching fraction of that class's frequency.

misconceptions: Giving the cumulative frequency at 65 as the number who scored more than 65 (it is the number at or below)
For the top 30, reading across from 30 on the vertical axis instead of from n − 30

skills.name: Draw and interpret a box-and-whisker diagram
examTypes: Draw a box-and-whisker diagram for the data
Write down the median and the IQR from the box plot
State, with a reason, whether the data could be normally distributed

methods.name: Five-number summary from the data
methods.summary: Order the data, find the minimum, Q1, median, Q3 and maximum, then draw the box from Q1 to Q3 with the median line and whiskers to the extremes (or to the furthest values that are not outliers).

methods.name: Read the five values from a cumulative frequency graph
methods.summary: Read Q1, the median and Q3 at n/4, n/2 and 3n/4, and the extremes from where the curve starts and finishes.

methods.name: 1-Var Stats or a box plot on the GDC
methods.summary: Enter the list and read minX, Q1, Med, Q3 and maxX, or draw the modified box plot, which marks outliers for you.

misconceptions: A longer section of the box or a longer whisker contains more data values (each quarter holds about 25% of the data)
Drawing the whisker out to an outlier instead of marking the outlier separately with a cross

threads.echo: A box plot with the median in the middle of the box and equal whiskers is symmetric, a hint the data could be normal, whose curve is symmetric about the mean.

skills.name: Test whether a value is an outlier using 1.5 × IQR
examTypes: Determine whether 52 is an outlier. Justify your answer
Show that the maximum value is an outlier
Find the smallest value that would be an outlier

methods.name: Compute both fences
methods.summary: Find Q1 − 1.5 × IQR and Q3 + 1.5 × IQR; any value outside these fences is an outlier.

methods.name: Compare the distance from the nearest quartile
methods.summary: For a 'show that', work out how far the value lies beyond its nearest quartile and show this distance exceeds 1.5 × IQR.

methods.name: Modified box plot on the GDC
methods.summary: Draw the modified box plot; points plotted on their own are outliers. Then confirm with the fence calculation to earn the marks.

misconceptions: Using 1.5 × Q3 as the upper fence instead of Q3 + 1.5 × IQR
Measuring 1.5 × IQR from the median instead of from the nearest quartile
Calling any value that looks far from the rest an outlier without doing the test

skills.name: Compare two distributions in context
examTypes: Compare the distributions of reaction times for the two groups
Using the box plots, state which class performed better. Justify your answer

methods.name: Compare medians and IQRs from the box plots
methods.summary: Make one comment on centre (the median is higher or lower) and one on spread (the IQR is larger or smaller, so less or more consistent), each in the language of the context.

methods.name: Compare means and standard deviations
methods.summary: When summary statistics are given, compare the means for centre and the standard deviations for consistency, again in context.

misconceptions: Comparing only the maximum or minimum values
Saying a larger IQR means a higher average
Quoting the numbers without saying what they mean in context

subtopics.title: Measures of central tendency and dispersion
subtopics.guide: Mean, median and mode; estimating the mean of grouped data and the modal class; IQR, standard deviation and variance (calculated with technology); the effect of adding or multiplying every value by a constant; quartiles of discrete data.

skills.name: Find the mean, median and mode of a data set or a discrete frequency table
examTypes: Find the mean of the data
Write down the median
Write down the mode

methods.name: Mean = Σx ÷ n (or Σfx ÷ Σf)
methods.summary: Add the values (or multiply each value by its frequency and add) and divide by the number of values.

methods.name: Median at position (n + 1)/2
methods.summary: Order the data and count to the (n + 1)/2-th value, averaging the two middle values when n is even; in a frequency table, use running totals to find that position.

methods.name: GDC 1-Var Stats
methods.summary: Enter the values (and a frequency list if needed) and read off x̄ and Med.

misconceptions: Taking the middle value of the unordered list as the median
Giving the position (n + 1)/2 as the median instead of the value in that position
Giving the highest frequency as the mode instead of the value that has that frequency

skills.name: Estimate the mean of grouped data and identify the modal class
examTypes: Write down the modal class
Write down the mid-interval value of the class 20 ≤ t < 30
Find an estimate of the mean

methods.name: Σfx ÷ Σf with mid-interval values
methods.summary: Replace each class by its mid-interval value x, multiply by the frequency f, add, and divide by the total frequency.

methods.name: Midpoints and frequencies in GDC lists
methods.summary: Put the midpoints in L1 and the frequencies in L2, then run 1-Var Stats with L2 as the frequency list.

misconceptions: Dividing by the number of classes instead of the total frequency
Using the upper class boundary instead of the mid-interval value
Calling the estimate the exact mean

skills.name: Use total = mean × n to find a missing value, a missing frequency or a combined mean
examTypes: The mean of 3, 7, k, 10, 12 is 8. Find k
The mean of the data in the frequency table is 2.4. Find p
Find the mean mark of the whole class, boys and girls combined

methods.name: Work with totals
methods.summary: Total = mean × n; subtract the known values to get the missing one, or add the group totals and divide by the combined n for a combined mean.

methods.name: Set Σfx ÷ Σf equal to the mean
methods.summary: With an unknown frequency p, write (Σfx including p) ÷ (Σf including p) = mean and solve the linear equation.

methods.name: Deviations from the mean add to zero
methods.summary: Subtract the mean from each known value; the missing value must balance these deviations so that they all add to zero.

misconceptions: Averaging the two group means for a combined mean when the groups are different sizes
Forgetting that the unknown frequency p also appears in the denominator Σf

skills.name: Find quartiles, range and IQR of discrete data
examTypes: Find the lower quartile and the upper quartile
Find the interquartile range
Write down the range

methods.name: Median of each half
methods.summary: Order the data, split it at the median (leaving the median out when n is odd), and take the median of the lower half and of the upper half.

methods.name: GDC 1-Var Stats
methods.summary: Enter the data and read Q1 and Q3 directly; IQR = Q3 − Q1.

misconceptions: Giving the IQR as Q1 + Q3, or as the pair of quartiles, instead of Q3 − Q1
Finding quartiles from the unordered list

skills.name: Find and interpret the standard deviation and the variance
examTypes: Write down the standard deviation
Find the variance
Interpret the standard deviation in context

methods.name: σx from GDC 1-Var Stats
methods.summary: Enter the data (with a frequency list if given) and read σx; square it for the variance.

methods.name: Square root of the mean squared deviation
methods.summary: For a small set, find each deviation from the mean, square, average and square-root: σ = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ n).

methods.name: Variance is the square of the SD
methods.summary: Convert between the two by squaring or square-rooting; whichever you are given, the other follows at once.

misconceptions: Reading Sx (which divides by n − 1) from the GDC instead of σx
Giving the standard deviation when the variance is asked for, or vice versa
Thinking the standard deviation can be negative because some values are below the mean

skills.name: Find the effect of adding or multiplying every value by a constant
examTypes: Each value is increased by 5. Write down the new mean and the new standard deviation
Each value is multiplied by 3. Find the new variance
Prices are converted using y = 1.2x + 3. Find the new mean and the new IQR

methods.name: Location shifts, spread scales
methods.summary: Adding k adds k to the mean, median, mode and quartiles but leaves the SD, IQR and range unchanged; multiplying by k multiplies all of these by k, and the variance by k².

methods.name: Picture the whole data set moving
methods.summary: Adding k slides the histogram k units along without changing its width; multiplying by k stretches it by factor k, so both the centre and the width scale.

methods.name: Test on a tiny data set
methods.summary: Try the change on a set such as {1, 2, 3} and see what happens to the mean and spread before applying the rule.

misconceptions: Adding a constant changes the standard deviation
Multiplying by k multiplies the variance by k (it is k²)
Adding k to every value adds k to the IQR

threads.echo: Adding 5 to every value translates the whole data set, just like y = f(x) + 5: the centre moves but the spread stays the same; multiplying by 3 is a stretch, so the spread stretches too.

skills.name: Choose and justify the most appropriate average or measure of spread
examTypes: Explain why the median may be a better measure of the centre than the mean
State which measure of spread is least affected by the outlier

methods.name: Check for outliers or skew
methods.summary: If there are outliers or the data are skewed, prefer the median and IQR; for roughly symmetric data without outliers, the mean and SD use all the information.

methods.name: Compare the mean with the median
methods.summary: A mean pulled well away from the median signals extreme values in that direction, so the median better represents a typical value.

misconceptions: The mean is always the best average because it uses every value
The mode is the most useful average for continuous data

subtopics.title: Correlation and the regression line of y on x
subtopics.guide: Scatter diagrams and linear correlation; Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficient r found with technology, and the difference between correlation and causation; lines of best fit by eye through the mean point; the regression line of y on x by technology, its use for prediction, and interpreting a and b in y = ax + b.

skills.name: Describe correlation from a scatter diagram or a value of r
examTypes: Describe the correlation shown in the scatter diagram
Interpret the value of r in context
State whether the data show that x causes y. Justify your answer

methods.name: Read direction and tightness from the scatter
methods.summary: Points rising to the right mean positive correlation, falling means negative; points hugging a straight line mean strong, a loose cloud means weak.

methods.name: Read the sign and size of r
methods.summary: The sign of r gives the direction; |r| close to 1 is strong, around 0.5 is moderate, and close to 0 is weak or no linear correlation.

misconceptions: r = −0.9 shows weak correlation because it is negative
Strong correlation proves that one variable causes the other
r ≈ 0 means there is no relationship at all (there may be a non-linear one)

skills.name: Calculate Pearson's r with technology and match r to a scatter diagram
examTypes: Find the value of r
Which of these is the most likely value of r for the scatter diagram?

methods.name: Linear regression on the GDC
methods.summary: Enter x and y in two lists, run LinReg (ax + b) with diagnostics on, and read r.

methods.name: Estimate from the shape of the scatter
methods.summary: Use the direction for the sign and how tightly the points follow a line for the size, then eliminate options that disagree.

misconceptions: Reporting r² from the GDC as r
Thinking r changes when the x and y lists are swapped (it does not; the regression line does)

skills.name: Find the mean point and use it with lines of best fit
examTypes: Write down the coordinates of the mean point
Draw a line of best fit on the scatter diagram
The regression line y = 1.4x + c passes through the mean point. Find c

methods.name: Find x̄ and ȳ
methods.summary: Average the x-values and the y-values separately to get the mean point (x̄, ȳ).

methods.name: Draw through the mean point by eye
methods.summary: Plot (x̄, ȳ), then draw a straight line through it that follows the trend with roughly equal numbers of points on each side.

methods.name: Substitute the mean point
methods.summary: Every regression line passes through (x̄, ȳ), so substitute it into y = ax + b to find a missing constant.

misconceptions: Forcing the line of best fit through the origin
Thinking the mean point must be one of the data points

skills.name: Find the equation of the regression line of y on x
examTypes: Write down the equation of the regression line of y on x
Find the equation of the regression line in the form y = ax + b

methods.name: LinReg with x as the first list
methods.summary: Enter the independent variable as x and the dependent variable as y, run LinReg (ax + b) and write a and b to 3 significant figures.

methods.name: Gradient plus the mean point
methods.summary: If the gradient a and the means are given, use y − ȳ = a(x − x̄), because the line passes through (x̄, ȳ).

misconceptions: Entering the lists the wrong way round and getting the line of x on y
Rounding a and b too early and losing accuracy in later predictions

skills.name: Use the regression line to predict, and judge whether the prediction is reliable
examTypes: Use the regression line to estimate y when x = 25
Explain why it is not valid to use the line to estimate y when x = 80
Comment on the reliability of your estimate

methods.name: Substitute into the equation
methods.summary: Put the given x into y = ax + b, using the unrounded a and b from the GDC where possible.

methods.name: Read from the drawn line
methods.summary: Go up from x to the line and across to the y-axis for a quick estimate or a check.

methods.name: Interpolation and strength check
methods.summary: A prediction is reliable only if x lies within the range of the data (interpolation) and the correlation is strong; otherwise say which condition fails.

misconceptions: Extrapolating far outside the data range and calling the result reliable
Rearranging the y-on-x line to predict x from a given y
Trusting a prediction when |r| is small

skills.name: Interpret a and b in y = ax + b in context
examTypes: Interpret the meaning of the gradient in context
Explain what the value of b represents
State whether b has a sensible meaning in this context

methods.name: 'For each extra unit of x, y changes by a'
methods.summary: Describe a as the change in y (with units) for every one-unit increase in x, and b as the predicted y when x = 0.

methods.name: Compare two predictions
methods.summary: Predict y at x and at x + 1; the difference is a, which shows what the gradient means in practice.

misconceptions: Interpreting b as the rate of change and a as the starting value
Saying 'a is the gradient' without any reference to the context or units
Treating b as meaningful when x = 0 is far outside the data

threads.echo: The a in y = ax + b is a gradient, the change in y per one unit of x, exactly the m in y = mx + c and the same idea as a derivative dy/dx.

subtopics.title: Basic probability
subtopics.guide: Trials, outcomes, equally likely outcomes, relative frequency, sample space U and events; P(A) = n(A)/n(U) for equally likely outcomes; complementary events A and A′; expected number of occurrences.

skills.name: Find a probability by counting equally likely outcomes
examTypes: Find the probability that the counter is red
A student is chosen at random from the table. Find the probability that they are left-handed
List the sample space and hence find P(A)

methods.name: n(A) ÷ n(U)
methods.summary: Count the outcomes in the event and divide by the total number of equally likely outcomes.

methods.name: List or tabulate the sample space
methods.summary: Write out every equally likely outcome systematically (or read the totals from a table), then pick out those in the event.

misconceptions: Treating outcomes that are not equally likely as if they were (for example, giving each total from 2 to 12 on two dice a probability of 1/11)
Dividing by a row total when the person is chosen from the whole group

skills.name: Use complementary events, including 'at least one'
examTypes: Write down P(A′)
Find the probability that at least one of the three components is faulty

methods.name: P(A′) = 1 − P(A)
methods.summary: A and A′ cover every outcome without overlapping, so their probabilities add to 1.

methods.name: Count the outcomes not in A
methods.summary: Count n(A′) directly and divide by n(U); a useful check on 1 − P(A).

methods.name: At least one = 1 − none
methods.summary: Instead of adding every case with one or more, find the single case 'none' and subtract it from 1.

misconceptions: Finding P(exactly one) when 'at least one' is asked for
P(at least one six in 3 rolls) = 3 × 1/6

skills.name: Estimate a probability from relative frequency
examTypes: Find the relative frequency of rolling a 4
Use the results to estimate the probability that a seed germinates
Explain which of the two estimates is more reliable

methods.name: Frequency ÷ number of trials
methods.summary: The relative frequency of an event is the number of times it happened divided by the number of trials.

methods.name: Read the long-run value
methods.summary: On a graph of relative frequency against number of trials, the value it settles towards is the best estimate of the probability.

misconceptions: The relative frequency from a handful of trials equals the true probability
After several heads in a row, a tail is 'due' (the gambler's fallacy)

skills.name: Find the expected number of occurrences
examTypes: The die is rolled 120 times. Find the expected number of sixes
In a town of 5000 people, find the expected number who are left-handed

methods.name: Expected number = n × P(A)
methods.summary: Multiply the number of trials by the probability of the event on each trial.

methods.name: Push counts through a tree or table
methods.summary: For a two-stage event, pass the n people through the tree as counts (40% of 300 is 120, then 5% of 120 is 6) instead of multiplying probabilities first.

misconceptions: Rounding the expected number to a whole number (it does not have to be one)
Giving the probability instead of the expected number

subtopics.title: Combined events: Venn, tree and sample space diagrams
subtopics.guide: Using Venn diagrams, tree diagrams, sample space diagrams and tables of outcomes to find probabilities, with and without replacement; combined events P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B); mutually exclusive events; conditional probability; independent events with P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B).

skills.name: Find P(A ∪ B) for combined events
examTypes: Find P(A ∪ B)
Find the probability that a student studies at least one of the two subjects
Find the probability that a student studies neither subject

methods.name: Addition rule
methods.summary: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B): add both, then subtract the overlap that was counted twice.

methods.name: Add the Venn diagram regions
methods.summary: Fill in the intersection first, then 'A only' and 'B only', and add the three regions inside the circles.

methods.name: 1 − P(neither)
methods.summary: If the region outside both circles is known, P(A ∪ B) = 1 − P(A′ ∩ B′).

methods.name: Two-way table
methods.summary: Add every cell in row A or column B, counting the shared cell only once, and divide by the grand total.

misconceptions: Adding P(A) + P(B) without subtracting the overlap (double counting)
Multiplying P(A) × P(B) for 'A or B'
Confusing 'A or B' (the union) with 'exactly one of A and B'

skills.name: Complete and use a Venn diagram, including finding an unknown
examTypes: Complete the Venn diagram
Find the value of x
Find P(A ∩ B′)
Find the probability that a student plays exactly one of the sports

methods.name: Fill from the middle outwards
methods.summary: Put the intersection in first, subtract it from each set total to get the 'only' regions, and put whatever is left of n(U) outside both circles.

methods.name: Regions add up to the total
methods.summary: Write each region in terms of x, set their sum equal to n(U) (or to 1), and solve.

methods.name: Set-notation identities
methods.summary: Use identities such as P(A ∩ B′) = P(A) − P(A ∩ B) without drawing every region.

misconceptions: Writing n(A) in the 'A only' region without subtracting the intersection
Forgetting the region outside both circles
Reading A ∩ B′ as 'neither A nor B'

skills.name: Use a tree diagram for multi-stage events, with and without replacement
examTypes: Complete the tree diagram
Find the probability that both sweets are red
Find the probability that the two sweets are different colours
Find the probability that the first six occurs on the third roll

methods.name: Multiply along, add between
methods.summary: Multiply the probabilities along each path to get that outcome, then add the paths that belong to the event.

methods.name: List the ordered outcomes
methods.summary: For small cases, list the ordered outcomes (RR, RB, BR, BB) with their probabilities and add the ones you need.

methods.name: Use the complement paths
methods.summary: When many paths qualify (different colours, at least one), find the few that do not and subtract from 1.

misconceptions: Not reducing the numerator and denominator on the second-stage branches when sampling without replacement
Adding along a path instead of multiplying
Counting only RB for 'different colours' and forgetting BR

threads.echo: Repeating the same branch multiplies by the same probability every time, so P(no six in n rolls) = (5/6)^n shrinks like a geometric sequence with ratio 5/6.
On a three-stage tree the number of paths with exactly two successes is 3C2 = 3, the same nCr that appears in Pascal's triangle and the binomial distribution.

skills.name: Use a sample space diagram or table of outcomes for two combined events
examTypes: Complete the sample space diagram for the sum of the two dice
Find the probability that the sum is 8
Find the probability that the product is greater than 10

methods.name: Fill a grid and count cells
methods.summary: Draw a 6 × 6 (or m × n) grid of outcomes, write the score in each cell, and count the cells that satisfy the event.

methods.name: List the ordered pairs
methods.summary: List the ordered pairs that give the event, e.g. (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2) for a sum of 8, out of 36 in total.

methods.name: Use the symmetry of the grid
methods.summary: Sums on two fair dice are symmetric about 7, so count the easier side: P(sum = 10) = P(sum = 4).

misconceptions: Counting (3,5) and (5,3) as a single outcome
Using 11 or 12 as the total number of outcomes for two dice instead of 36

threads.echo: The two-dice sum grid is symmetric about 7, so P(sum = 4) = P(sum = 10): count one side and reuse it, just as a parabola's axis of symmetry lets you reuse one half.

skills.name: Recognise and use mutually exclusive events
examTypes: State whether A and B are mutually exclusive. Justify your answer
A and B are mutually exclusive. Find P(A ∪ B)

methods.name: Check P(A ∩ B) = 0
methods.summary: Mutually exclusive means P(A ∩ B) = 0, so P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B); test either condition.

methods.name: Non-overlapping Venn circles
methods.summary: Draw the events; if the circles cannot overlap, the events are mutually exclusive.

methods.name: Can both happen at once?
methods.summary: Ask whether one single outcome could be in both events (rolling a 2 and rolling an odd number cannot).

misconceptions: Mutually exclusive means the same as independent
If P(A) + P(B) < 1 then A and B must be mutually exclusive

skills.name: Find a conditional probability from a table, Venn diagram or tree diagram
examTypes: A student is chosen from those who play tennis. Find the probability that they also play football
Given that the first sweet is red, find the probability that the second sweet is red
Use the Venn diagram to find P(A | B)

methods.name: Restrict to the table row or column
methods.summary: The 'given' group becomes the new total: divide the cell count by the total of that row or column only.

methods.name: Restrict to the given circle
methods.summary: Look only inside circle B; the fraction of it that is also in A is n(A ∩ B) ÷ n(B).

methods.name: Read the second-stage branch
methods.summary: On a tree, each second-stage branch probability is already conditional on the first-stage branch it grows from.

methods.name: P(A ∩ B) ÷ P(B)
methods.summary: Divide the probability of both by the probability of the given event.

misconceptions: Dividing by the grand total instead of the total of the 'given' group
Confusing P(A | B) with P(B | A)

skills.name: Use P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B) for independent events
examTypes: A and B are independent. Find P(A ∩ B)
Two machines fail independently with probabilities 0.1 and 0.05. Find the probability that both fail

methods.name: Multiply the probabilities
methods.summary: For independent events, P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B).

methods.name: Tree with identical second-stage branches
methods.summary: Because B does not depend on A, the branches for B are the same after A and after A′; multiply along the path you need.

misconceptions: Adding P(A) + P(B) for 'A and B'
Giving P(A) + P(B) − P(A)P(B), which is P(A ∪ B), when the intersection is asked for
Taking P(A ∩ B) = 0 for independent events (that is mutually exclusive)

subtopics.title: Discrete random variables
subtopics.guide: Discrete random variables and their probability distributions, given as a table or as a function; probabilities add to 1; expected value E(X) = Σ x P(X = x); applications, including fair games, where E(X) = 0 for the player's gain.

skills.name: Use ΣP(X = x) = 1 to find an unknown probability or constant
examTypes: Find the value of k
P(X = x) = k(x + 1) for x = 1, 2, 3, 4. Find k
Show that k = 0.1

methods.name: Set the sum of the probabilities to 1
methods.summary: Add all the probabilities (in terms of k), set the total equal to 1, and solve.

methods.name: Tabulate the function first
methods.summary: When P(X = x) is given as a formula, substitute each x to build the table, then add.

methods.name: Reject invalid solutions
methods.summary: If the equation gives two values of k (for example a quadratic), reject any value that makes a probability negative or greater than 1.

misconceptions: Adding the x-values (or the products x × P) instead of the probabilities
Keeping a value of k that makes one of the probabilities negative

skills.name: Construct a probability distribution from a context
examTypes: Two dice are rolled and X is the larger score. Complete the probability distribution table
Show that P(X = 2) = 3/10
Write down the possible values of X

methods.name: Sample space grid, then tally each value
methods.summary: Write the value of X in every cell of the outcome grid, count how often each value appears, and divide by the total.

methods.name: Tree diagram paths
methods.summary: For sequential draws, add the probabilities of all the paths that give each value of X.

methods.name: Fill the last entry by subtraction
methods.summary: Find the easier probabilities first and get the last one as 1 minus the rest, then check every entry lies between 0 and 1.

misconceptions: Missing a possible value of X, often X = 0
Treating every possible value of X as equally likely

skills.name: Find probabilities such as P(X ≥ a) from a distribution
examTypes: Find P(X > 2)
Find P(1 ≤ X < 4)
Find P(X = 3 | X > 1)

methods.name: Add the relevant entries
methods.summary: Pick out exactly the x-values that satisfy the inequality and add their probabilities.

methods.name: 1 minus the rest
methods.summary: When most values qualify, subtract the probabilities of the few that do not from 1.

misconceptions: Including the endpoint for a strict inequality, e.g. using X = 2 in P(X > 2)
For a conditional probability, not dividing by P(given event)

skills.name: Calculate and interpret E(X)
examTypes: Find E(X)
Interpret E(X) in context
Find the expected total winnings after 50 games

methods.name: E(X) = Σ x P(X = x)
methods.summary: Multiply each value by its probability and add the products.

methods.name: GDC with probabilities as weights
methods.summary: Put the x-values in L1 and the probabilities in L2 and run 1-Var Stats with L2 as the frequency list; x̄ is E(X).

methods.name: Centre of a symmetric distribution
methods.summary: If the probabilities are symmetric about a value, E(X) is that value, with no calculation needed.

misconceptions: Taking the plain average of the x-values and ignoring the probabilities
Believing E(X) must be one of the possible values of X
Dividing Σ x P(X = x) by the number of values

threads.echo: If a probability table is symmetric about a value, E(X) sits right on that line of symmetry, just as the vertex of a parabola sits on its axis.

skills.name: Find unknown probabilities or values given E(X)
examTypes: Given that E(X) = 2.3, find p and q
Given that the expected value is 5, find the value of x

methods.name: ΣP = 1 and Σ x P = E(X)
methods.summary: Write one equation from the probabilities adding to 1 and one from the expected value, then solve simultaneously by elimination or substitution.

methods.name: GDC simultaneous equation solver
methods.summary: Enter the two linear equations in p and q into the solver.

misconceptions: Using only the E(X) equation and forgetting that the probabilities add to 1
Setting Σ x P(X = x) equal to 1 instead of to E(X)

skills.name: Model a game with a random variable and decide whether it is fair
examTypes: Show that the game is not fair
Find the cost to play so that the game is fair
Find the player's expected profit per game

methods.name: Distribution of net gain, set E(X) = 0
methods.summary: Let X be the player's gain (prize minus stake) for each outcome, build its distribution and solve E(X) = 0 for the unknown.

methods.name: Expected winnings equal the cost
methods.summary: Find the expected prize money per game; the game is fair exactly when this equals the cost to play.

misconceptions: Using the prize as the gain without subtracting the stake
Thinking a fair game means winning and losing are equally likely

subtopics.title: The binomial distribution
subtopics.guide: Recognising when X ~ B(n, p) is a suitable model; finding binomial probabilities with technology; mean E(X) = np and variance Var(X) = np(1 − p).

skills.name: Recognise a binomial situation and state n and p
examTypes: Write down the distribution of X
State two assumptions needed for X to follow a binomial distribution
Explain why X cannot be modelled by a binomial distribution

methods.name: Check the four conditions
methods.summary: A fixed number of trials n, each either success or failure, a constant probability p, and independent trials; if all hold, X ~ B(n, p).

methods.name: Look for the condition that breaks
methods.summary: Ask what could change p from trial to trial (drawing without replacement, fatigue, weather) or whether the number of trials is not fixed.

misconceptions: Writing B(p, n) instead of B(n, p)
Using the probability that every trial succeeds, such as 0.5^8, as the parameter p
Treating draws without replacement from a small bag as binomial

skills.name: Find P(X = r) for a binomial distribution
examTypes: Find P(X = 3)
Find the probability that exactly 2 of the 10 seeds germinate
Write down an expression for P(X = 4)

methods.name: Binomial pdf on the GDC
methods.summary: Enter n, p and r into binompdf to get P(X = r) directly.

methods.name: nCr p^r (1 − p)^(n − r)
methods.summary: Choose which r trials succeed (nCr ways), then multiply by p for each success and by 1 − p for each failure.

methods.name: Count the tree paths
methods.summary: For small n, count the paths with exactly r successes; each has the same probability, so multiply one path's probability by the number of paths.

misconceptions: Leaving out the nCr factor and giving just p^r (1 − p)^(n − r)
Swapping the powers: p^(n − r) (1 − p)^r
Using the cumulative function (binomcdf) for 'exactly r'

threads.echo: The nCr in P(X = r) is the same coefficient as in the binomial expansion of (q + p)^n: each term of that expansion is one probability of the distribution.

skills.name: Find cumulative binomial probabilities: at most, at least, between
examTypes: Find P(X ≤ 3)
Find the probability that at least 4 are defective
Find P(2 < X ≤ 6)
Find the probability that at least one seed germinates

methods.name: Binomial cdf on the GDC
methods.summary: binomcdf gives P(X ≤ k); for a range, use the lower and upper bound version or subtract two cumulative values.

methods.name: Complement for 'at least'
methods.summary: P(X ≥ k) = 1 − P(X ≤ k − 1); 'at least one' is 1 − P(X = 0) = 1 − (1 − p)^n.

methods.name: Add the individual probabilities
methods.summary: For a short range, add P(X = r) for each r in the range.

misconceptions: P(X ≥ 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 3) (it should be 1 − P(X ≤ 2))
Using P(X ≤ 5) for P(X < 5)
P(2 < X ≤ 6) = P(X ≤ 6) − P(X ≤ 3) (it should subtract P(X ≤ 2))

threads.echo: All the P(X = r) together are the terms of (q + p)^n = 1^n = 1 from the binomial theorem, which is exactly why the complement 1 − P(X ≤ k − 1) works.
When p = 0.5, nCr = nC(n − r) makes the distribution symmetric, so for B(10, 0.5), P(X ≤ 3) = P(X ≥ 7).

skills.name: Find the mean, variance and standard deviation of a binomial distribution
examTypes: Find E(X)
Find Var(X)
Find the expected number of defective items in a batch of 200

methods.name: E(X) = np and Var(X) = np(1 − p)
methods.summary: Multiply n by p for the mean; multiply by (1 − p) as well for the variance, and square-root that for the standard deviation.

methods.name: Generate the distribution and use 1-Var Stats
methods.summary: Put x = 0 to n in L1 and binompdf(n, p) in L2, then 1-Var Stats with L2 as frequencies gives x̄ = np and σx = √(np(1 − p)) as a check.

misconceptions: Var(X) = np (forgetting the factor 1 − p)
Giving np(1 − p) when the standard deviation is asked for
Rounding E(X) to a whole number

skills.name: Find n or p from given information about a binomial distribution
examTypes: Given E(X) = 6 and Var(X) = 4.2, find n and p
Find the least number of trials so that P(at least one success) > 0.95
Given n = 4 and P(X = 0) = 0.0256, find p

methods.name: Divide Var(X) by E(X) to get 1 − p
methods.summary: np(1 − p) ÷ np = 1 − p, so p follows at once, and then n = E(X) ÷ p.

methods.name: Solve 1 − (1 − p)^n > c with logs
methods.summary: Rearrange to (1 − p)^n < 1 − c, take logs, divide by the negative log (reversing the inequality), and round n up.

methods.name: GDC table of values in n
methods.summary: Tabulate 1 − (1 − p)^n (or binomcdf as a function of n) and read off the first n that satisfies the condition.

misconceptions: Not reversing the inequality when dividing by the log of a number less than 1
Rounding n down instead of up to the next whole number
Taking p = Var(X) ÷ E(X) (that gives 1 − p)

threads.echo: Finding the least n with 0.9^n < 0.05 means undoing an exponent with logarithms, the same move as finding how many years compound interest takes to reach a target.
P(no successes in n trials) = (1 − p)^n is a decaying geometric sequence: every extra trial multiplies the chance of 'none' by the same factor.

skills.name: Build a binomial model from an earlier probability, including conditional and 'kth success' questions
examTypes: Ten bags are chosen at random. Using your answer to (a), find the probability that more than 2 are underweight
Find the probability that the third defective item is the eighth item tested
Given that at least one seed germinates, find the probability that exactly two germinate

methods.name: Find p first, then use B(n, p) on the GDC
methods.summary: Use a normal, tree or table calculation to find p for one trial (kept to full accuracy), then use binompdf or binomcdf with that p.

methods.name: Split off the last trial
methods.summary: For 'the kth success is on trial m', require exactly k − 1 successes in the first m − 1 trials (binomial), then multiply by p for trial m.

methods.name: Conditional probability as a ratio
methods.summary: For a 'given that' question, divide P(both conditions) by P(given condition), simplifying the intersection first (X = 2 and X ≥ 1 is just X = 2).

misconceptions: Using a rounded p from the earlier part and losing accuracy
Finding P(X = 3) in 8 trials for 'the third success is on the eighth trial'
Multiplying the two probabilities in a conditional instead of dividing

subtopics.title: The normal distribution
subtopics.guide: The normal curve and its properties: symmetric about the mean, mean = median = mode, and approximately 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations; sketching and shading diagrams; normal probabilities and inverse normal values found with technology.

skills.name: Use the shape and properties of the normal curve, including the 68-95-99.7 rule
examTypes: Write down the percentage of values within one standard deviation of the mean
Sketch the normal curve and shade the region representing P(X > 40)
Which diagram shows N(50, 4) and N(50, 16) on the same axes?

methods.name: 68-95-99.7 rule
methods.summary: About 68% of values lie within μ ± σ, 95% within μ ± 2σ and 99.7% within μ ± 3σ.

methods.name: Sketch, label μ and shade
methods.summary: Draw a bell curve centred on μ, mark μ ± σ, shade the required region and check whether the answer should be more or less than 0.5.

methods.name: μ moves the curve, σ stretches it
methods.summary: Changing μ slides the curve along without changing its shape; a larger σ makes it wider and lower, because the total area stays 1.

misconceptions: 95% of the values lie within one standard deviation of the mean
A larger σ gives a taller curve
P(X = a) is non-zero for a continuous normal variable

threads.echo: The normal curve is symmetric about μ just as a parabola is symmetric about its axis, so the mean, median and mode all sit on that line.
Changing μ translates the bell curve horizontally and changing σ stretches it, the same translations and stretches you apply to y = f(x).

skills.name: Find normal probabilities from given ones using symmetry, without a calculator
examTypes: Write down P(X < μ)
Find P(X < 7)

methods.name: Mirror the tail
methods.summary: Values equally far either side of μ cut off equal tails: P(X < μ − a) = P(X > μ + a).

methods.name: Total area 1, each half 0.5
methods.summary: Write the required region in terms of known areas, using total area = 1 and P(X < μ) = 0.5.

methods.name: Sketch and shade
methods.summary: Draw the curve, mark μ and the symmetric points, shade the known tails, and read the required region as what is left.

misconceptions: P(7 < X < 13) = 0.2 + 0.2 (adding the tails instead of subtracting them from 1)
Forgetting that P(X < μ) = 0.5
Applying symmetry about 0 instead of about μ

threads.echo: Mirroring a tail across μ halves the work, the same trick as using a parabola's axis or the related angles on the unit circle.
Each probability is an area under the curve, and the areas of separate pieces add up to the whole area of 1.

skills.name: Calculate normal probabilities with technology, including expected numbers
examTypes: Find P(X < 42)
Find the probability that a randomly chosen bag weighs between 495 g and 510 g
In a sample of 400 bags, find the expected number that weigh more than 510 g

methods.name: normalcdf with μ and σ
methods.summary: Enter the lower bound, upper bound, μ and σ, using a very large number such as 10^99 for an open end.

methods.name: Sketch to sense-check
methods.summary: Shade the region on a quick sketch; for example, a tail beyond μ + σ must give less than about 0.16.

methods.name: Standardise, then use Z
methods.summary: Convert the bounds to z = (x − μ)/σ and find the same area under N(0, 1).

misconceptions: Entering the variance instead of the standard deviation into the GDC
Using 0 as the lower bound for P(X < a) when the variable can be negative (for example temperatures)
Leaving an expected number as a probability instead of multiplying by n

threads.echo: A normal probability is the area under the bell curve between two values, the same 'add up thin strips' idea as a definite integral.

skills.name: Find a value of X from a given probability (inverse normal)
examTypes: Find a such that P(X < a) = 0.75
