The top 10% of students receive a distinction. Find the minimum mark for a distinction
Find the upper quartile of X

methods.name: invNorm with the left-tail area
methods.summary: invNorm needs the area to the left; for 'top 10%' enter 0.9 (or use the RIGHT tail setting with 0.1).

methods.name: Find z, then x = μ + zσ
methods.summary: Find z with invNorm on N(0, 1), then move z standard deviations from the mean.

methods.name: Sketch the tail first
methods.summary: Shade the given area to see whether the answer must lie above or below μ before using the GDC.

misconceptions: Entering 0.10 for the top 10% without converting to the left-tail area 0.90
Giving the z-value or the probability as the answer instead of the x-value
Using normalcdf when a value of x is wanted

threads.echo: normalcdf turns a boundary into an area and invNorm undoes it, turning an area back into a boundary, just as f⁻¹ takes an output back to its input.

skills.name: Find an interval symmetric about the mean that contains a given probability
examTypes: Find k such that P(μ − k < X < μ + k) = 0.9
Find the interval, symmetric about the mean, that contains 95% of the masses

methods.name: Split what is left into two equal tails
methods.summary: The 0.1 outside the interval splits into 0.05 in each tail, so μ + k = invNorm(0.95, μ, σ).

methods.name: GDC centre-tail inverse normal
methods.summary: Use the CENTER tail option of invNorm with area 0.9 to get both endpoints at once.

methods.name: Solve normalcdf(μ − k, μ + k, μ, σ) = 0.9
methods.summary: Solve the equation in k numerically with the GDC solver or by intersecting graphs.

misconceptions: Using invNorm(0.9) for the upper endpoint instead of invNorm(0.95)
Giving the endpoint μ + k when k is asked for

threads.echo: A central interval leaves two equal tails, so the curve's symmetry about μ turns one unknown boundary into a mirror-image pair.

subtopics.title: The regression line of x on y
subtopics.guide: Finding the regression line of x on y with technology and using it to predict x from a given y; knowing that y on x predicts y from x and x on y predicts x from y, and that both lines pass through the mean point.

skills.name: Find the regression line of x on y
examTypes: Find the equation of the regression line of x on y
Write down the regression line of x on y in the form x = cy + d

methods.name: LinReg with the lists swapped
methods.summary: Run LinReg with the y-data as the first list and the x-data as the second, then write the result as x = cy + d.

methods.name: Gradient plus the mean point
methods.summary: If the gradient c is given, use x − x̄ = c(y − ȳ), because the line passes through (x̄, ȳ).

misconceptions: Rearranging the y-on-x line to make x the subject (it is a different line unless r = ±1)
Copying the GDC output as y = ax + b without swapping the variables back

skills.name: Choose the correct regression line for a prediction
examTypes: Explain which regression line should be used to estimate x when y = 30
State why the line of y on x should not be used here

methods.name: The variable you predict is the subject
methods.summary: Identify which variable is given and which is to be estimated, and use the line that has the estimated variable as its subject (x on y to estimate x).

misconceptions: The y-on-x line can always be used if you rearrange it
Choosing a line by which variable is on the horizontal axis, regardless of which one is being predicted

skills.name: Predict x from y with the x-on-y line and judge reliability
examTypes: Use the appropriate regression line to estimate the age of a tree that is 12 m tall
Comment on the validity of this estimate

methods.name: Substitute y into x = cy + d
methods.summary: Put the given y-value straight into the x-on-y equation.

methods.name: Interpolation and strength check
methods.summary: The estimate is reliable only if y lies within the range of the y-data and the correlation is strong.

misconceptions: Substituting the y-value into the y-on-x line and solving for x
Calling an extrapolated estimate reliable because r is strong

skills.name: Use the fact that both regression lines pass through the mean point
examTypes: The regression lines are y = 0.8x + 2 and x = 1.1y − 1. Find x̄ and ȳ
Write down the coordinates of the point where the two regression lines meet
Given that x̄ = 12, use the regression line of y on x to find ȳ

methods.name: Solve the two lines simultaneously
methods.summary: Substitute one equation into the other; the solution (x, y) is the mean point (x̄, ȳ).

methods.name: Graph both lines and find the intersection
methods.summary: Rearrange x = cy + d to y = (x − d)/c, graph both lines and use the intersect tool.

methods.name: Substitute one known mean
methods.summary: If x̄ is known, substitute it into either regression line to get ȳ.

misconceptions: Thinking the two regression lines are parallel or perpendicular
Substituting x̄ into the x-on-y equation as if it were a y-value

threads.echo: The mean point is where the two regression lines cross, so you can find it by solving the pair simultaneously or by graphing both and reading off the intersection.

subtopics.title: Conditional probability and independence (formal)
subtopics.guide: Formal definition and use of P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B); for independent events P(A | B) = P(A) = P(A | B′); testing whether events are independent.

skills.name: Calculate P(A | B) using the formula
examTypes: Find P(A | B)
Find P(B | A′)
Find the probability that a student studies Mathematics, given that they study Biology

methods.name: P(A ∩ B) ÷ P(B)
methods.summary: Find the probability of both happening and divide by the probability of the given event.

methods.name: Restrict to circle B on a Venn diagram
methods.summary: Fill in the Venn diagram; within circle B, the share that is also in A is the answer.

methods.name: Imagine 100 people
methods.summary: Turn the probabilities into counts out of 100, then divide the count in both by the count in the given group.

misconceptions: Dividing by P(A) instead of P(B)
Giving P(A ∩ B) as the answer without dividing
Computing P(A | B) as P(A) × P(B)

skills.name: Find a 'reversed' conditional probability from a tree diagram
examTypes: Given that the test result is positive, find the probability that the person has the disease
Given that the second ball is red, find the probability that the first ball was red

methods.name: Wanted path over all paths giving the condition
methods.summary: On the tree, add every path that ends in the given event for the denominator; the path that is also in the wanted event is the numerator.

methods.name: Formula, with P(B) found by adding branches
methods.summary: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) ÷ P(B), where P(B) = P(A ∩ B) + P(A′ ∩ B) is read from the tree.

methods.name: Imagine 1000 people
methods.summary: Push 1000 people through the tree to get counts, then divide the count of 'A and B' by the count of 'B'.

misconceptions: Reading P(B | A) off a branch and giving it as P(A | B)
Using only one path for P(B) in the denominator

skills.name: Rearrange the conditional formula to find P(A ∩ B) or another unknown
examTypes: Given P(A | B) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.5, find P(A ∩ B)
Hence find P(A ∪ B)
Given P(A ∩ B) and P(A | B), find P(B)

methods.name: P(A ∩ B) = P(A | B) × P(B)
methods.summary: Rearrange the definition to get the intersection, then use it in the addition rule or a Venn diagram.

methods.name: Multiply along the tree branch
methods.summary: Draw B first and then A given B on a tree; the path probability P(B) × P(A | B) is P(A ∩ B).

methods.name: Fill a Venn diagram
methods.summary: Place P(A ∩ B) in the middle, then complete the other regions to read off whatever else is asked.

misconceptions: P(A ∩ B) = P(A | B) ÷ P(B)
Treating P(A | B) as if it were P(A ∩ B)

skills.name: Determine whether two events are independent, with justification
examTypes: Determine whether A and B are independent. Justify your answer
Show that A and B are not independent
Are the events 'studies Mathematics' and 'studies Biology' independent? Justify

methods.name: Compare P(A ∩ B) with P(A)P(B)
methods.summary: A and B are independent exactly when P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B); show both numbers.

methods.name: Compare P(A | B) with P(A)
methods.summary: Independent means knowing B does not change the probability of A: P(A | B) = P(A), equivalently P(A | B) = P(A | B′).

methods.name: Compare proportions across the rows of a table
methods.summary: In a two-way table, if the proportion in A is the same in row B and in row B′, the events are independent.

misconceptions: Events that overlap cannot be independent
Mutually exclusive events (with non-zero probabilities) are independent
Concluding 'not independent' without quoting both numbers being compared

skills.name: Use independence to find an unknown probability
examTypes: A and B are independent, P(A) = 0.3 and P(A ∪ B) = 0.65. Find P(B)
Given that A and B are independent, find P(A′ ∩ B)

methods.name: Substitute P(A)P(B) into the addition rule
methods.summary: Write P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A)P(B) with P(B) = x and solve the linear equation.

methods.name: Use independence of the complements
methods.summary: If A and B are independent then so are A′ and B′, so 1 − P(A ∪ B) = P(A′)P(B′); solve for P(B′).

methods.name: Venn diagram in terms of x
methods.summary: Let P(B) = x, put 0.3x in the intersection, and set the total inside the circles equal to P(A ∪ B).

misconceptions: Using P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) as if the events were mutually exclusive
Setting P(A ∩ B) = 0 because the events are independent

skills.name: Find conditional probabilities involving normal, binomial or discrete distributions
examTypes: Given that a fish is longer than 30 cm, find the probability that it is longer than 35 cm
Given that at least one seed germinates, find the probability that exactly two germinate
Find P(X > 40 | X > 30)

methods.name: Simplify the intersection, then divide
methods.summary: Work out the overlap of the two conditions (X > 35 and X > 30 is just X > 35), then divide its probability by P(given).

methods.name: Shade both regions on a sketch
methods.summary: Shade the 'given' region and the part of it that is also wanted; the answer is the smaller area as a fraction of the larger.

methods.name: GDC for numerator and denominator
methods.summary: Use normalcdf or binomcdf for each probability separately, keeping full accuracy before dividing.

misconceptions: Multiplying P(X > 35) × P(X > 30) for the numerator
Giving P(30 < X < 35) as the answer
Forgetting to divide by P(given)

threads.echo: A conditional normal probability is a ratio of two areas under the curve: the wanted area as a fraction of the 'given' area.

subtopics.title: Standardisation and inverse normal with unknown parameters
subtopics.guide: Standardising normal variables with z = (x − μ)/σ, where z is the number of standard deviations from the mean; using z-values from technology to find an unknown mean and/or standard deviation.

skills.name: Calculate and interpret a z-value, and convert back to x
examTypes: Find the z-value for x = 74
Interpret z = −1.5 in context
A value has z = 2.1. Find the value of x

methods.name: z = (x − μ)/σ
methods.summary: Subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation; reverse with x = μ + zσ.

methods.name: Count standard deviations along the axis
methods.summary: Mark μ and steps of σ on the axis; z is how many steps x is from μ, negative if x is below the mean.

misconceptions: Dividing by the variance instead of the standard deviation
Writing (μ − x)/σ and getting the sign wrong
Thinking a negative z-value is impossible

threads.echo: z = (x − μ)/σ translates by −μ and then stretches by 1/σ, turning any normal curve into N(0, 1), the same translate-then-stretch you apply to graphs of f(x).

skills.name: Compare values from different normal distributions using z
examTypes: Determine in which test Ana performed better relative to her classmates. Justify your answer
Justify which athlete's time was more exceptional

methods.name: Compare the z-values
methods.summary: Standardise each value within its own distribution; the larger z is the relatively better performance (unless lower is better, as for race times).

methods.name: Compare the proportion below each value
methods.summary: Find P(X < x) in each distribution with normalcdf; the higher proportion beaten is the better relative performance.

misconceptions: Comparing the raw scores instead of the standardised values
Comparing x − μ without dividing by σ
Forgetting that for times a more negative z is better

skills.name: Rewrite a probability for X as an equivalent probability for Z
examTypes: Show that P(X < 40) = P(Z < −1.25)
Write down the probability for Z equivalent to P(X > 70)
Given P(Z < z) = 0.8, find z

methods.name: Standardise each bound
methods.summary: Replace each x in the inequality by (x − μ)/σ; the inequality keeps its direction because σ > 0.

methods.name: Check both sides on the GDC
methods.summary: Compute normalcdf for X with μ and σ and for Z with 0 and 1; equal areas confirm the conversion.

misconceptions: Reversing the inequality sign when standardising
Standardising with the variance instead of the standard deviation

threads.echo: Standardising slides and squashes the bell curve into N(0, 1) but leaves the shaded area, the probability, unchanged, just as a translated graph keeps its shape.

skills.name: Find an unknown mean or standard deviation from one probability
examTypes: Given that P(X < 30) = 0.2 and μ = 35, find σ
15% of bags weigh more than 510 g and σ = 6 g. Find μ

methods.name: invNorm on Z, then solve z = (x − μ)/σ
methods.summary: Find z = invNorm(left-tail area, 0, 1), substitute x and the known parameter into z = (x − μ)/σ, and solve for the unknown.

methods.name: Solve normalcdf = p for the unknown
methods.summary: Use the GDC solver, or graph y = normalcdf(−10^99, 30, 35, s) against y = 0.2, to find the unknown parameter numerically.

misconceptions: Trying invNorm(0.2, 35, σ) when σ is the unknown
Using the upper-tail area in invNorm without converting, so z has the wrong sign
Getting a negative σ and not noticing the sign error

threads.echo: invNorm undoes the area to recover z, then you undo the standardisation with x = μ + zσ to reach the unknown: two inverses in a row.
You can solve for σ algebraically from z = (x − μ)/σ, or graph the probability as a function of σ and intersect it with y = 0.2: two routes, same answer.

skills.name: Find both μ and σ from two probabilities
examTypes: Given that P(X < 20) = 0.1 and P(X > 50) = 0.2, find μ and σ
Show that μ + 0.842σ = 50
Given that P(X < 12) = P(X > 28) = 0.15, write down μ

methods.name: Two equations x = μ + zσ, solved simultaneously
methods.summary: Find each z with invNorm, write μ + z₁σ = x₁ and μ + z₂σ = x₂, then subtract to eliminate μ.

methods.name: GDC simultaneous equation solver
methods.summary: Enter the two linear equations in μ and σ into the solver.

methods.name: Equal tails put μ in the middle
methods.summary: If P(X < a) = P(X > b), the mean is exactly (a + b)/2, which leaves only σ to find.

misconceptions: Giving both conditions a positive z when one value is below the mean
Writing (x − μ)/σ = probability instead of = z
Rounding the z-values to 1 decimal place and losing accuracy

threads.echo: If P(X < a) = P(X > b), the mean sits exactly halfway at (a + b)/2, just like the axis of symmetry halfway between a parabola's two roots.
Each condition is a straight line in μ and σ, so the answer is where the two lines cross, found by elimination or with a GDC solver.

subtopics.title: Limits and the derivative as a rate of change
subtopics.guide: An informal idea of a limit, estimated from a table or a graph. The derivative is the gradient function of a curve (the limiting gradient of chords) and a rate of change, written dy/dx, f′(x), ds/dt and so on.

skills.name: Estimate a limit from a table, a graph or simple algebra
examTypes: Use the table to estimate the value of lim (x→2) f(x)
Use the graph to write down lim (x→∞) f(x)
Find lim (x→3) (x² − 9)/(x − 3)

methods.name: Read the trend in a table of values
methods.summary: Look at f(x) as x gets closer to a from both sides and see which value the outputs settle towards.

methods.name: Trace the graph towards x = a
methods.summary: Follow the curve towards x = a (or out to large x) and read the height it approaches, even if there is a hole or an asymptote there.

methods.name: Generate the table on the GDC
methods.summary: Use the GDC table with x-values such as 1.9, 1.99, 2.01, 2.001 to produce the values yourself.

methods.name: Factorise and cancel, then substitute
methods.summary: Cancel the common factor that causes 0/0 (or divide through by the highest power of x for limits at infinity), then substitute.

misconceptions: The limit does not exist because f(a) itself is undefined (0/0)
The limit always equals f(a), even when the graph has a hole or jump at x = a
Checking values on one side of x = a only

skills.name: Find the gradient of a curve as the limit of chord gradients
examTypes: Find the gradient of the chord PQ, where Q has x-coordinate 1 + h
Complete the table of chord gradients and hence estimate the gradient of the tangent at P
Write down the limit of the chord gradient as h → 0

methods.name: Shrink the chord numerically
methods.summary: Compute rise over run for chords with Q ever closer to P (h = 0.1, 0.01, 0.001) and spot the value the gradients approach.

methods.name: Simplify (f(a + h) − f(a))/h
methods.summary: Expand the numerator, cancel the factor h, then let h → 0.

methods.name: Confirm with the GDC dy/dx
methods.summary: Use the GDC numerical derivative at x = a to confirm the limiting value.

methods.name: Draw the tangent and measure it
methods.summary: Rule the tangent at P on the graph and divide its rise by its run.

misconceptions: Putting h = 0 before cancelling, giving 0/0
Taking one chord gradient as the exact gradient of the tangent
Computing run over rise (Δx/Δy)

threads.echo: The gradient of a straight line was rise over run; the derivative is the same rise over run, taken over a chord so short it becomes the tangent.
Each chord is a small movement, h across and f(a + h) − f(a) up, and its gradient is the up part divided by the across part, just like a gradient from a movement vector.

skills.name: Interpret a derivative as a rate of change in context, with units and sign
examTypes: Interpret the meaning of dV/dt = −3 in context
Write down the units of dP/dt
Explain what f′(5) = 12 represents
Write 'the area is increasing at 4 cm² per second' using derivative notation

methods.name: Read dy/dx as 'units of y per unit of x'
methods.summary: State how fast y changes per unit of x at that instant, with units such as cm² per second.

methods.name: Use the sign for direction
methods.summary: Positive means y increases as x increases, negative means it decreases; then quote the size of the rate.

methods.name: Picture the tangent
methods.summary: Imagine the tangent to the y-against-x graph at that point; its gradient is the rate.

misconceptions: Reading f′(5) = 12 as 'the value of f at 5 is 12'
Ignoring the negative sign, so dV/dt = −3 is read as increasing by 3
Giving the units of y only (cm²) instead of y per unit x (cm² per second)

threads.echo: Like the slope b in a regression line y = a + bx (change in y per unit of x), a derivative says how much the output changes per unit of input, but at a single instant.

skills.name: Estimate the gradient at a point from a graph or with technology
examTypes: Use the graph to estimate the gradient of the curve at x = 2
Use your GDC to find the gradient of the curve at x = 1.5
State whether the gradient at A is greater than the gradient at B

methods.name: Draw a tangent and use rise over run
methods.summary: Rule a tangent touching the curve at the point and divide its rise by its run between two well-separated grid points.

methods.name: Use a short chord either side
methods.summary: Join two points just either side of x = a and use that chord's gradient as the estimate.

methods.name: GDC dy/dx at the point
methods.summary: Use the graph's dy/dx (or nDeriv) feature at x = a.

methods.name: Compare steepness and direction
methods.summary: For comparisons, decide whether each tangent slopes up or down and which is steeper.

misconceptions: Using the y-value at the point as the gradient
Using the chord from the origin to the point instead of the tangent
Thinking a steeper downhill tangent has a larger gradient

threads.echo: The gradient of a line becomes the gradient of the tangent for a curve: the same rise over run, now changing from point to point.

subtopics.title: Increasing and decreasing functions
subtopics.guide: Increasing and decreasing functions, identified from the sign of the derivative. Graphical interpretation of f′(x) > 0, f′(x) = 0 and f′(x) < 0.

skills.name: Find the intervals on which f is increasing or decreasing
examTypes: Find the values of x for which f is decreasing
Find the interval on which f is increasing
Hence write down the set of values of x for which f′(x) > 0

methods.name: Solve f′(x) > 0 or f′(x) < 0
methods.summary: Differentiate, solve f′(x) = 0 for the critical values, then use the shape of f′ (e.g. its parabola) to decide where it is positive or negative.

methods.name: Sign table for f′
methods.summary: Mark the roots of f′ on a number line and test one x-value in each interval.

methods.name: Read the graph of f′
methods.summary: Plot or sketch y = f′(x); f increases where that graph is above the x-axis and decreases where it is below.

methods.name: Find turning points of f on the GDC
methods.summary: Graph f, find its maximum and minimum points, and read the intervals between them.

methods.name: Use the vertex of a quadratic
methods.summary: For f(x) = ax² + bx + c, f changes direction only at x = −b/(2a); with a > 0 it decreases to the left and increases to the right.

misconceptions: Giving an interval of y-values rather than x-values
Solving f(x) < 0 (below the axis) instead of f′(x) < 0 (going down)
Getting the inequality the wrong way round when the leading coefficient of f′ is negative

threads.echo: The vertex of a parabola is exactly where it switches from decreasing to increasing, which is where f′(x) = 0.
Solving f′(x) > 0 is a quadratic inequality like in SL2.7: solve it by algebra or read it from where the graph of f′ sits above the x-axis.

skills.name: Read the sign of f′(x) from the graph of f
examTypes: On the graph, indicate the intervals where f′(x) < 0
Write down the value of f′(x) at the point A
Which statement about f′ is true at x = 2?

methods.name: Walk along the curve left to right
methods.summary: Uphill means f′ > 0, flat at a turning point means f′ = 0, downhill means f′ < 0.

methods.name: Lay a tangent at the point
methods.summary: Hold a ruler as a tangent at the point and see whether it slopes up, slopes down or is horizontal.

methods.name: Build a sign diagram
methods.summary: Mark the turning points on the x-axis and write +, 0 or − under each stretch of the curve.

misconceptions: Confusing f′(x) < 0 with f(x) < 0 (being below the axis)
Thinking f′ = 0 at the x-intercepts rather than at the turning points
Thinking f′(x) = 0 means the function value is zero

threads.echo: Uphill, flat and downhill are the positive, zero and negative gradients of a straight line, now read point by point along a curve.

skills.name: Decide whether f is increasing or decreasing at a given point
examTypes: Determine whether f is increasing or decreasing at x = 1. Justify your answer
Is the temperature rising or falling at t = 3? Give a reason

methods.name: Evaluate f′(a) and use its sign
methods.summary: Find f′(a) and write 'increasing because f′(a) > 0' (or decreasing because f′(a) < 0).

methods.name: GDC numerical derivative
methods.summary: Find dy/dx at x = a on the GDC and interpret its sign.

methods.name: Compare nearby values
methods.summary: Compare f(a − 0.01) and f(a + 0.01); if the output rises, f is increasing there.

misconceptions: Using the sign of f(a) instead of f′(a)
Justifying with 'the graph goes up' without referring to the derivative

skills.name: Show that a function is increasing (or decreasing) for all x in its domain
examTypes: Show that f is increasing for all x
Show that f′(x) > 0 for x > 0, and hence explain why f has an inverse
Justify that g is a decreasing function

methods.name: Complete the square on f′(x)
methods.summary: Write f′(x) = a(x − h)² + k with a > 0 and k > 0, so f′(x) ≥ k > 0 for every x.

methods.name: Discriminant of f′ is negative
methods.summary: For a quadratic f′ with positive leading coefficient, show b² − 4ac < 0, so f′ never reaches zero and stays positive.

methods.name: Argue term by term
methods.summary: Show f′ is a sum of terms that cannot be negative, e.g. 3x² + eˣ + 1 > 0 because x² ≥ 0 and eˣ > 0.

methods.name: Graph f′ and find its minimum
methods.summary: On P2, plot y = f′(x) and show that its lowest point is above the x-axis.

misconceptions: Checking f′ at a few points and concluding it is positive everywhere
Showing f(x) > 0 instead of f′(x) > 0
Claiming x² > 0 for all x (it equals 0 at x = 0)

threads.echo: The 'no real roots' discriminant test from quadratics returns: if f′ never hits zero, f has no turning points at all.
Completing the square on f′(x) is the same move that revealed the vertex of a parabola; here it reveals that f′ can never be negative.
A function that is always increasing is one-to-one, so it passes the horizontal line test and has an inverse.

skills.name: Find a parameter so that f is increasing (or decreasing) everywhere
examTypes: f(x) = x³ + kx² + 3x. Find the values of k for which f is increasing for all x
Find the range of values of p for which f′(x) ≥ 0 for all x

methods.name: Require discriminant of f′ ≤ 0
methods.summary: Differentiate, then require the quadratic f′(x) (positive leading coefficient) to have b² − 4ac ≤ 0, and solve the inequality in k.

methods.name: Require the minimum of f′ to be ≥ 0
methods.summary: Complete the square on f′(x) and require its minimum value to be at least zero.

methods.name: Explore k on the GDC
methods.summary: Graph f′ for several values of k (or use a slider) to find the boundary where the parabola just touches the x-axis, then confirm by algebra.

misconceptions: Using the discriminant of f(x) instead of f′(x)
Using b² − 4ac > 0 (two roots) instead of ≤ 0
Solving k² ≤ 9 as k ≤ 3 only, losing −3 ≤ k

threads.echo: f′ just touching the x-axis is the discriminant = 0 tangency case from SL2.7: the boundary between 'always increasing' and 'has turning points'.

subtopics.title: Differentiating ax^n (n ∈ ℤ)
subtopics.guide: The derivative of f(x) = axⁿ is f′(x) = anxⁿ⁻¹ for integer n, including negative powers. Derivatives of sums of such terms, and gradients of curves at given points.

skills.name: Differentiate axⁿ and sums of such terms
examTypes: Find f′(x)
Write down dy/dx
Differentiate 4x³ − 5x + 7

methods.name: Power rule term by term
methods.summary: Multiply each term by its power and reduce the power by one; constant terms differentiate to 0.

misconceptions: Reducing the coefficient instead of multiplying: d/dx(5x³) = 4x² rather than 15x²
Raising the power: d/dx(axⁿ) = anxⁿ⁺¹
Leaving a constant unchanged instead of making it 0, or writing d/dx(7x) = 7x

threads.echo: Adding a constant translates the graph up or down, which changes no gradients at all, so the derivative of a constant is 0.

skills.name: Rewrite reciprocals and fractions as powers of x, then differentiate
examTypes: Differentiate f(x) = 3/x² + 2x
Find dy/dx for y = (x² + 4)/x
Find f′(x) where f(x) = (x + 2)(x − 3)

methods.name: Write each term as axⁿ
methods.summary: Rewrite 3/x² as 3x⁻², apply the power rule (−2 becomes −3), and rewrite with positive powers if asked.

methods.name: Split the fraction first
methods.summary: Divide every term of the numerator by the denominator, e.g. (x² + 4)/x = x + 4x⁻¹, then differentiate.

methods.name: Expand brackets first
methods.summary: Multiply out to a sum of powers of x, then differentiate term by term.

methods.name: Quotient rule
methods.summary: Treat the fraction as u/v and use the quotient rule from SL5.6; valid but slower.

misconceptions: Differentiating the denominator: d/dx(1/x²) = 1/(2x)
Getting the new power wrong: x⁻² → −2x⁻¹ instead of −2x⁻³
Dividing only the first term of the numerator by x

threads.echo: 3/x² and 3x⁻² are the same expression, as with log laws and quadratic forms, but only the power form lets the power rule work.

skills.name: Find the gradient of a curve at a given point
examTypes: Find the gradient of the curve at x = 2
Find f′(−1)
Find the rate of change of y with respect to x when x = 3

methods.name: Differentiate, then substitute
methods.summary: Find f′(x), then substitute x = a.

methods.name: GDC dy/dx at the point
methods.summary: On P2, use the GDC's dy/dx (numerical derivative) at x = a directly.

methods.name: Very short chord as a check
methods.summary: Estimate with (f(a + 0.001) − f(a))/0.001 to check your exact answer.

misconceptions: Substituting into f(x) instead of f′(x)
Substituting first and then differentiating the number f(a), giving 0
Sign slips with negatives, e.g. 3(−2)² evaluated as −12

threads.echo: f′(a) is a single number, the gradient of the tangent at x = a, just as m is the gradient of a straight line.

skills.name: Find the point(s) where a curve has a given gradient
examTypes: Find the x-coordinates of the points where the gradient of the curve is 4
Find the coordinates of the point on the curve where the gradient is −2
The gradient of the curve at P is 7. Find the coordinates of P

methods.name: Solve f′(x) = k
methods.summary: Set the derivative equal to the given gradient, solve for x, then substitute into f for y.

methods.name: Intersect y = f′(x) with y = k
methods.summary: Graph the derivative and the horizontal line y = k on the GDC and find the intersections.

methods.name: Scan for parallel tangents
methods.summary: Look along y = f(x) for tangents parallel to a line of gradient k, useful for counting how many such points exist.

misconceptions: Solving f(x) = k instead of f′(x) = k
Finding x but not substituting into f(x) for the y-coordinate
Substituting x into f′(x) to get the y-coordinate

threads.echo: f′(x) = k is the intersection of y = f′(x) with the horizontal line y = k, solvable by algebra or by GDC.

skills.name: Find unknown coefficients from gradient and point conditions
examTypes: f(x) = ax³ + bx, f′(1) = 5 and f(1) = 3. Find a and b
The gradient of y = kx² − 3x at x = 2 is 9. Find k

methods.name: Turn each condition into an equation
methods.summary: Differentiate with the unknowns in place, write one equation per condition, and solve (simultaneously if needed).

methods.name: Solve the system on the GDC
methods.summary: Form the equations by hand, then solve the linear system with the GDC's simultaneous-equation solver.

misconceptions: Using the gradient condition in f(x) instead of f′(x)
Treating k as a variable and differentiating it

subtopics.title: Tangents and normals
subtopics.guide: Equations of the tangent and the normal to a curve at a given point. The tangent's gradient is f′(a) and the normal's is the negative reciprocal.

skills.name: Find the equation of the tangent at a given point
examTypes: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve at x = 2
Give your answer in the form y = mx + c
Find the equation of the tangent at the point where the curve crosses the y-axis

methods.name: Point-gradient form
methods.summary: Find the point (a, f(a)) and the gradient m = f′(a), then use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).

methods.name: Substitute into y = mx + c
methods.summary: Put m, x = a and y = f(a) into y = mx + c and solve for c.

methods.name: GDC draw-tangent feature
methods.summary: Use the GDC's tangent tool at x = a, which displays the tangent's equation.

misconceptions: Using the expression f′(x) as the gradient instead of the number f′(a)
Using f′(a) as the y-coordinate of the point
Using the normal's gradient with the tangent's point (mixing the two lines)

threads.echo: The tangent is the straight line with the curve's instantaneous gradient, so close to the point it is the best straight-line version of the curve.

skills.name: Find the equation of the normal at a given point
examTypes: Find the equation of the normal to the curve at x = 1
Give your answer in the form ax + by + d = 0
The normal at P meets the x-axis at Q. Find the coordinates of Q

methods.name: Negative reciprocal, then point-gradient form
methods.summary: Find m = f′(a), use −1/m for the normal, then y − f(a) = (−1/m)(x − a).

methods.name: Write (x − a) + m(y − f(a)) = 0 directly
methods.summary: This form of the normal avoids fractions, lands in ax + by + d = 0 form, and still works when m = 0 (giving x = a).

methods.name: GDC for the tangent gradient
methods.summary: Get f′(a) from the GDC's dy/dx, then form the normal by hand.

misconceptions: Using −m or 1/m instead of −1/m for the normal's gradient
Reusing the tangent's y-intercept c in the normal's equation
Trying to compute −1/0 when the tangent is horizontal, instead of writing the vertical normal x = a

skills.name: Use a given tangent line to read off f(a) and f′(a)
examTypes: The line y = 3x − 2 is tangent to the graph of f at x = 1. Write down f′(1)
Find f(1)
Hence find the gradient of the normal at this point

methods.name: Gradient of the tangent is f′(a)
methods.summary: Read m from y = mx + c; that number is f′(a).

methods.name: The tangent touches the curve at x = a
methods.summary: Substitute x = a into the tangent: its y-value equals f(a).

methods.name: Read the diagram
methods.summary: From a diagram, read the point of contact and compute the tangent's rise over run.

misconceptions: Taking f(a) to be the tangent's y-intercept c
Thinking f′(a) is the y-coordinate of the point of contact

skills.name: Find where the tangent (or normal) is parallel or perpendicular to a given line
examTypes: Find the point on the curve at which the tangent is parallel to y = 2x + 1
Find the coordinates of the points where the tangent is horizontal
Find the x-coordinate of the point where the normal is parallel to x + 4y = 3

methods.name: Turn the condition into a gradient
methods.summary: Parallel means equal gradients, perpendicular means the negative reciprocal; set f′(x) equal to the required value and solve.

methods.name: Intersect f′ with the target gradient
methods.summary: Plot y = f′(x) and y = k on the GDC; the intersections give the x-values.

methods.name: Convert a normal condition first
methods.summary: If the normal must have gradient n, the tangent must have gradient −1/n, so only f′ is needed.

misconceptions: Rearranging x + 4y = 3 and taking the gradient as 1/4 instead of −1/4
Setting the required normal gradient equal to f′(x) directly
Stopping at the x-value when the coordinates are asked for

skills.name: Use a tangent or normal to find intercepts, an area, or a second intersection
examTypes: The tangent at P meets the x-axis at A and the y-axis at B. Find the area of triangle OAB
The tangent at P meets the curve again at Q. Find the coordinates of Q
Find the coordinates of the point where the normal at P meets the curve again

methods.name: Put x = 0 and y = 0 in the tangent
methods.summary: Get both intercepts from the line's equation, then use ½ × base × height for the triangle.

methods.name: Use the double root at the point of contact
methods.summary: Setting curve = tangent gives (x − a)² as a factor, so for a cubic the remaining root comes from comparing coefficients.

methods.name: GDC intersect
methods.summary: Graph the curve and the line and use the intersect tool.

misconceptions: Finding the intercepts of the curve instead of the tangent
Not using the double root, so the cubic looks unsolvable without a calculator
Using a negative intercept as a negative length in the triangle area

threads.echo: Where a tangent meets the curve again is just the intersection of two graphs: solve curve = line by algebra or read it from the GDC.

skills.name: Find an unknown constant given that a line is tangent to a curve
examTypes: The line y = 4x + k is a tangent to the curve y = x² + 1. Find k
The tangent to the curve at x = a passes through the origin. Find a
Find the value of m for which the line y = mx is tangent to y = eˣ

methods.name: Match gradients to find the point of contact
methods.summary: Set f′(x) equal to the line's gradient to find the point of contact, then substitute into both equations to find the constant.

methods.name: Discriminant = 0
methods.summary: Equate line and curve to get a quadratic; a tangent meets the curve exactly once there, so set b² − 4ac = 0.

methods.name: Tangent at a general point
methods.summary: Write the tangent at x = a as y − f(a) = f′(a)(x − a) and impose that it passes through the given point.

methods.name: Vary the constant on the GDC
methods.summary: Change the constant until the line just touches the curve, then confirm algebraically.

misconceptions: Setting the line equal to f′(x) instead of f(x)
Using b² − 4ac > 0 instead of = 0
Matching gradients but forgetting the line must also pass through the point on the curve

threads.echo: Discriminant = 0 meant a quadratic has exactly one root; here it means the line touches the curve instead of cutting through it.
Tangency is a special intersection of two graphs: the equation line = curve has a repeated root.

subtopics.title: Introduction to integration
subtopics.guide: Integration as anti-differentiation of sums of axⁿ (n ∈ ℤ, n ≠ −1), with a boundary condition to find the constant. Definite integrals using technology, and the area between a curve and the x-axis where f(x) > 0.

skills.name: Anti-differentiate sums of axⁿ (n ∈ ℤ, n ≠ −1)
examTypes: Find ∫ (6x² − 4x + 1) dx
Find ∫ 3/x² dx
Find ∫ (x + 2)(x − 1) dx

methods.name: Reverse power rule
methods.summary: Raise each power by one, divide by the new power, and add + C.

methods.name: Guess, differentiate, adjust
methods.summary: Write a candidate antiderivative, differentiate it, and adjust the coefficient until you get back the integrand.

methods.name: Expand or rewrite first
methods.summary: Multiply out brackets, or rewrite 3/x² as 3x⁻², before integrating term by term.

misconceptions: Dividing by the old power n instead of n + 1
Forgetting + C
Integrating 3/x² as 3/(x³/3) or as 3 ln(x²)

threads.echo: Anti-differentiation undoes differentiation, as ln undoes eˣ: integrate, then differentiate, and you are back where you started.
The + C means the answer is a whole family of curves, each a vertical translation of the others, all with the same gradient at every x.

skills.name: Use a boundary condition to find the constant of integration
examTypes: Given f′(x) = 3x² − 2 and f(1) = 5, find f(x)
A curve has gradient function dy/dx = 4x − 1 and passes through (2, 3). Find the equation of the curve
Find f(3)

methods.name: Integrate, then substitute the point
methods.summary: Integrate with + C, substitute the known point into f, and solve for C.

methods.name: Start value plus accumulated change
methods.summary: Use f(b) = f(a) + ∫ from a to b of f′(x) dx to go from the known value to the required one without finding C.

methods.name: Choose the right vertical shift
methods.summary: Sketch y = F(x) + C for a few values of C and pick the shift that passes through the given point.

misconceptions: Substituting the point into f′(x) instead of f(x)
Leaving + C in the final answer, or setting C = 0
Substituting the y-value in place of x

threads.echo: Each value of C is a vertical translation of the same curve; the boundary condition picks the one translation that passes through the given point.
f(b) = f(a) + ∫ f′(x) dx is 'starting value plus everything added since', like a running total of a series.

skills.name: Evaluate a definite integral using technology
examTypes: Write down the value of ∫ from 0 to 2 of eˣ sin x dx
Use your GDC to find ∫ from 1 to 3 of f(x) dx
Find the value of the integral, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures

methods.name: Numerical integration template
methods.summary: Enter the integrand and the limits into the GDC's ∫dx (fnInt) template.

methods.name: ∫f(x)dx tool on the graph
methods.summary: Graph y = f(x) and use the graph screen's integral tool between the two x-values, which also shades the region.

methods.name: Integrate by hand to check
methods.summary: If the integrand is a polynomial, integrate exactly and compare to confirm the GDC entry.

misconceptions: Leaving the calculator in degree mode for trig integrands
Entering the limits the wrong way round, giving the negative of the answer
Missing brackets, e.g. entering e^x+1 when e^(x+1) is meant

threads.echo: Like a series total, the integral adds up the pieces f(x) dx across the interval; the GDC just does the adding for you.

skills.name: Write an integral expression for a shaded area under a curve
examTypes: Write down an integral that represents the area of the shaded region R
Write down the limits of integration for the region
Hence find the area of R

methods.name: Read the boundaries from the diagram
methods.summary: The left and right edges of the region (axis crossings or given vertical lines) are the limits; the curve is the integrand.

methods.name: Solve f(x) = 0 for the limits
methods.summary: If the edges are x-intercepts, solve f(x) = 0 to find them exactly.

methods.name: GDC zero finder
methods.summary: Use the GDC's zero/root feature to locate the limits.

misconceptions: Using y-values as the limits
Putting the larger limit at the bottom
Using the derivative of f as the integrand, or leaving out dx

threads.echo: The limits are where the curve meets the x-axis: solutions of f(x) = 0, found by algebra or by reading the graph.

skills.name: Find the area between a curve and the x-axis where f(x) > 0
examTypes: Find the area enclosed by the curve, the x-axis and the lines x = 1 and x = 3
Find the area of the region bounded by the curve and the x-axis
The region R is bounded by the curve, the x-axis and the y-axis. Find the area of R

methods.name: Anti-differentiate and evaluate
methods.summary: Find F and compute F(b) − F(a) by hand.

methods.name: GDC definite integral
methods.summary: After finding the limits, evaluate ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx on the GDC.

methods.name: Use triangles and trapezia
methods.summary: If the boundary is straight or piecewise linear, split the region into simple shapes.

misconceptions: Computing F(a) − F(b)
Using 0 as the lower limit when the region starts at an x-intercept
Rounding the limits too early on P2 and losing accuracy

threads.echo: The area is built from very thin strips of height f(x) and width dx added together, the same 'add many small pieces' idea as a series sum.

skills.name: Interpret the definite integral of a rate as a total change in context
examTypes: Water flows into a tank at r(t) litres per minute. Find the volume that flows in during the first 10 minutes
Interpret ∫ from 0 to 5 of r(t) dt in context
Find the time at which the total amount reaches 100 litres

methods.name: Integrate the rate on the GDC
methods.summary: Evaluate ∫ r(t) dt over the time interval numerically.

methods.name: Anti-differentiate the rate
methods.summary: Find the amount function from the rate, then subtract its values at the two times.

methods.name: Area under a rate graph
methods.summary: For a piecewise-linear rate graph, add the areas of triangles and trapezia under it.

misconceptions: Evaluating the rate at the end time instead of integrating
Adding the starting amount when only the change is asked for, or forgetting it when the total is asked for
Giving the answer in units per minute instead of units

threads.echo: Total change = the sum of (rate × tiny time) pieces, the same idea as distance from velocity: integration turns a rate back into an amount.
The rate is the derivative of the amount, so integrating the rate undoes that differentiation and recovers the change in amount.

subtopics.title: Further differentiation: standard functions, chain, product and quotient rules
subtopics.guide: Derivatives of xⁿ (n ∈ ℚ), sin x, cos x, eˣ and ln x, and of sums and multiples of these. Differentiation of composite functions (chain rule), products (product rule) and quotients (quotient rule).

skills.name: Differentiate √x, x^(p/q), sin x, cos x, eˣ and ln x, with sums and multiples
examTypes: Differentiate f(x) = 4√x − 3 cos x
Find dy/dx for y = 2eˣ + 5 ln x
Find f′(x) where f(x) = 6/∛x

methods.name: Standard results term by term
methods.summary: Apply the formula booklet results (d/dx sin x = cos x, d/dx cos x = −sin x, d/dx ln x = 1/x, d/dx eˣ = eˣ) to each term.

methods.name: Rewrite roots as rational powers
methods.summary: Write √x = x^(1/2) and 6/∛x = 6x^(−1/3) before using the power rule.

methods.name: Simplify logs first
methods.summary: Use log laws, e.g. ln(x³) = 3 ln x and ln(5x) = ln 5 + ln x, so the derivative is immediate.

misconceptions: d/dx cos x = sin x (missing the minus sign)
d/dx eˣ = x eˣ⁻¹, treating eˣ as a power of x
Getting a fractional power wrong: x^(−1/3) → −⅓x^(2/3) instead of −⅓x^(−4/3)

threads.echo: eˣ is the exponential whose gradient equals its own value: the bigger it gets, the faster it grows, which is why it models continuous growth.
Rewriting √x as x^(1/2) or ln(x³) as 3 ln x uses the exponent and log laws of SL1.7 to pick the form that is easiest to differentiate.

skills.name: Differentiate composite functions using the chain rule
examTypes: Differentiate y = (3x² + 1)⁴
Find f′(x) where f(x) = e^(2x − 1)
Find dy/dx for y = ln(x² + 4)
Differentiate sin(3x)

methods.name: Outer derivative × inner derivative
methods.summary: Differentiate the outer function leaving the inside unchanged, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.

methods.name: Substitute u for the inside
methods.summary: Let u be the inner function, find dy/du and du/dx, then dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx.

methods.name: Expand a small power first
methods.summary: For something like (2x + 1)³, expand (binomial theorem) and differentiate term by term.

methods.name: Split logs before differentiating
methods.summary: For ln of a product, power or quotient, use log laws first, e.g. ln((2x + 1)³) = 3 ln(2x + 1).

misconceptions: Forgetting the inner derivative: d/dx (3x² + 1)⁴ = 4(3x² + 1)³
d/dx ln(3x) = 1/(3x) instead of 1/x
Replacing the inside by its derivative: 4(6x)³

threads.echo: f(ax + b) is f stretched horizontally by factor 1/a, which makes every gradient a times steeper: that factor a is the chain rule's inner derivative.

skills.name: Differentiate products using the product rule
examTypes: Differentiate y = x² ln x
Find f′(x) where f(x) = x eˣ, giving your answer in factorised form
Differentiate y = eˣ sin x

methods.name: Product rule
methods.summary: With y = uv, use dy/dx = u dv/dx + v du/dx, then factorise common terms.

methods.name: Multiply out first
methods.summary: If both factors are polynomials, expand and use the power rule instead.

methods.name: Combine into one power
methods.summary: Products like x²√x are just x^(5/2), so no product rule is needed.

misconceptions: (uv)′ = u′v′
Writing only one of the two terms
Factorising wrongly, e.g. 2x ln x + x = x(2 ln x)

skills.name: Differentiate quotients using the quotient rule
examTypes: Differentiate y = (ln x)/x
Find f′(x) where f(x) = (2x + 1)/(x − 3)
Find the gradient of y = (sin x)/x at x = π

methods.name: Quotient rule
methods.summary: With y = u/v, use (v u′ − u v′)/v², keeping v u′ first.

methods.name: Rewrite as u × v⁻¹
methods.summary: Use the product rule with the chain rule on v⁻¹, then simplify over a common denominator.

methods.name: Split when the denominator is a single term
methods.summary: If the denominator is a power of x, divide each term and use the power rule.

misconceptions: Reversing the numerator to u v′ − v u′, which flips the sign of the answer
Forgetting to square the denominator

skills.name: Show that a derivative simplifies to a given form
examTypes: Show that f′(x) = (1 − ln x)/x²
Show that dy/dx = eˣ(x + 1)
Show that f′(x) can be written in the form a/(x − 3)², stating the value of a

methods.name: Differentiate, then simplify to the target
methods.summary: Apply the right rule(s), then factorise or put over a common denominator until it matches the given form.

methods.name: Pick the rule that lands nearest the target
methods.summary: Choose the route that makes the target easiest to reach, e.g. product rule with a negative power instead of the quotient rule.

methods.name: Meet in the middle
methods.summary: Simplify your derivative and rearrange the given answer, showing both sides reach the same expression in an LHS = RHS layout.

misconceptions: Working backwards from the given answer without actually differentiating
Cancelling single terms across a sum in the numerator and denominator
Sign slips when expanding −u v′ in the quotient rule

threads.echo: Like a trig identity or an LHS = RHS proof, a 'show that' derivative asks you to turn one form into an equivalent one that shows the structure.

skills.name: Use the chain, product or quotient rule with given values of functions and derivatives
examTypes: The table gives values of f, g, f′ and g′. Find h′(2) where h(x) = f(x)g(x)
Given h(x) = f(g(x)), find h′(1)
Find the gradient of the curve y = f(x)/g(x) at x = 3

methods.name: Write the general rule, then substitute
methods.summary: Write h′ in general (e.g. f′g + fg′, or f′(g(x)) × g′(x)), then substitute values from the table.

methods.name: Read values and gradients from graphs
methods.summary: When f and g are drawn as straight-line pieces, read function values and gradients from the graphs, then substitute.

misconceptions: For a composite, using f′(1) instead of f′(g(1))
For a product, multiplying f′(a) × g′(a)
Reading g′(1) from the table when g(1) is needed

subtopics.title: The second derivative
subtopics.guide: The second derivative f″(x), or d²y/dx², and concavity. The relationships between the graphs of f, f′ and f″.

skills.name: Find and evaluate the second derivative
examTypes: Find f″(x)
Find the value of d²y/dx² when x = 2
Show that f″(x) = 6x − 4

methods.name: Differentiate f′(x) again
methods.summary: Differentiate the first derivative with the same rules (often the product or chain rule a second time).

methods.name: Gradient of the f′ graph on the GDC
methods.summary: On P2, graph y = f′(x) (or nDeriv of f) and find its gradient at the point, giving f″(a).

misconceptions: Squaring f′(x) instead of differentiating it
Differentiating f(x) again instead of f′(x)
Reading d²y/dx² as (dy/dx)²

threads.echo: f″ is the rate of change of the gradient, just as acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.

skills.name: Determine where a graph is concave up or concave down
examTypes: Find the values of x for which the graph of f is concave down
Determine whether the curve is concave up or concave down at x = 1
Justify that the graph of f is concave up for x > 2

methods.name: Solve f″(x) > 0 or f″(x) < 0
methods.summary: Concave up where f″(x) > 0, concave down where f″(x) < 0.

methods.name: Is f′ increasing?
methods.summary: Concave up exactly where f′ is increasing, which you can read from the graph of f′.

methods.name: Curve above or below its tangents
methods.summary: Concave up means the curve lies above its tangents (it holds water); concave down means it lies below them.

methods.name: Look at the GDC graph
methods.summary: Plot f and look at the bending, confirming with the sign of f″ at test points.

misconceptions: Confusing concave up (f″ > 0) with increasing (f′ > 0)
Thinking concave down means decreasing
Using f(x) > 0 instead of f″(x) > 0

threads.echo: Concave up means the gradient itself is increasing, so the rate of change is changing, like a car that keeps speeding up.

skills.name: Match or sketch the graphs of f, f′ and f″
examTypes: The graph of f is shown. Sketch the graph of f′
Match each graph of f with the graph of its derivative
Which of the graphs could be y = f″(x)?

methods.name: Turning points become zeros
methods.summary: Turning points of f are x-intercepts of f′; where f rises, f′ is above the axis; where f falls, f′ is below.

methods.name: Degree drops by one
methods.summary: The derivative of a cubic is a parabola and the derivative of a parabola is a straight line.

methods.name: Sign rows for f′ and f″
methods.summary: Build sign rows for f′ and f″ from the shape of f, then draw graphs that fit the signs.

methods.name: Graph the numerical derivative
methods.summary: When f is given as a formula, graph nDeriv(f(x)) on the GDC to see f′.

misconceptions: Drawing f′ as a shifted copy of f
Putting the zeros of f′ at the x-intercepts of f instead of at its turning points
Thinking f′ must be positive wherever f is above the x-axis

threads.echo: Every maximum or minimum of f shows up as a root on the graph of f′, so the derivative graph is a map of where the extremes are.

skills.name: Use the graph of f′ (or f″) to deduce features of f
examTypes: The graph of f′ is shown. Find the x-coordinate of the local maximum of f. Justify your answer
Find the x-coordinate of the point of inflexion of f. Justify your answer
Write down the interval on which the graph of f is concave up

methods.name: Look for sign changes of f′
methods.summary: A maximum of f is where f′ crosses from positive to negative; a minimum is where it crosses from negative to positive.

methods.name: Turning points of f′ give inflexions
methods.summary: Points of inflexion of f occur at the maxima and minima of the f′ graph, where f″ changes sign.

methods.name: Sign diagram from the f′ graph
methods.summary: Convert the f′ graph into sign rows for f′ and f″, then read the behaviour of f.

methods.name: Signed area under f′
methods.summary: Compare values of f using f(b) − f(a) = ∫ from a to b of f′(x) dx, the signed area under the f′ graph.

misconceptions: Taking the maximum point of the f′ graph as the maximum of f
Claiming a maximum where f′ touches zero without changing sign
Justifying with 'f′ = 0' alone, without the sign change

threads.echo: The signed area under the f′ graph is the change in f, so the f′ graph tells you how f builds up between two points.

skills.name: Interpret the second derivative in context
examTypes: Explain what P″(t) < 0 means for the population
The temperature is rising but at a decreasing rate. Write this using derivatives
Interpret the sign of d²h/dt² at t = 3

methods.name: Read the two layers in words
methods.summary: f′ says whether the quantity is going up or down; f″ says whether that rate is itself going up or down; combine them in a sentence.

methods.name: Sketch a small piece of curve
methods.summary: Draw a short curve with the right slope (sign of f′) and the right bend (sign of f″) and describe it.

misconceptions: Reading f″ < 0 as 'the quantity is decreasing'
Treating 'increasing at a decreasing rate' as 'decreasing'

threads.echo: A second derivative is a rate of a rate, as in kinematics where acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.

subtopics.title: Stationary points, optimisation and points of inflexion
subtopics.guide: Local maximum and minimum points, found from f′(x) = 0 and tested with the first or second derivative. Optimisation in context, and points of inflexion with zero and non-zero gradient.

skills.name: Find the coordinates of stationary points
examTypes: Find the x-coordinates of the stationary points of f
Find the coordinates of the local minimum point
Show that f has a stationary point at x = 2

methods.name: Solve f′(x) = 0
methods.summary: Differentiate, set f′(x) = 0, solve (factorise or quadratic formula), then substitute each x into f for y.

methods.name: GDC maximum/minimum tool
methods.summary: Graph f and use the maximum and minimum features to read the turning points.

methods.name: Zeros of the f′ graph
methods.summary: Graph f′ and find where it crosses the x-axis, then evaluate f at those x-values.

methods.name: Vertex of a quadratic
methods.summary: For a quadratic the only stationary point is the vertex: x = −b/(2a), or read (h, k) from a(x − h)² + k.

misconceptions: Solving f(x) = 0 instead of f′(x) = 0
Losing the negative root when solving x² = 4
Substituting the x-value into f′ instead of f to get the y-coordinate

threads.echo: The vertex of a parabola, found from −b/(2a) in SL2.6, is exactly where f′(x) = 0: calculus finds the same point and works for any curve.
Solving f′(x) = 0 by factorising and reading turning points off the GDC give the same answer, so use one to check the other.

skills.name: Determine the nature of stationary points
examTypes: Use the second derivative to show that this point is a local maximum
Determine the nature of each stationary point. Justify your answer
Explain why f has a local minimum at x = 3

methods.name: Second derivative test
methods.summary: Evaluate f″ at the point: f″ > 0 gives a local minimum, f″ < 0 a local maximum, and f″ = 0 is inconclusive.

methods.name: First derivative sign table
methods.summary: Check the sign of f′ just either side: + then − is a maximum, − then + is a minimum, no change is a point of inflexion.

methods.name: Use the shape of the cubic
methods.summary: For a cubic with two stationary points and a positive x³ coefficient, the left one is the maximum and the right one the minimum.

methods.name: Look at the GDC graph
methods.summary: Graph f and look at the shape near the point; good supporting evidence, but not a full justification on its own.

misconceptions: f″ > 0 means a maximum (sign reversed)
f″(a) = 0 proves a point of inflexion (x⁴ has a minimum at 0 with f″(0) = 0)
Checking the sign of f rather than f′ either side of the point

threads.echo: For a parabola the sign of a decided max or min; for any curve the sign of f″ does the same job, and for a quadratic f″ is exactly 2a.

skills.name: Find points of inflexion, with zero or non-zero gradient
examTypes: Find the coordinates of the point of inflexion
Show that the curve has a point of inflexion at x = 1
Explain why (0, 0) is a point of inflexion with zero gradient

methods.name: f″ = 0 with a sign change
methods.summary: Solve f″(x) = 0, then check that f″ changes sign either side (the concavity changes).

methods.name: Turning points of the f′ graph
methods.summary: Graph f′ on the GDC; the points of inflexion of f are at its maximum and minimum points.

methods.name: Cubic symmetry point
methods.summary: A cubic's inflexion is at x = −b/(3a), exactly midway between its two stationary points.

methods.name: Check the gradient there
methods.summary: Evaluate f′ at the inflexion: f′ = 0 gives a stationary (horizontal) inflexion, f′ ≠ 0 a non-stationary one.

misconceptions: Treating f″(a) = 0 as enough, without checking for a sign change
Assuming every point with f′ = 0 and f″ = 0 is a point of inflexion
Thinking a point of inflexion must have zero gradient

threads.echo: Every cubic has half-turn symmetry about its point of inflexion, just as every parabola has mirror symmetry about its vertex.

skills.name: Find a maximum or minimum of a given model in context
examTypes: The profit is P(x) = −2x³ + 27x² − 84x. Find the value of x that maximises the profit
Find the maximum height reached by the ball
Justify that this value of x gives a maximum

methods.name: Derivative = 0, then justify
methods.summary: Solve the derivative = 0, justify the maximum or minimum (f″ or sign change), then answer the question asked (the x-value or the optimum value).

methods.name: GDC maximum/minimum tool
methods.summary: Graph the model on a sensible window and use the maximum or minimum feature.

methods.name: Vertex of a quadratic model
methods.summary: If the model is quadratic, the optimum is at x = −b/(2a) or read from completed-square form.

misconceptions: Giving the x-value when the maximum value is asked for (or the other way round)
Ignoring the domain, e.g. accepting a negative or non-integer number of items
Assuming the stationary point is a maximum without justifying it

threads.echo: Maximum profit and maximum height are vertex questions in disguise; f′ = 0 finds the top whether or not the model is a parabola.

skills.name: Set up and solve an optimisation problem from a description
examTypes: A closed cylinder has volume 250 cm³. Show that its surface area is A = 2πr² + 500/r
An open box is made from a 20 cm by 30 cm sheet by cutting squares of side x from each corner. Find the maximum volume
Find the dimensions that minimise the cost

methods.name: Eliminate a variable with the constraint
methods.summary: Use the fixed quantity (volume, perimeter, area) to write one variable in terms of the other, giving a function of a single variable.

methods.name: Differentiate and justify
methods.summary: Differentiate the one-variable function, solve = 0, and justify the maximum or minimum.

methods.name: Graph on the feasible domain
methods.summary: Graph the single-variable function over the values that make physical sense and read the optimum with the max/min tool.

methods.name: Midpoint of the roots for a quadratic model
methods.summary: If the function is quadratic, e.g. A = x(50 − x), the optimum is midway between its roots (x = 25).

misconceptions: Differentiating before eliminating the second variable
Ignoring the feasible domain, e.g. allowing x > 10 on a 20 cm sheet
Giving the constraint value or the optimal x when the optimal value is asked for

threads.echo: Fencing a field for the largest area was a parabola-vertex problem; calculus extends the same 'find the top' idea to boxes, cans and costs.
For a quadratic model like x(50 − x), the axis of symmetry halfway between the roots gives the optimum without differentiating.

skills.name: Find the greatest and least values of f on a closed interval (and its range)
examTypes: Find the maximum value of f for 0 ≤ x ≤ 4
Find the range of f on the given domain
Explain why the least value of f occurs at an endpoint

methods.name: Compare stationary values and endpoints
methods.summary: Evaluate f at every stationary point inside the interval and at both endpoints, then pick the largest and smallest.

methods.name: Set the GDC window to the interval
methods.summary: Graph f only over the interval and read the highest and lowest points, including the ends.

methods.name: No turning points means endpoints
methods.summary: If f′ has no zeros in the interval, f is monotonic there and its extremes are at the endpoints.

misconceptions: Ignoring the endpoints and quoting only the local maximum and minimum
Including stationary points that lie outside the interval
Giving x-values instead of function values for the range

threads.echo: On a restricted domain the biggest value can sit at an end rather than at a turning point, like a parabola restricted to one side of its vertex.

skills.name: Find unknown constants given a stationary point or inflexion
examTypes: f(x) = ax³ + bx² + 1 has a stationary point at (1, 3). Find a and b
Given that f has a local minimum at x = 2, find k
The graph of f has a point of inflexion at x = −1. Find p

methods.name: Form equations from the conditions
methods.summary: Use f′(a) = 0 (plus f(a) = b for the coordinates, or f″(a) = 0 for an inflexion) and solve simultaneously.

methods.name: Solve the system on the GDC
methods.summary: Form the equations by hand and solve the linear system with the GDC.

methods.name: Write f′ in factor form
methods.summary: If both stationary x-values are known, write f′(x) = k(x − p)(x − q) and compare coefficients.

misconceptions: Using f(a) = 0 instead of f′(a) = 0
Using only one condition when two unknowns need two equations
Substituting the y-coordinate into f′

subtopics.title: Kinematics
subtopics.guide: Motion in a straight line: displacement s, velocity v = ds/dt and acceleration a = dv/dt = d²s/dt². Displacement from velocity by integration, and total distance travelled as the integral of speed |v|.

skills.name: Find velocity and acceleration from displacement
examTypes: Find the velocity of the particle when t = 2
Find an expression for the acceleration of the particle
Find the acceleration at the time when the velocity is zero

methods.name: Differentiate with respect to t
methods.summary: v = ds/dt and a = dv/dt = d²s/dt²; differentiate, then substitute the time.

methods.name: GDC dy/dx at the time
methods.summary: Graph s (or v) against t and use dy/dx at the required time.

methods.name: Gradient of a motion graph
methods.summary: Velocity is the gradient of the s–t graph; acceleration is the gradient of the v–t graph.

misconceptions: Substituting t into s to get the velocity
Computing average velocity s/t instead of ds/dt
Assuming acceleration is constant when it depends on t

threads.echo: Velocity is the rate of change of displacement and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: the derivative with time as the input.

skills.name: Find when a particle is at rest, changes direction, or is speeding up
examTypes: Find the times when the particle is at rest
Find the value of t at which the particle changes direction
Determine whether the particle is speeding up or slowing down at t = 3. Justify your answer

methods.name: Solve v(t) = 0
methods.summary: Solve v = 0 for the times at rest, keeping only times in the given domain.

methods.name: Sign of v either side
methods.summary: Check v before and after each root: a sign change means a change of direction.

methods.name: Zeros of the v–t graph
methods.summary: Graph v against t on the GDC and find where it crosses the t-axis.

methods.name: Compare signs of v and a
methods.summary: Speeding up when v and a have the same sign, slowing down when they have opposite signs.

misconceptions: At rest means a = 0
Speeding up means a > 0, even when v < 0
Counting every zero of v as a change of direction, even where v touches zero without changing sign

threads.echo: In one dimension velocity behaves like a vector: its sign gives the direction, and it must pass through zero for the particle to turn round.

skills.name: Find displacement (or velocity) by integrating with initial conditions
examTypes: Given v = 3t² − 4 and s = 2 when t = 0, find an expression for s
Find the displacement of the particle between t = 1 and t = 4
Given a = 6t and v = 5 when t = 1, find v in terms of t

methods.name: Integrate and use the initial condition
methods.summary: Integrate v (or a) with + C, then use the given starting value to find C.

methods.name: Start position plus definite integral
methods.summary: Use s(T) = s(0) + ∫ from 0 to T of v dt to get the position at a given time directly.

methods.name: GDC definite integral of v
methods.summary: Evaluate ∫ v dt numerically for the change in displacement over the interval.

misconceptions: Assuming the constant is 0 (or that s = 0 at t = 0) without being told
Differentiating v instead of integrating to get s
Confusing the displacement over an interval with the position at the end of it

threads.echo: Differentiation takes s to v; integration undoes it and takes v back to s.
Without a starting position, s is only known up to + C, a vertical shift of its graph; the initial condition fixes which shift.

skills.name: Find the total distance travelled
examTypes: Find the total distance travelled by the particle in the first 5 seconds
Write down an expression for the distance travelled between t = 0 and t = 4
Explain why the distance travelled is greater than the displacement

methods.name: Integrate |v| on the GDC
methods.summary: Evaluate ∫ from t₁ to t₂ of |v(t)| dt in one step.

methods.name: Split where v = 0
methods.summary: Find the times the particle is at rest, integrate v over each piece separately, and add the absolute values.

methods.name: Add areas on the v–t graph
methods.summary: For a piecewise-linear v–t graph, add the areas of the triangles and trapezia, all counted as positive.

methods.name: Track the positions
methods.summary: Find s at the start, at each turning time and at the end, and add the distances between consecutive positions.

misconceptions: Using ∫ v dt (the displacement) as the distance
Not splitting the integral where the particle changes direction
Subtracting the area below the t-axis instead of adding it

threads.echo: Distance is built up from tiny speed × time pieces, the same 'add up many small pieces' idea as a series sum or an area under a curve.
Displacements in opposite directions cancel like opposite vectors, but distance adds the size of every leg of the journey.

skills.name: Find the maximum or minimum velocity, or the maximum speed
examTypes: Find the maximum velocity of the particle for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4
Find the maximum speed of the particle
Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and the velocity at that time

methods.name: Set a = 0
methods.summary: Solve a = dv/dt = 0 for the turning points of v, then compare with the values at the ends of the time interval.

methods.name: GDC max/min of v or |v|
methods.summary: Graph v over the time interval and use the max/min tool; for speed, graph |v|.

methods.name: Vertex of a quadratic velocity
methods.summary: If v is quadratic in t, its extreme value is at t = −b/(2a).

misconceptions: Treating maximum speed as maximum velocity (a large negative velocity is a high speed)
Ignoring the endpoints of the time interval
Setting v = 0 to find the maximum velocity

threads.echo: Maximum velocity is a stationary point of v, found where its derivative (the acceleration) is zero, like any other maximum.

skills.name: Interpret displacement–time and velocity–time graphs
examTypes: The diagram shows the v–t graph. Find the acceleration at t = 2
Use the graph to find the displacement after 6 seconds
Write down the time intervals when the particle is moving in the negative direction

methods.name: Read gradients
methods.summary: The gradient of an s–t graph is velocity; the gradient of a v–t graph is acceleration.

methods.name: Signed area under the v–t graph
methods.summary: Area above the t-axis is positive displacement and area below is negative; use triangles and trapezia.

methods.name: Above or below the axis
methods.summary: Where the v–t graph is above the axis the particle moves in the positive direction; below, in the negative direction.

misconceptions: Reading the height of a v–t graph as the displacement
Thinking a downward-sloping v–t graph means moving backwards
Counting area below the axis as positive displacement

threads.echo: The area under a v–t graph is the displacement built up over time, the same link between area and adding up that the definite integral formalises.

subtopics.title: Further indefinite integration
subtopics.guide: Indefinite integrals of xⁿ (n ∈ ℚ), sin x, cos x, 1/x and eˣ, and of their composites with ax + b. Integration by inspection (reverse chain rule) or substitution for integrals of the form ∫ k g′(x) f(g(x)) dx.

skills.name: Integrate xⁿ (n ∈ ℚ), sin x, cos x, 1/x and eˣ
examTypes: Find ∫ (3√x + 2/x) dx
Find ∫ (eˣ − 4 sin x) dx
Find ∫ 1/√x dx

methods.name: Standard results term by term
methods.summary: Use the formula booklet results: ∫ cos x dx = sin x + C, ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + C, ∫ 1/x dx = ln x + C, ∫ eˣ dx = eˣ + C.

methods.name: Rewrite roots as powers
methods.summary: Write √x = x^(1/2) and 1/√x = x^(−1/2) before using the reverse power rule.

methods.name: Differentiate to check
methods.summary: Differentiate your answer to make sure you get back the integrand; this catches sign errors with sin and cos.

misconceptions: ∫ sin x dx = cos x + C (wrong sign)
Using the power rule on 1/x: ∫ x⁻¹ dx = x⁰/0
Multiplying by the new power instead of dividing: ∫ x^(1/2) dx = (3/2)x^(3/2)

threads.echo: Every result here is a derivative read backwards: d/dx sin x = cos x, so ∫ cos x dx = sin x + C.

skills.name: Integrate composites with ax + b
examTypes: Find ∫ e^(3x + 1) dx
Find ∫ 1/(2x − 5) dx
Find ∫ cos(4x) dx
Find ∫ (3x + 2)⁵ dx

methods.name: Integrate, then divide by a
methods.summary: Integrate as if the inside were just x, then divide by a, the derivative of ax + b.

methods.name: Substitute u = ax + b
methods.summary: Let u = ax + b so dx = du/a, integrate in u, then substitute back.

methods.name: Differentiate to check
methods.summary: Differentiate the candidate; the chain rule should produce exactly the integrand.

methods.name: Expand a low power
methods.summary: For something like (2x + 1)², expand and integrate term by term; the answer differs only in the constant.

misconceptions: Multiplying by a as in differentiation: ∫ cos(4x) dx = 4 sin(4x) + C
Missing the factor ½: ∫ 1/(2x − 5) dx = ln|2x − 5| + C
Dividing by the exponent: ∫ e^(3x + 1) dx = e^(3x + 1)/(3x + 1) + C

threads.echo: Replacing x by ax squeezes the graph horizontally by factor 1/a, so areas shrink by a factor of a: that is why you divide by a.
This is the chain rule run backwards: differentiating multiplies by a, so integrating divides by a.

skills.name: Integrate ∫ k g′(x) f(g(x)) dx by inspection or substitution
examTypes: Find ∫ x e^(x²) dx
Find ∫ 6x/(x² + 1) dx
Use the substitution u = x² + 3 to find ∫ x(x² + 3)⁴ dx
Find ∫ sin x cos⁴ x dx

methods.name: Inspection (reverse chain rule)
methods.summary: Spot an inner function and a multiple of its derivative, guess the answer, differentiate it, and adjust the constant.

methods.name: Substitution u = g(x)
methods.summary: Let u = g(x), replace g′(x) dx with du, integrate in u, then substitute back.

methods.name: Recognise g′(x)/g(x)
methods.summary: Use ∫ g′(x)/g(x) dx = ln|g(x)| + C directly, adjusting for any constant multiple.

misconceptions: Integrating the outer function but leaving the extra x in place
Forgetting to divide by 2: ∫ 6x/(x² + 1) dx = 6 ln(x² + 1) + C
Forgetting to substitute back from u to x

threads.echo: Inspection is the chain rule in reverse: you ask which function, when differentiated, produced this one.

skills.name: Rewrite an integrand in a standard form before integrating
examTypes: Find ∫ (x² + 3)/x dx
Find ∫ (2 + √x)² dx
Find ∫ sin x cos x dx
Find ∫ (eˣ + 1)² dx

methods.name: Split the fraction
methods.summary: Divide each term of the numerator by the denominator: (x² + 3)/x = x + 3/x.

methods.name: Expand the square
methods.summary: Multiply out, e.g. (eˣ + 1)² = e^(2x) + 2eˣ + 1, and integrate each term.

methods.name: Use a trig identity
methods.summary: Use sin x cos x = ½ sin 2x to reach a standard integral.

methods.name: Spot a reverse chain rule instead
methods.summary: ∫ sin x cos x dx = ½ sin² x + C by inspection; different-looking correct answers differ only by a constant.

misconceptions: Integrating numerator and denominator separately: ∫ (x² + 3)/x dx = (x³/3 + 3x)/(x²/2)
Missing the middle term: (eˣ + 1)² = e^(2x) + 1
Thinking two answers that differ by a constant cannot both be correct

threads.echo: The same integrand written another way (split, expanded, or with a double angle identity) turns an awkward integral into standard ones.
½ sin² x and −¼ cos 2x are both correct antiderivatives because their graphs are vertical translations of each other.

skills.name: Find f from f′ or f″ and given conditions
examTypes: Given f′(x) = cos 2x and f(π/4) = 3, find f(x)
The gradient of a curve is 2/(x + 1) and the curve passes through (0, 4). Find its equation
Given f″(x) = 6x + eˣ, f′(0) = 2 and f(0) = 1, find f(x)

methods.name: Integrate and fit the constant(s)
methods.summary: Integrate, then substitute the known point to find C; from f″, integrate twice and use one condition at each stage.

methods.name: Start value plus GDC integral
methods.summary: On P2, if only one value is needed, compute f(b) = f(a) + ∫ from a to b of f′(x) dx on the GDC.

misconceptions: Using a single constant for both integrations from f″
Mis-evaluating exact values when finding C, e.g. taking sin(π/2) = 0
Substituting the point into f′ instead of f

threads.echo: Each + C is a vertical translation; starting from f″ there are two constants, so you need two conditions to pin down a single curve.

skills.name: Use a given derivative to find an integral ('hence')
examTypes: Find d/dx (x ln x). Hence find ∫ ln x dx
Differentiate x eˣ and hence find ∫ x eˣ dx
Given that d/dx (e^(x²)) = 2x e^(x²), find ∫ from 0 to 1 of x e^(x²) dx

methods.name: Integrate the derivative result and rearrange
methods.summary: From d/dx (x ln x) = ln x + 1, integrate both sides to get x ln x = ∫ ln x dx + x, so ∫ ln x dx = x ln x − x + C.

methods.name: Differentiate your answer
methods.summary: Differentiate the proposed antiderivative to confirm it gives the integrand.

misconceptions: Taking the derivative itself as the integral: ∫ ln x dx = ln x + 1
Forgetting to move across the integral of the extra term (the + 1 becomes − x)
Dropping + C

threads.echo: Every derivative fact is also an integral fact read backwards, the same 'undo' relationship as f and f⁻¹.

subtopics.title: Definite integrals and areas
subtopics.guide: Definite integrals evaluated analytically, including their properties. Areas between a curve and the x-axis where f(x) may be negative (without technology), and areas between two curves.

skills.name: Evaluate a definite integral exactly
examTypes: Find the exact value of ∫ from 0 to π/2 of cos x dx
Show that ∫ from 1 to 3 of 2/(2x − 1) dx = ln 5
Evaluate ∫ from 1 to 4 of √x dx

methods.name: F(upper) − F(lower)
methods.summary: Find an antiderivative F, then compute F(b) − F(a), using brackets for each value.

methods.name: Odd and even functions
methods.summary: An odd integrand over −a to a gives 0; an even one gives twice the integral from 0 to a.

methods.name: Signed area of simple shapes
methods.summary: For a linear integrand, the integral is the signed area of a triangle or trapezium.

methods.name: GDC check
methods.summary: On P2, or as a check, evaluate numerically and compare with your exact answer.

misconceptions: Computing F(lower) − F(upper)
Assuming the lower limit contributes 0, e.g. treating e⁰ or cos 0 as 0
Writing + C in the answer to a definite integral

threads.echo: An odd function over −a to a has equal positive and negative areas that cancel exactly, so symmetry can give the answer with no integration.

skills.name: Use properties of definite integrals
examTypes: Given ∫ from 1 to 4 of f(x) dx = 7, find ∫ from 1 to 4 of (3f(x) + 2) dx
Write down ∫ from 4 to 1 of f(x) dx
Given ∫ from 0 to 3 of f(x) dx = 5 and ∫ from 0 to 6 of f(x) dx = 12, find ∫ from 3 to 6 of f(x) dx

methods.name: Apply the rules
methods.summary: Split ∫ (3f + 2) into 3∫ f + ∫ 2, use ∫ from a to b of k dx = k(b − a), add adjacent intervals, and change sign when swapping limits.

methods.name: Picture the areas
methods.summary: Multiplying f by 3 triples the area, adding 2 adds a rectangle of height 2 and width b − a, and adjacent intervals add.

misconceptions: ∫ from 1 to 4 of (f(x) + 2) dx = 7 + 2 instead of 7 + 2 × 3
Not changing the sign when the limits are reversed
Assuming ∫ (f(x))² dx = (∫ f(x) dx)²

threads.echo: 3f(x) is a vertical stretch, which triples every height and so the area; f(x) + 2 is a vertical translation, which adds a rectangle of height 2.

skills.name: Find areas where the curve is partly below the x-axis
examTypes: Find the total area enclosed by the curve and the x-axis between x = 0 and x = 3
Explain why ∫ from 0 to 2π of sin x dx does not give the area between the curve and the x-axis
Find the area of the shaded region below the x-axis
